topics: Hydrogen bonds and cohesion/adhesion
Water as universal solvent — polarity and dissolving
pH scale and buffers in biological systems
lessons.examTip: Students know water is polar but can't explain WHY hydrogen bonds form or how a pH drop affects enzyme function mechanistically

topics: Carbon's four bonds and functional groups
Structural vs. molecular formulas
How functional groups determine molecule behavior
lessons.examTip: Confusing structural isomers with different compounds — same formula, different properties, and AP asks about the property difference

topics: Monosaccharides, disaccharides, polysaccharides via dehydration synthesis
Glycosidic linkages (α vs β) and structural consequences
Starch vs. cellulose: same monomer, different linkage, different function
lessons.examTip: Students say 'cellulose for structure, starch for energy' without explaining that β-1,4-linkages create straight chains — AP free response wants the mechanism

topics: Saturated vs. unsaturated fatty acids and membrane fluidity
Phospholipid bilayer formation via hydrophobic exclusion
Steroids as signaling molecules — cholesterol's membrane role
lessons.examTip: Confusing that cholesterol both stabilizes and fluidizes membranes depending on temperature — AP tests this context-dependence directly

topics: Four levels of protein structure and stabilizing forces at each level
Denaturation — which bonds break and why
Enzymes as proteins: active site, substrate specificity
lessons.examTip: Saying denaturation 'breaks all bonds' — primary structure (peptide bonds) survives denaturation; only secondary/tertiary/quaternary collapse

lessons.lessonTitle: Nucleic Acids — Storing and Transmitting Information
topics: Nucleotide structure: sugar, phosphate, nitrogenous base
DNA double helix: antiparallel, complementary base pairing
RNA types and their roles vs. DNA
lessons.examTip: Confusing the directionality rules — DNA replication always 5'→3' synthesis; AP gives you a template strand and expects you to know the new strand's polarity

lessons.lessonTitle: Enzymes: Lowering the Activation Energy Barrier
topics: Enzyme kinetics: substrate concentration, Vmax, Km
Competitive vs. noncompetitive inhibition — effect on Km and Vmax
Allosteric regulation and feedback inhibition
lessons.examTip: Mixing up competitive (raises apparent Km, same Vmax) vs. noncompetitive (lowers Vmax, same Km) — especially on graphs where you must read the shift correctly

topics: Fluid mosaic model — protein types and functions
Osmosis, tonicity, and water potential in cells
Active vs. passive transport — energy requirements and direction
lessons.examTip: Confusing osmosis direction — water moves toward higher solute concentration (lower water potential), not 'toward where there's more water'

lessons.lessonTitle: Prokaryotes vs. Eukaryotes — What the Difference Actually Means
topics: Membrane-bound organelles as the defining eukaryote feature
Endosymbiotic theory — evidence for mitochondria/chloroplast origins
Surface area-to-volume ratio and cell size constraints
lessons.examTip: Stating endosymbiotic theory without citing the evidence (double membranes, own DNA, 70S ribosomes) — AP free response explicitly asks for supporting evidence

topics: Endomembrane system: ER → Golgi → vesicle secretion pathway
Mitochondria structure linked to function (cristae = more surface area)
Chloroplast structure: thylakoid vs. stroma and their roles
lessons.examTip: Generic answers like 'mitochondria makes energy' — AP wants 'inner membrane folds increase surface area for ATP synthase concentration'

lessons.lessonTitle: The Cytoskeleton — More Than a Scaffold
topics: Microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments: structure and function
Motor proteins: kinesin and dynein moving cargo along microtubules
Cell division: spindle fibers and cytokinesis roles
lessons.examTip: Treating cytoskeleton as static — AP tests that it is dynamic, assembling/disassembling for cell movement and division

lessons.lessonTitle: Cell Signaling — Receptors and Second Messengers
topics: Signal transduction cascade: ligand → receptor → relay → response
G-protein coupled receptors and cAMP as second messenger
Signal amplification through kinase cascades
lessons.examTip: Confusing the signal (ligand) with the receptor — the lipid-soluble signal crosses the membrane and binds intracellular receptor; protein signals cannot cross and need surface receptors

lessons.lessonTitle: Membrane Transport — Moving Molecules In and Out
topics: Facilitated diffusion via channel and carrier proteins
Na⁺/K⁺ pump as the canonical active transport example
Endocytosis and exocytosis — bulk transport mechanics
lessons.examTip: Not distinguishing channel proteins (ion channels, gated) from carrier proteins (conformational change) — AP experiments often hinge on this distinction

lessons.lessonTitle: Water Potential and Osmosis in Plant vs. Animal Cells
topics: Water potential equation: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp
Turgor pressure in plant cells vs. lysis/crenation in animal cells
Plasmolysis vs. flaccid vs. turgid states
lessons.examTip: Applying animal cell logic to plant cells — plant cells don't burst in hypotonic solution because the cell wall provides pressure potential that stops net water entry

lessons.lessonTitle: Cell Communication: Direct Contact, Local, and Long-Distance
topics: Gap junctions and plasmodesmata for direct cell-to-cell signaling
Paracrine vs. endocrine signaling: distance and speed tradeoffs
Apoptosis as a signal-triggered programmed response
lessons.examTip: Thinking all signaling requires the bloodstream — paracrine signals act locally without entering circulation; AP tests which pathway applies in a scenario

topics: Negative feedback: the mechanism that stabilizes set points
Positive feedback: amplification toward a completion point
Receptor → control center → effector as the universal homeostasis circuit
lessons.examTip: Calling positive feedback 'bad' — AP scenarios include childbirth and blood clotting as normal, functional positive feedback loops

lessons.lessonTitle: Energy, Entropy, and Why Reactions Happen
topics: Free energy (ΔG): spontaneous vs. nonspontaneous reactions
Exergonic coupling to endergonic reactions via ATP
Entropy in biological systems — order maintained at energy cost
lessons.examTip: Thinking living cells violate thermodynamics by creating order — they don't; they export entropy by consuming energy; AP FRQ often asks you to explain this

lessons.lessonTitle: ATP: The Currency of Cellular Work
topics: ATP hydrolysis: where energy comes from (phosphate bond release)
ATP synthase mechanism — chemiosmosis not substrate-level phosphorylation
ATP regeneration pathways in different conditions
lessons.examTip: Saying ATP 'stores energy in bonds' — energy is released from electrostatic repulsion relief when the bond breaks, not from breaking a high-energy bond

topics: 10 steps produce 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP, 2 NADH from 1 glucose
Investment phase (uses 2 ATP) vs. payoff phase (produces 4 ATP)
Glycolysis occurs in cytoplasm — no oxygen or mitochondria required
lessons.examTip: Forgetting glycolysis doesn't require mitochondria — on AP experiments with mitochondria-inhibiting drugs, glycolysis still runs

lessons.lessonTitle: Pyruvate Oxidation and the Citric Acid Cycle
topics: Pyruvate → Acetyl-CoA: CO₂ released, NADH made, CoA attached
Krebs cycle: 2 turns per glucose, produces 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 ATP
Carbon accounting: all 6 carbons of glucose leave as CO₂ by end of Krebs
lessons.examTip: Placing Krebs in the cytoplasm — it occurs in the mitochondrial matrix; AP questions about location of specific steps test this directly

lessons.lessonTitle: Electron Transport Chain and ATP Synthesis
topics: ETC: NADH/FADH₂ donate electrons → O₂ as final acceptor → H₂O
Proton gradient across inner membrane drives ATP synthase
32-34 ATP yield estimate — why it's an estimate, not exact
lessons.examTip: Saying oxygen is 'burned' in the ETC — oxygen accepts electrons (acts as electron acceptor), not fuel; this distinction appears in multiple-choice constantly

topics: Lactic acid vs. ethanol fermentation: same purpose, different products
NAD⁺ regeneration is the actual goal — not ATP production
Why only 2 ATP net: ETC unavailable, only substrate-level phosphorylation
lessons.examTip: Thinking fermentation produces more energy than aerobic — it produces 0 additional ATP beyond glycolysis; the point is solely to recycle NAD⁺

topics: Photosystems I and II: P700 vs. P680, their sequence and roles
Linear electron flow: H₂O → PSII → ETC → PSI → NADP⁺
ATP and NADPH produced in thylakoid; O₂ is a byproduct of water splitting
lessons.examTip: Getting PSI and PSII order backward — PSII comes first in the pathway despite the numbering (named by discovery, not function order)

lessons.lessonTitle: Calvin Cycle — Fixing Carbon into Sugar
topics: Three stages: carbon fixation (RuBisCO), reduction, RuBP regeneration
ATP and NADPH inputs from light reactions consumed here
C3 vs. C4 vs. CAM: adaptations to reduce photorespiration
lessons.examTip: Confusing C3 plants with the Calvin cycle step name — C3 refers to the 3-carbon product (3-PGA), not that only 3 steps occur; C4 is a CO₂ concentrating adaptation, not a different Calvin cycle

lessons.lessonTitle: Cellular Respiration vs. Photosynthesis: The Energy Accounting
topics: Comparing inputs/outputs: net equations and what each step produces
How ETC in chloroplast mirrors ETC in mitochondria mechanistically
Experimental design: measuring O₂, CO₂, or radioactive carbon as tracers
lessons.examTip: Treating photosynthesis and respiration as opposites that cancel out — they don't balance in all conditions; AP labs often require you to measure both simultaneously

lessons.lessonTitle: Signal Transduction: From Reception to Response
topics: Three-stage cascade: reception → transduction → response
Phosphorylation cascades as signal amplification mechanism
Specificity: why different cells respond differently to same signal
lessons.examTip: Describing signal transduction as linear when it's a cascade with amplification — one receptor activation can phosphorylate thousands of proteins

lessons.lessonTitle: Cell Cycle: Phases, Checkpoints, and Control
topics: G1, S, G2, M phases and what happens in each
Checkpoints: G1/S, G2/M, spindle assembly — what each monitors
Cyclin-CDK complexes as the molecular clock
lessons.examTip: Not knowing what each checkpoint specifically checks — G1 checks size/nutrients, G2 checks DNA replication completion, spindle checks chromosome attachment

topics: PMAT phases and what moves/happens at each
Sister chromatids vs. homologous chromosomes — when each separates
Spindle fibers, centromeres, kinetochores as mechanical machinery
lessons.examTip: Confusing mitosis with meiosis chromosome movement — in mitosis sister chromatids separate; homologs never separate in mitosis

topics: Meiosis I: homolog separation (reductive division)
Meiosis II: sister chromatid separation (like mitosis)
Crossing over during prophase I — when and where recombination occurs
lessons.examTip: Saying meiosis produces 4 genetically identical cells — crossing over and independent assortment ensure no two products are identical

lessons.lessonTitle: Cancer: When Cell Cycle Control Fails
topics: Proto-oncogenes vs. tumor suppressor genes: accelerator vs. brake model
Multiple mutations required for cancer — not a single-hit disease
Metastasis: loss of cell adhesion and invasion of new tissues
lessons.examTip: Confusing oncogenes (gain-of-function mutations, dominant) with tumor suppressors (loss-of-function, recessive) — AP explicitly tests this distinction

lessons.lessonTitle: Apoptosis — Programmed Cell Death as a Survival Strategy
topics: Intrinsic vs. extrinsic apoptosis pathways
Caspases as executioner proteins — proteolytic cascade
Role of apoptosis in development, immunity, and cancer prevention
lessons.examTip: Viewing apoptosis as always harmful — AP scenarios include normal uses: finger web removal in embryos, T-cell selection, virus-infected cell elimination

topics: Totipotent vs. pluripotent vs. multipotent stem cells
Differential gene expression: same DNA, different proteins expressed
Epigenetic controls: methylation silences genes without changing sequence
lessons.examTip: Thinking differentiated cells have different DNA — all somatic cells have the same genome; differentiation is about which genes are expressed, not which genes exist

topics: Tight junctions, desmosomes, gap junctions: when each is used
ECM components (collagen, fibronectin) and cell adhesion signaling
Contact inhibition loss in cancer cells
lessons.examTip: Not connecting cell junctions to function — AP asks which junction allows passage of ions/molecules (gap junctions) vs. which seals epithelial layers (tight junctions)

lessons.lessonTitle: Mendelian Genetics — The Rules of Inheritance
topics: Segregation and independent assortment as chromosome behavior
Monohybrid and dihybrid cross probability calculations
Test cross: determining unknown genotype
lessons.examTip: Treating Mendel's laws as pure math without connecting to meiosis — AP FRQ asks you to explain WHY alleles segregate (homologs separate in meiosis I)

topics: Incomplete dominance vs. codominance: blending vs. both expressed
Multiple alleles: ABO blood type system and allele interactions
Pleiotropy: one gene affecting multiple traits
lessons.examTip: Confusing incomplete dominance (new phenotype) with codominance (both phenotypes visible) — AP uses blood type (codominance) vs. flower color (incomplete) as test cases

topics: Linked genes violate independent assortment — lower recombination frequency
Map units (cM) calculated from recombination frequency
Chi-square test to determine if genes are linked or independent
lessons.examTip: Assuming 50% recombination for linked genes — only unlinked genes show 50%; linked genes show <50%, and the value gives you map distance

topics: X-linked traits: hemizygous males express all X-linked alleles
Criss-cross inheritance pattern in X-linked recessive traits
X-inactivation (Lyon hypothesis) in females — mosaic expression
lessons.examTip: Not recognizing X-linked patterns in pedigrees — if all affected individuals are male and the trait passes through carrier females, that's X-linked recessive

topics: Autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked: diagnostic rules
Identifying carriers vs. affected individuals in pedigrees
Probability calculation for offspring genotypes from pedigree data
lessons.examTip: Skipping the elimination process — AP pedigree questions require ruling out each pattern systematically; guessing pattern without justification loses all FRQ points

topics: Nondisjunction in meiosis I vs. meiosis II — different products
Trisomy 21, Turner syndrome, Klinefelter: phenotype linked to mechanism
Deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations at chromosomal level
lessons.examTip: Not distinguishing meiosis I vs. II nondisjunction — meiosis I nondisjunction means BOTH homologs go to same cell; meiosis II means both sister chromatids go together

topics: DNA methylation silencing gene expression without mutation
Histone acetylation/deacetylation and chromatin accessibility
Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance — passing acquired marks
lessons.examTip: Treating epigenetics as permanent — most epigenetic marks are reversible; AP scenarios ask whether a change is heritable across generations or just within a lifetime

lessons.lessonTitle: Quantitative Genetics — Polygenic Traits and Environment
topics: Multiple genes + environment producing continuous distribution
Heritability: proportion of variation due to genetic differences
Norm of reaction: one genotype → different phenotypes in different environments
lessons.examTip: Confusing heritability with how genetic a trait is — high heritability means variation IN A POPULATION is genetic; it says nothing about whether the trait itself requires genes

lessons.lessonTitle: DNA Replication — Accuracy and the Machinery
topics: Helicase, primase, DNA polymerase III, ligase — order and function
Leading vs. lagging strand synthesis: why Okazaki fragments form
Proofreading and mismatch repair keeping mutation rate low
lessons.examTip: Not explaining WHY the lagging strand is discontinuous — DNA pol only adds to 3' end, so lagging strand must be synthesized in short 5'→3' fragments away from the fork

topics: Promoter recognition, RNA pol binding, elongation, termination
Template vs. coding strand — which one RNA pol reads
Pre-mRNA processing: 5' cap, poly-A tail, splicing out introns
lessons.examTip: Confusing template strand with coding strand — RNA pol reads 3'→5' template and produces mRNA identical to coding strand (except T→U)

topics: Ribosome structure: A, P, E sites and their roles
tRNA anticodon matching to mRNA codon — wobble position
Start codon (AUG), stop codons, reading frame shifts
lessons.examTip: Confusing codon (mRNA, 5'→3') with anticodon (tRNA, 3'→5') orientation — AP gives you an mRNA sequence and asks you to derive the anticodon and amino acid

topics: Point mutations: missense, nonsense, silent — effect on protein
Frameshift mutations from insertions/deletions — catastrophic downstream
DNA repair mechanisms: base excision, nucleotide excision
lessons.examTip: Thinking silent mutations have no effect — AP now includes questions about synonymous mutations affecting splicing or mRNA stability, not just protein sequence

lessons.lessonTitle: Gene Regulation in Prokaryotes — The Operon Model
topics: lac operon: inducible — repressor removed by allolactose
trp operon: repressible — repressor activated by tryptophan
Catabolite repression: CAP-cAMP system and glucose vs. lactose preference
lessons.examTip: Mixing up lac operon states — when glucose is absent AND lactose is present, BOTH the repressor is off AND CAP is on; AP tests knowing both requirements for maximal transcription

lessons.lessonTitle: Gene Regulation in Eukaryotes — Chromatin to Translation
topics: Transcription factors binding enhancers and promoters — combinatorial control
miRNA and siRNA: post-transcriptional silencing mechanisms
Chromatin remodeling: nucleosome positioning controls gene access
lessons.examTip: Treating eukaryotic gene regulation as a single on/off switch — regulation occurs at transcription, RNA processing, translation, and post-translation simultaneously

topics: PCR: denature → anneal primers → extend; exponential amplification
Gel electrophoresis: smaller fragments migrate farther
Restriction enzymes creating sticky ends for recombinant DNA
lessons.examTip: Not understanding why specific primers are needed for PCR — primers define the region amplified; wrong primer = no amplification; AP lab questions test primer design

lessons.lessonTitle: Gene Editing and CRISPR — Mechanism and Applications
topics: CRISPR-Cas9: guide RNA directs Cas9 to cut specific DNA sequence
HDR vs. NHEJ repair pathways after cutting — different outcomes
Applications: disease treatment, agriculture, ethical considerations
lessons.examTip: Thinking CRISPR always inserts a new gene — without a repair template, NHEJ creates random insertions/deletions (knockouts); a specific insertion requires HDR with a template

topics: Four postulates: variation, heritability, differential survival, trait change
Natural selection acts on phenotype but evolution changes allele frequencies
Fitness defined as reproductive success — not strength or survival alone
lessons.examTip: Saying organisms 'try to adapt' — natural selection is not goal-directed; individuals don't change; populations change over generations through differential reproduction

topics: H-W equation: p² + 2pq + q² = 1; p + q = 1
Five conditions for equilibrium — which violations cause evolution
Using H-W to calculate allele frequencies from phenotype data
lessons.examTip: Using H-W when the population IS evolving — H-W is the null hypothesis; if selection is occurring, H-W frequencies won't match observed; AP tests recognizing when to use it

lessons.lessonTitle: Types of Natural Selection — Directional, Stabilizing, Disruptive
topics: Directional: shifts mean phenotype toward one extreme
Stabilizing: eliminates extremes, narrows variation around mean
Disruptive: eliminates intermediate phenotypes, may lead to speciation
lessons.examTip: Confusing stabilizing (reduces variation) with directional (shifts mean) — AP gives a graph and asks which type, requiring you to look at change in mean AND variance

topics: Genetic drift: random allele frequency change, stronger in small populations
Bottleneck vs. founder effect: different causes of drift
Gene flow: migration homogenizes populations, opposes local adaptation
lessons.examTip: Treating genetic drift as selection — drift is random and can fix harmful alleles; selection is directional; AP explicitly tests whether a scenario is drift or selection

topics: Intrasexual (male-male competition) vs. intersexual (female choice) selection
Runaway selection (Fisher's process): honest vs. arbitrary signals
Non-random mating changes genotype frequencies but not allele frequencies alone
lessons.examTip: Thinking sexual selection always increases fitness — costly traits like peacock tails decrease survival fitness while increasing mating success; AP tests this tradeoff

topics: Allopatric vs. sympatric speciation: geographic isolation vs. reproductive isolation in place
Prezygotic vs. postzygotic barriers — types and examples
Adaptive radiation: rapid speciation from single ancestor in new environments
lessons.examTip: Confusing geographic isolation with speciation — isolation is a mechanism, not speciation itself; speciation occurs when reproductive isolation becomes complete

lessons.lessonTitle: Phylogenetics — Reading the Tree of Life
topics: Cladograms: shared derived characters define clades
Homology vs. analogy: shared ancestry vs. convergent evolution
Molecular clocks: mutation rates as evolutionary timekeepers
lessons.examTip: Reading cladograms as 'ladders of progress' — the tree shows branching, not ranking; two species at the same branch level are equally 'advanced' relative to their common ancestor

lessons.lessonTitle: Evidence for Evolution — Fossils, Biogeography, Molecular
topics: Fossil record: transitional forms and stratigraphic dating
Comparative anatomy: homologous structures, vestigial organs
Molecular evidence: cytochrome c sequence similarity as evolutionary distance
lessons.examTip: Treating molecular evidence as less reliable than fossils — AP values all lines of evidence equally; multiple converging lines strengthen an evolutionary hypothesis

lessons.lessonTitle: Population Ecology — Growth Models and Limiting Factors
topics: Exponential vs. logistic growth: J-curve vs. S-curve
Carrying capacity (K) and density-dependent limiting factors
r vs. K selected species: life history tradeoffs
lessons.examTip: Applying exponential growth to K-selected species — logistic growth only approaches K asymptotically; AP gives you data and asks which model fits and why

topics: Competition, predation, mutualism, commensalism, parasitism: + /- /0 effects
Competitive exclusion vs. character displacement and niche partitioning
Keystone species disproportionate effect on community structure
lessons.examTip: Confusing mutualism (+/+) with commensalism (+/0) — AP scenarios require you to determine effect on BOTH species, not just the one that appears to benefit

lessons.lessonTitle: Ecosystem Ecology — Energy Flow and Trophic Levels
topics: 10% rule: ~10% energy transferred between trophic levels
Gross vs. net primary productivity — why they differ
Food web vs. food chain: energy flow and complexity
lessons.examTip: Applying the 10% rule too rigidly — AP acknowledges variation (5-20%) and asks you to calculate from data rather than assuming exactly 10%

topics: Carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, fossil fuels
Nitrogen cycle: fixation → nitrification → assimilation → denitrification
Phosphorus cycle: no atmospheric phase, weathering-dependent
lessons.examTip: Forgetting that phosphorus has no significant atmospheric component — it cycles through rock weathering and biological uptake only; AP tests this uniqueness

topics: Primary succession: bare rock → climax community over centuries
Secondary succession: faster recovery from disturbance on existing soil
Pioneer species characteristics and facilitation model
lessons.examTip: Treating the climax community as permanent — disturbances continuously reset succession; AP scenarios include fire ecology where disturbance is part of the normal cycle

topics: Species richness, evenness, and diversity indices
Island biogeography: immigration rate vs. extinction rate equilibrium
Habitat fragmentation effects on minimum viable population size
lessons.examTip: Not applying island biogeography to habitat patches — fragmented habitats function like islands; larger, less isolated patches have higher biodiversity equilibrium

topics: Greenhouse effect mechanism: CO₂ absorbs IR radiation, re-radiates
Invasive species disrupting food webs and competitive balance
Sixth mass extinction: habitat loss as primary driver
lessons.examTip: Explaining climate change vaguely ('more CO₂ = warmer') — AP FRQ wants the mechanism: CO₂ absorbs outgoing longwave radiation and re-emits it toward Earth

topics: Proximate (mechanism) vs. ultimate (evolutionary) causation
Fixed action patterns, imprinting, and associative learning
Kin selection and Hamilton's rule: altruism explained by inclusive fitness
lessons.examTip: Answering 'why' questions with only proximate mechanisms — AP explicitly tests whether you can give BOTH a proximate and ultimate explanation for the same behavior

lessons.lessonTitle: Electron Configuration and the Periodic Table
topics: Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion, Hund's rule — filling order
Orbital shapes: s, p, d and their energy levels
Periodic trends derived from electron configuration: atomic radius, IE, EN
lessons.examTip: Writing electron configurations for ions — students often forget to remove from the highest n orbital (4s before 3d for transition metal cations)

topics: PES peaks: position = binding energy, height = relative number of electrons
Connecting PES spectrum to electron configuration
Shielding and effective nuclear charge (Zeff) explaining peak positions
lessons.examTip: Reading PES graphs — lower binding energy peaks are on the RIGHT (valence electrons); students read left-to-right and misidentify which electrons are valence

lessons.lessonTitle: Periodic Trends — Why They Exist, Not Just What They Are
topics: Atomic radius: Zeff increase across period, shielding increase down group
Ionization energy exceptions: half-filled subshell stability (N vs. O)
Electronegativity as measure of nuclear pull on bonding electrons
lessons.examTip: Memorizing trends without the mechanism — AP FRQ always asks 'explain in terms of' nuclear charge and electron shielding, not just state the trend

topics: Isotopes: same Z, different mass number — effect on atomic mass
MS: m/z values, relative abundance peaks, molecular ion
Average atomic mass calculation from isotope data
lessons.examTip: Confusing mass number with atomic mass — mass number is an integer (protons+neutrons); atomic mass is a weighted average and rarely an integer

lessons.lessonTitle: Moles, Molar Mass, and Stoichiometry Foundations
topics: Mole as Avogadro's number of particles — connecting mass to count
Molar mass from periodic table; empirical vs. molecular formula
Percent composition and empirical formula determination
lessons.examTip: Finding molecular formula from empirical — must divide molar mass by empirical formula mass to get the multiplier; AP gives both values and expects this calculation

lessons.lessonTitle: Mixtures, Pure Substances, and Separation Techniques
topics: Homogeneous vs. heterogeneous mixtures at the particle level
Chromatography, distillation, filtration — which property each exploits
Colligative properties as mixture properties
lessons.examTip: Treating chromatography as purely a separation technique — AP asks you to explain WHICH intermolecular forces cause components to travel at different rates

topics: Coulomb's law: force ∝ charge product / distance²
Isoelectronic series — size determined by nuclear charge alone
Ion radius vs. atomic radius: cations smaller, anions larger than neutral
lessons.examTip: Not applying Coulomb's law to explain trends — AP expects 'higher nuclear charge pulls electrons closer, reducing radius' not just 'the radius decreases'

lessons.lessonTitle: Quantum Mechanical Model of the Atom
topics: Wave-particle duality and the de Broglie relationship
Heisenberg uncertainty principle — position and momentum tradeoff
Quantum numbers (n, l, ml, ms) and orbital designation
lessons.examTip: Treating quantum numbers as arbitrary labels — AP tests that n determines energy, l determines shape, and ml determines spatial orientation in a magnetic field

topics: Formal charge minimization to select best Lewis structure
Expanded octets for period 3+ elements (PCl5, SF6)
Resonance structures and their meaning for bond order
lessons.examTip: Drawing any valid Lewis structure without checking formal charge — AP always prefers the structure where formal charges are closest to zero

topics: Electron geometry vs. molecular geometry — lone pairs count for geometry, not name
Bond angles and how lone pairs compress them
Polarity from geometry: symmetric vs. asymmetric electron distribution
lessons.examTip: Using electron geometry name instead of molecular geometry name — a molecule with 4 electron pairs and 1 lone pair is 'trigonal pyramidal' not 'tetrahedral'

lessons.lessonTitle: Ionic vs. Covalent Bonding — Why the Difference Matters
topics: Electronegativity difference as predictor of bond character
Lattice energy: why ionic compounds have high melting points
Network covalent solids (diamond, quartz) — no ions, no discrete molecules
lessons.examTip: Treating ionic/covalent as binary — AP expects a continuum; polar covalent bonds have partial charges and the degree matters for property prediction

lessons.lessonTitle: Metallic Bonding and Properties of Metals
topics: Electron sea model: delocalized electrons explain conductivity and malleability
Metallic character trends on periodic table
Alloys as modified metallic structures
lessons.examTip: Explaining metal properties without the electron sea — AP FRQ asks to connect malleability/conductivity to the specific bonding model, not just state they're metals

topics: sp, sp2, sp3 hybridization linked to molecular geometry
Sigma and pi bonds: sigma = head-on overlap, pi = side-by-side
Bond order, bond length, and bond energy relationships
lessons.examTip: Confusing sigma and pi bond counts — a double bond = 1σ + 1π; triple bond = 1σ + 2π; AP asks total sigma or pi bonds in a molecule

topics: Stock notation for transition metal ions (Fe²⁺ vs. Fe³⁺)
Polyatomic ions: formula and charge memorization
Acid naming: binary acids (hydro-...ic) vs. oxyacids (-ic/-ous)
lessons.examTip: Ignoring transition metal oxidation states — AP gives you a formula and asks for name; you must determine charge from anion to name the cation correctly

topics: Bond dipoles vs. molecular dipole: vector addition of individual bonds
How lone pairs and molecular symmetry affect overall polarity
Polarity predicting physical properties (boiling point, solubility)
lessons.examTip: Calling any molecule with polar bonds 'polar' — CO₂ has two polar bonds but is nonpolar because they cancel; AP tests the vector cancellation argument

topics: PES as evidence for energy level structure within atoms
How bond formation shifts orbital energies in molecules
Connecting spectroscopic data to atomic/molecular structure conclusions
lessons.examTip: Not connecting PES data to periodic trends — AP gives an unknown element's PES and expects you to identify it by matching peak pattern to electron configuration

lessons.lessonTitle: London Dispersion Forces — The Universal IMF
topics: Induced dipole formation — instantaneous dipole mechanism
Polarizability: larger, heavier molecules have stronger LDFs
LDF as the ONLY force between noble gases and nonpolar molecules
lessons.examTip: Ignoring LDF in polar molecules — polar molecules have BOTH dipole-dipole AND LDF; large nonpolar molecules can have stronger IMFs than small polar ones

topics: Requirements: H bonded to N, O, or F; with lone pair on N, O, or F
Anomalous properties of water from H-bonding (high bp, density maximum)
H-bonding in biological molecules: DNA base pairing, protein secondary structure
lessons.examTip: Calling any O-H interaction a hydrogen bond — the H must be between two electronegative atoms (donor AND acceptor required); C-H does not form true hydrogen bonds

topics: Boiling point, vapor pressure, viscosity, surface tension all correlate with IMF strength
Vapor pressure inversely related to IMF strength
Comparing across different IMF types: H-bond > dipole-dipole > LDF for similar-sized molecules
lessons.examTip: Comparing molecules of vastly different sizes — a large nonpolar molecule can have a higher boiling point than a small polar molecule due to greater LDF; always consider BOTH IMF type and molecular size

topics: Four solid types: ionic, molecular, metallic, network covalent — properties of each
Unit cells: simple cubic, BCC, FCC — particles per cell calculation
Melting point and hardness correlated to bonding type
lessons.examTip: Treating all hard solids as ionic — diamond and quartz are network covalent (no ions); their hardness comes from covalent bonds extending in 3D, not electrostatic attraction

topics: Like dissolves like: matching polarity/H-bonding for solubility
Enthalpy of solution: solute-solute + solvent-solvent vs. solute-solvent interactions
Solubility of gases: Henry's law — pressure dependence
lessons.examTip: Predicting solubility from polarity alone without energy considerations — an endothermic dissolution can still be spontaneous if entropy increase is sufficient

topics: Boiling point elevation, freezing point depression: ΔT = iKm
Osmotic pressure and semipermeable membranes
Van't Hoff factor (i) for electrolytes vs. nonelectrolytes
lessons.examTip: Forgetting the van't Hoff factor for electrolytes — NaCl dissociates into 2 particles (i=2), so its colligative effect is double a nonelectrolyte at the same molality

lessons.lessonTitle: Phase Diagrams — Pressure, Temperature, and State
topics: Triple point, critical point, normal boiling/melting points on phase diagram
Clausius-Clapeyron equation: ln(P2/P1) = -ΔHvap/R × (1/T2 - 1/T1)
Sublimation, deposition, and supercritical fluid regions
lessons.examTip: Misreading phase boundaries — the line between liquid and gas shows equilibrium vapor pressure at each temperature; AP gives you a phase diagram and asks what happens along a path

lessons.lessonTitle: Spectroscopy — IR, NMR, and Mass Spec in Structure Determination
topics: IR spectroscopy: functional groups absorb specific wavelengths
Mass spectrum: molecular ion peak and fragmentation patterns
Using spectral data to identify unknowns
lessons.examTip: Treating spectroscopy as trivia — AP gives spectral data and asks you to identify a compound or confirm a structure; this requires actually interpreting peak positions

lessons.lessonTitle: Balancing Chemical Equations and Reaction Types
topics: Conservation of mass and charge in balancing
Synthesis, decomposition, single/double displacement, combustion patterns
Net ionic equations: eliminating spectator ions
lessons.examTip: Writing full ionic equation instead of net ionic — AP always wants spectator ions removed; if you include them, the equation is wrong even if balanced

lessons.lessonTitle: Stoichiometry — Limiting Reagents and Percent Yield
topics: Mole ratio from balanced equation as conversion factor
Identifying limiting reagent: compare actual ratio to stoichiometric ratio
Theoretical vs. actual yield; sources of percent yield <100%
lessons.examTip: Calculating limiting reagent by comparing masses instead of moles — must convert to moles first; the reagent that produces LESS product is limiting

topics: Molarity calculations: M = mol/L
Titration: equivalence point, endpoint, and indicator choice
Dilution equation: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂
lessons.examTip: Confusing equivalence point with endpoint — equivalence point is when stoichiometric amounts react (calculated); endpoint is when indicator changes (observed); they're close but not identical

topics: Oxidation state assignment rules; identifying oxidizing vs. reducing agents
Half-reaction method for balancing redox in acidic/basic solution
Activity series predicting spontaneous displacement reactions
lessons.examTip: Confusing oxidation state with charge — Fe³⁺ has an oxidation state of +3 and a charge of +3, but in FeCl₃ the iron has oxidation state +3 with no actual ionic charge listed

topics: Solubility rules for common ions — which combinations precipitate
Ksp expression and its relationship to solubility
Common ion effect reducing solubility
lessons.examTip: Applying Ksp as if it were Keq for a generic reaction — Ksp only applies to dissolution equilibrium; if Ksp is exceeded, precipitation occurs until the product drops back to Ksp

topics: Brønsted-Lowry: proton donor/acceptor; Lewis: electron pair donor/acceptor
Strong acid + strong base → neutral; weak acid/base → depends on Ka/Kb
Equivalence point pH for different acid-base combinations
lessons.examTip: Assuming all neutralizations produce pH 7 — only strong acid + strong base gives pH 7 at equivalence; weak acid + strong base gives basic pH because the conjugate base hydrolyzes

topics: Ideal gas law: PV = nRT — which variable to solve for
Molar volume at STP: 22.4 L/mol (0°C, 1 atm)
Dalton's law of partial pressures and mole fractions
lessons.examTip: Using STP molar volume (22.4 L) at non-STP conditions — must use PV=nRT when temperature ≠ 0°C or pressure ≠ 1 atm

topics: Galvanic vs. electrolytic cell direction of electron flow
Standard reduction potentials and cell voltage: E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode
Nernst equation: non-standard conditions
lessons.examTip: Drawing electron flow going from cathode to anode — electrons flow from anode (oxidation) to cathode (reduction) through the wire; ions move through the salt bridge

topics: Rate = -Δ[reactant]/Δt = +Δ[product]/Δt with stoichiometric coefficients
Average rate vs. instantaneous rate from concentration-time graphs
Initial rate method for determining rate law
lessons.examTip: Forgetting stoichiometric coefficients when relating rates — if 2A → B, rate of disappearance of A is twice the rate of appearance of B

topics: Rate = k[A]m[B]n — determining m and n from experimental data
Zero, first, second order: different integrated rate laws and graphs
Half-life equations for first-order vs. second-order reactions
lessons.examTip: Determining order from stoichiometry instead of experimental data — reaction order must be determined experimentally; coefficients in balanced equation do NOT give the order (unless it's an elementary step)

lessons.lessonTitle: The Arrhenius Equation — Temperature and Rate
topics: k = Ae^(-Ea/RT): activation energy and frequency factor
ln(k) vs. 1/T plot: slope = -Ea/R
How catalysts lower Ea without changing ΔG or ΔH
lessons.examTip: Saying catalysts 'speed up reactions by providing energy' — catalysts lower activation energy by providing an alternate pathway; they don't add energy or change thermodynamics

topics: Elementary steps must add to give overall balanced equation
Rate law comes from slow (rate-determining) step
Intermediates appear in mechanism steps but not the overall equation
lessons.examTip: Writing rate law from the overall balanced equation — rate law only comes from the mechanism's slow step; the overall equation coefficients mean nothing for kinetics

topics: Three requirements: sufficient energy, correct orientation, collision frequency
How concentration, temperature, surface area affect collision frequency
Transition state (activated complex) at the energy maximum
lessons.examTip: Not distinguishing collision frequency from reaction rate — increasing concentration increases collision frequency, but only a fraction of collisions are effective (correct energy + orientation)

topics: Homogeneous: catalyst in same phase as reactants (H⁺ in solution)
Heterogeneous: surface catalysis (Pt in catalytic converter)
Enzymes as biological catalysts — active site and substrate specificity
lessons.examTip: Confusing catalyst consumption — catalysts are NOT consumed overall (they're regenerated), even though they participate in the mechanism

lessons.lessonTitle: Integrated Rate Laws and Half-Life Calculations
topics: First order: ln[A]t = -kt + ln[A]₀; t½ = 0.693/k (constant)
Second order: 1/[A]t = kt + 1/[A]₀; t½ = 1/(k[A]₀) (concentration-dependent)
Identifying order from linearization of [A] vs. t data
lessons.examTip: Applying first-order half-life to second-order reactions — only first-order reactions have constant half-lives; second-order half-life changes as concentration changes

lessons.lessonTitle: Kinetics vs. Thermodynamics — Controlling the Outcome
topics: Kinetic product (faster forming) vs. thermodynamic product (more stable)
A reaction can be thermodynamically favorable but kinetically inert
How temperature shifts product distribution toward thermodynamic control
lessons.examTip: Assuming fast reactions are thermodynamically favorable — diamond-to-graphite conversion is thermodynamically favorable but kinetically prevented at room temperature

topics: Endothermic vs. exothermic: sign of ΔH and system vs. surroundings perspective
Hess's Law: ΔH is state function, additive over multiple steps
Standard enthalpies of formation and their use in calculation
lessons.examTip: Flipping Hess's Law signs wrong — when you reverse a reaction, flip the sign of ΔH; when you multiply, multiply ΔH; AP gives multiple steps and requires careful sign tracking

topics: q = mcΔT for solution calorimetry
Coffee cup vs. bomb calorimeter: constant pressure vs. constant volume
Heat of reaction from temperature change and specific heat
lessons.examTip: Using water's specific heat (4.18 J/g·°C) for all solutions — AP specifies the solution's specific heat in the problem; using water's value for a salt solution introduces error

topics: Entropy as measure of microstates/disorder, not just 'messiness'
Predicting sign of ΔS: gas formation, dissolving, increased particles
Third law: entropy of perfect crystal at 0 K is zero
lessons.examTip: Predicting ΔS only from state changes — dissolving a salt increases entropy (more particles, more disorder) even though liquid→dissolved appears 'less ordered' visually

topics: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS: when each term dominates at high/low T
ΔG° = -RT ln K: connecting thermodynamics to equilibrium
ΔG° = -nFE°: connecting thermodynamics to electrochemistry
lessons.examTip: Confusing ΔG° (standard conditions) with ΔG (actual conditions) — reaction spontaneity under standard conditions (ΔG°) differs from actual conditions (ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q)

topics: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) - Σ(bonds formed): gaseous species only
Bond energy tables and their limitations
Why bond energy method gives estimates, not exact values
lessons.examTip: Using bond energies for aqueous or liquid species — bond energy method only works for gas-phase species; for condensed phases, use Hess's Law with formation enthalpies

topics: Four ΔH/ΔS sign combinations and their spontaneity by temperature
Crossover temperature where ΔG changes sign: T = ΔH/ΔS
Entropy-driven vs. enthalpy-driven reactions
lessons.examTip: Thinking exothermic reactions are always spontaneous — endothermic, entropy-driven reactions (like dissolving ammonium nitrate) are spontaneous at high enough temperature

lessons.lessonTitle: Entropy and the Second Law in Chemical Systems
topics: Second law: total entropy of universe increases for spontaneous processes
ΔSuniverse = ΔSsystem + ΔSsurroundings
Exothermic reactions increase entropy of surroundings
lessons.examTip: Applying second law only to the system — a reaction can decrease system entropy and still be spontaneous if it increases surroundings entropy sufficiently

lessons.lessonTitle: Thermodynamic Cycles and Hess's Law Applications
topics: Born-Haber cycle for ionic compound formation energy
Multi-step Hess's Law calculations with state function properties
Connecting ΔHf° values to stability of compounds
lessons.examTip: Not checking that intermediate steps cancel correctly in Hess's Law — AP gives steps that require reversal and scaling; careless algebra errors are the #1 error here

lessons.lessonTitle: Dynamic Equilibrium and the Equilibrium Constant
topics: Equilibrium: forward rate = reverse rate, concentrations constant but nonzero
Kc expression: products over reactants, raised to stoichiometric powers
K > 1 means product-favored; K < 1 means reactant-favored
lessons.examTip: Including pure solids and liquids in K expressions — solids and pure liquids have constant concentration (activity = 1) and are omitted from K; AP tests this in heterogeneous equilibria

topics: ICE table setup: Initial, Change, Equilibrium concentrations
Small x approximation: valid when K << initial concentration
Quadratic formula application when x is not negligible
lessons.examTip: Applying the 5% approximation without checking — if x/[initial] > 5%, must solve the quadratic; AP problems are often designed to make the approximation invalid

lessons.lessonTitle: Le Chatelier's Principle — Predicting Equilibrium Shifts
topics: Concentration changes: adding/removing reactant or product
Pressure/volume changes: shifts toward side with fewer/more moles of gas
Temperature changes: treat ΔH as reactant or product
lessons.examTip: Applying Le Chatelier to solids/liquids — adding or removing a pure solid has NO effect on equilibrium position (it doesn't appear in K and doesn't change concentration)

topics: Q calculated same way as K but at non-equilibrium conditions
Q < K: reaction proceeds forward; Q > K: reaction proceeds reverse
Q = K: system is at equilibrium
lessons.examTip: Forgetting to compare Q to K direction — AP gives initial concentrations and asks which way equilibrium shifts; must calculate Q first, then compare to K

topics: Ksp expression for ionic dissolution; calculating molar solubility
Common ion effect: shared ion reduces solubility
Precipitation: ion product Q > Ksp triggers precipitation
lessons.examTip: Confusing molar solubility (mol/L of compound that dissolves) with Ksp (equilibrium product) — for Ca₃(PO₄)₂, the relationship between s and Ksp involves powers of 3 and 2

lessons.lessonTitle: Kp vs. Kc and Gas Equilibria
topics: Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn where Δn = moles gas products - reactants
When Kp = Kc: when Δn = 0
Partial pressure and mole fraction in gas equilibrium calculations
lessons.examTip: Using Kc values in Kp calculations or vice versa without conversion — AP sometimes gives Kp data for a Kc calculation requiring the conversion; always check which constant is given

lessons.lessonTitle: Coupled Equilibria and Complex Ion Formation
topics: Sequential equilibria: multiply K values when steps are combined
Complex ion formation increasing solubility of sparingly soluble salts
Acid-base effects on solubility of salts with acidic/basic anions
lessons.examTip: Treating complex ion formation as separate from solubility — AgCl dissolves MORE in ammonia because Ag⁺ is consumed forming Ag(NH₃)₂⁺, pulling the dissolution equilibrium right

lessons.lessonTitle: Gibbs Free Energy and Equilibrium Connection
topics: ΔG° = -RT ln K: quantitative relationship between thermodynamics and equilibrium
ΔG = 0 at equilibrium under actual conditions
How temperature affects K through ΔH and ΔS
lessons.examTip: Confusing ΔG° = 0 with ΔG = 0 — at equilibrium it's ΔG = 0 (not ΔG°); ΔG° = 0 means K = 1, which is a specific coincidence, not the general equilibrium condition

lessons.lessonTitle: pH, Ka, and the Strength Scale
topics: pH = -log[H⁺]; Ka measures degree of ionization for weak acids
Strong acids: 100% ionization (no Ka expression needed)
Relationship: pKa = -log Ka; lower pKa = stronger acid
lessons.examTip: Calculating pH for weak acids using pH = -log[HA] instead of finding [H⁺] via Ka — for weak acids must use Ka and ICE table; [H⁺] ≠ initial concentration

topics: Conjugate pair: differ by one proton only
Ka × Kb = Kw for conjugate pairs at 25°C
Amphoteric species (like water and HCO₃⁻) acting as both acid and base
lessons.examTip: Forgetting Ka × Kb = Kw relationship — if given Ka of a weak acid, Kb of its conjugate base = Kw/Ka; AP titration problems require this conversion

topics: Buffer = weak acid + its conjugate base (or weak base + conjugate acid)
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA])
Buffer capacity: maximized when pH ≈ pKa, depleted by excess strong acid/base
lessons.examTip: Using Henderson-Hasselbalch for non-buffer mixtures — H-H only applies when significant amounts of BOTH weak acid AND conjugate base are present; doesn't work at equivalence point

lessons.lessonTitle: Titration Curves — Anatomy of the Graph
topics: Initial pH, half-equivalence point (pH = pKa), equivalence point, buffer region
Strong acid/strong base: sharp equivalence point at pH 7
Weak acid/strong base: equivalence point above 7; half-eq pH = pKa
lessons.examTip: Reading half-equivalence point incorrectly — at half-equivalence, exactly half the acid is neutralized; moles acid = moles conjugate base; pH = pKa directly at that point

topics: Ka1 >> Ka2 >> Ka3: each successive proton harder to remove
Dominant species at each pH in a diprotic acid system
Amphiprotic intermediate species: pH = (pKa1 + pKa2)/2
lessons.examTip: Calculating pH for polyprotic acids using all Ka values simultaneously — only Ka1 matters for pH of weak polyprotic acid solution; Ka2 contribution is negligible

topics: Binary acids: bond strength and electronegativity across/down periodic table
Oxyacids: more oxygens = stronger acid (electron withdrawal from O-H)
Resonance stabilization of conjugate base increases acid strength
lessons.examTip: Ranking only by electronegativity for binary acids — down a group, bond strength decreases more than electronegativity increases, making HI stronger than HF despite F being more electronegative

lessons.lessonTitle: Lewis Acids and Bases — Beyond Protons
topics: Lewis acid: electron pair acceptor (not just proton donors)
Lewis base: electron pair donor (all Brønsted-Lowry bases are Lewis bases)
Metal ions as Lewis acids in coordination chemistry
lessons.examTip: Limiting acid-base thinking to proton transfer — AP specifically tests Lewis definition for reactions without protons, like BF₃ + NH₃ or metal-ligand complex formation

lessons.lessonTitle: Acid-Base Indicators and Titration Endpoint Selection
topics: Indicator = weak acid where HIn and In⁻ have different colors
Choose indicator with pKa ≈ equivalence point pH
Why universal indicator differs from single indicators
lessons.examTip: Choosing any indicator for any titration — phenolphthalein (range 8.2-10) is wrong for strong acid/strong base if the equivalence point is at pH 7; must match indicator range to equivalence point pH

topics: Galvanic cell: spontaneous redox, positive E°cell, negative ΔG°
Electrolytic cell: non-spontaneous, requires external voltage
Standard cell voltage: E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode
lessons.examTip: Drawing electron flow incorrectly — electrons always flow from anode to cathode through external circuit; in solution, cations move toward cathode (same direction as electron 'destination')

topics: E = E° - (RT/nF)ln Q: how concentration affects cell voltage
At 25°C: E = E° - (0.0592/n)log Q simplified form
Dead battery: E = 0 when Q = K (equilibrium reached)
lessons.examTip: Using Nernst with ΔG° instead of E° — Nernst applies to cell potential (E), not free energy directly; also forgetting n (moles of electrons) in the denominator

topics: Charge = current × time (Q = It) in coulombs
Moles of electrons = Q/F where F = 96,485 C/mol
Moles of product from stoichiometry of half-reaction
lessons.examTip: Not accounting for n in electrolysis — depositing Cu²⁺ requires 2 mol e⁻ per mol Cu; Al³⁺ requires 3; students often calculate moles of electrons but forget to divide by n

lessons.lessonTitle: Free Energy, Equilibrium, and Electrochemistry Triangle
topics: ΔG° = -nFE° = -RT ln K: three-way relationship
Using one quantity to calculate the other two
How spontaneity prediction is consistent across all three approaches
lessons.examTip: Forgetting sign conventions — ΔG° negative = spontaneous = K > 1 = E°cell positive; AP gives one value and asks for another; sign errors are the most common mistake

lessons.lessonTitle: Batteries and Fuel Cells — Applied Electrochemistry
topics: Primary (non-rechargeable) vs. secondary (rechargeable) batteries
Hydrogen fuel cell: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O with electrical energy output
Internal resistance and real vs. theoretical cell voltage
lessons.examTip: Treating all batteries as equivalent — AP distinguishes by asking which type uses which reaction and why rechargeable batteries can be reversed (product can be reconverted)

topics: Iron corrosion as electrochemical cell: anodic and cathodic regions
Sacrificial anode: more active metal preferentially oxidizes
Galvanic corrosion between dissimilar metals in contact
lessons.examTip: Not explaining corrosion mechanistically — AP FRQ asks to identify which metal acts as anode and why (standard reduction potential comparison), not just state that corrosion occurs

topics: ATP coupling to drive endergonic reactions via shared intermediate
Chemiosmosis as electrochemical gradient driving ATP synthesis
Gibbs free energy of metabolic reactions and efficiency
lessons.examTip: Treating biological thermodynamics as different from chemical thermodynamics — same ΔG rules apply; ATP hydrolysis is simply a highly exergonic reaction coupled to less favorable ones

topics: Designing reactions to be spontaneous: choosing conditions to favor ΔG < 0
Industrial synthesis tradeoffs: Le Chatelier vs. kinetics vs. thermodynamics
Haber process as case study: high P (Le Chatelier), moderate T (kinetics/thermodynamics balance)
lessons.examTip: Applying only thermodynamics to industrial processes — Haber process uses moderate temperature despite K being larger at low T because kinetics requires activation energy; AP tests this tradeoff explicitly

lessons.lessonTitle: Ecosystem Structure — Who Eats Whom and Why It Matters
topics: Producers, consumers, decomposers — roles in energy and nutrient cycling
Food webs vs. food chains: complexity and stability
Trophic cascade: removing a predator ripples through the web
lessons.examTip: Describing food webs only as 'who eats what' — AP FRQ asks about CONSEQUENCES of removing a species; must trace effects through multiple trophic levels

topics: Only ~10% of energy transferred between trophic levels
Gross primary productivity (GPP) vs. net primary productivity (NPP)
Why terrestrial ecosystems have higher NPP than open ocean
lessons.examTip: Applying the 10% rule to matter/nutrients — nutrients recycle, energy does not; the 10% rule is energy-only; confusing these on FRQ loses full credit

lessons.lessonTitle: Biogeochemical Cycles — Carbon, Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Water
topics: Carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion, ocean buffering
Nitrogen cycle: fixation (N₂ → NH₃), nitrification, denitrification pathways
Phosphorus cycle: no atmospheric reservoir; slow weathering release
lessons.examTip: Confusing nitrogen fixation with nitrification — fixation converts N₂ gas to usable NH₃ (only bacteria do this); nitrification converts NH₃ to NO₃⁻

topics: Temperature and precipitation as the two axes determining biome type
Biome characteristics: tropical rainforest, temperate deciduous, grassland, desert, tundra
Latitude, altitude, and continentality effects on biome distribution
lessons.examTip: Memorizing biome lists without understanding the climate logic — AP gives a climate graph (climatograph) and asks you to identify the biome; must know precipitation seasonality patterns

topics: Marine zones: intertidal, photic, aphotic, benthic, pelagic
Freshwater: lakes (stratification, turnover), rivers, wetlands
Estuaries as highly productive transition zones
lessons.examTip: Forgetting that estuaries combine freshwater and marine inputs — AP tests why estuaries are so productive (nutrient input from both, shallow water, high light penetration)

topics: Fundamental vs. realized niche: what's possible vs. what's achieved
Competitive exclusion principle and niche partitioning as its resolution
Mutualism, commensalism, parasitism: fitness effects on each partner
lessons.examTip: Confusing fundamental (potential) with realized (actual) niche — competitive exclusion shrinks the realized niche; AP asks which is wider and why

topics: Provisioning, regulating, cultural, supporting services — categories and examples
Valuing ecosystem services economically for policy arguments
Wetlands as case study: flood control, water purification, carbon storage
lessons.examTip: Listing ecosystem services without connecting them to mechanisms — AP FRQ asks to explain HOW wetlands filter water (plant uptake, microbial processing of nutrients), not just that they do

topics: NPP = GPP - respiration; units in g C/m²/yr or kcal/m²/yr
Calculating energy available at each trophic level
Comparing productivity across biomes using data tables
lessons.examTip: Using GPP instead of NPP for available energy — consumers can only use NPP (what's left after plant respiration); AP math FRQ always requires NPP as the starting value

lessons.lessonTitle: Biodiversity — Three Levels and Why Each Matters
topics: Genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity — distinct but interconnected
Why genetic diversity matters for disease resistance and adaptation
Biodiversity hotspots: high endemism + high threat
lessons.examTip: Treating biodiversity as just species count — AP distinguishes all three levels and asks which type is affected by a specific threat (inbreeding reduces genetic diversity; habitat loss reduces species diversity)

lessons.lessonTitle: Evolution and Natural Selection as Biodiversity Engine
topics: Speciation mechanisms: allopatric vs. sympatric
Adaptive radiation and why island/isolated environments accelerate it
Extinction vs. speciation rate determining net biodiversity
lessons.examTip: Treating evolution as slow and irrelevant to current conservation — rapid evolution (antibiotic resistance, pesticide resistance) is a current AP topic

lessons.lessonTitle: Island Biogeography — A Model for Habitat Patches
topics: Immigration rate and extinction rate reaching equilibrium species number
Size effect: larger islands have lower extinction rates
Distance effect: closer islands have higher immigration rates
lessons.examTip: Not applying island biogeography to fragmented habitats — AP explicitly tests that forest fragments, parks, and reserves function as ecological islands

topics: Habitat destruction as #1 threat globally
Invasive species: competitive, predatory, and disease mechanisms
Overexploitation, pollution, climate change as additional drivers
lessons.examTip: Ranking threats without supporting data — AP FRQ asks to justify which threat is greatest using specific evidence; 'habitat destruction' without mechanism loses points

topics: Keystone species: disproportionate impact relative to biomass
Trophic cascade: top predator removal increases herbivore, decreases vegetation
Sea otter / sea urchin / kelp as the canonical AP case study
lessons.examTip: Confusing keystone with apex predator — a keystone species has outsized community impact but isn't necessarily the top predator; starfish and sea otters are classic AP keystone examples

lessons.lessonTitle: Conservation Strategies — Protected Areas and Corridors
topics: SLOSS debate: one large vs. several small reserves
Habitat corridors allowing gene flow between fragmented populations
Minimum viable population and extinction vortex
lessons.examTip: Assuming larger reserves are always better — AP tests nuances: multiple small reserves may cover more habitat types; edge effects reduce effective interior area of large reserves

lessons.lessonTitle: Invasive Species — Mechanisms and Case Studies
topics: Why invasives succeed: enemy release, novel weapons, phenotypic plasticity
AP case studies: zebra mussels, kudzu, cane toads, Asian carp
Economic and ecological costs of invasive species
lessons.examTip: Saying invasives succeed 'because they have no predators' — that's enemy release hypothesis, one explanation; AP may ask for multiple mechanisms or ask you to evaluate evidence

topics: IUCN Red List categories: criteria for critically endangered vs. vulnerable
CITES: trade restrictions for threatened species
Captive breeding and reintroduction programs — success factors
lessons.examTip: Confusing CITES (trade) with ESA (domestic US protection) — AP tests which treaty applies to international vs. domestic species protection scenarios

topics: Exponential growth (J-curve): unlimited resources, r = biotic potential
Logistic growth (S-curve): K as carrying capacity, growth slows near K
Per capita growth rate changes with density under logistic model
lessons.examTip: Using exponential model when logistic applies — AP gives data showing slowing growth and asks which model fits; must recognize S-curve features in data, not just graphs

topics: Clumped, uniform, and random distribution — causes of each
Density-dependent vs. density-independent limiting factors
Population sampling methods: mark-recapture, transects, quadrats
lessons.examTip: Confusing density-dependent (disease, competition, predation — intensity increases with density) with density-independent (weather, natural disasters — occur regardless of density)

lessons.lessonTitle: Age Structure Diagrams — Predicting the Future
topics: Pyramid shapes: growing, stable, declining populations
Dependency ratio: proportion of working-age to non-working-age population
How current age structure predicts future growth momentum
lessons.examTip: Reading age pyramids as snapshots not predictors — a country with many young people will CONTINUE growing even if fertility drops to replacement level immediately (population momentum)

topics: Four stages: high birth+death → falling death → falling birth → stable
Total fertility rate (TFR) vs. replacement fertility (2.1)
Factors driving fertility decline: education, urbanization, women's rights
lessons.examTip: Applying demographic transition uniformly to all countries — different countries are in different stages; AP gives TFR and death rate data and asks which stage and what policy would be effective

topics: Type I (late loss — humans, elephants), Type II (constant — birds), Type III (early loss — fish, plants)
Connecting curve type to life history strategy (r vs. K selection)
Survivorship data interpretation from tables
lessons.examTip: Memorizing examples without understanding mechanism — AP asks WHY fish are Type III (massive egg production, minimal parental care, most die young) not just that they are Type III

topics: Ecological footprint: land area required to support a lifestyle
IPAT equation: Impact = Population × Affluence × Technology
Per capita resource consumption differences between developed and developing nations
lessons.examTip: Blaming only population size for environmental impact — AP tests IPAT; a small wealthy population can have more impact than a large poor population due to affluence factor

topics: Maximum sustainable yield (MSY): harvesting at K/2 for fastest regrowth
Tragedy of the commons: individual incentive vs. collective optimum
ITQs and catch limits as management tools
lessons.examTip: Thinking MSY means harvest as much as possible — MSY is at K/2 where population growth rate is maximum; overfishing past MSY depletes the population

topics: China's one-child policy: demographic consequences (sex ratio, aging)
Pro-natalist vs. anti-natalist policies — when each is used
Education and access to family planning as most effective interventions
lessons.examTip: Evaluating policies only on effectiveness without ethical dimensions — AP FRQ often asks for both effectiveness AND tradeoffs/consequences; China's policy reduced growth but created aging crisis

topics: Plate boundaries: divergent, convergent, transform — landforms at each
Convection in mantle driving plate movement
Earthquakes and volcanoes concentrated at plate boundaries
lessons.examTip: Confusing subduction (oceanic under continental or oceanic under oceanic) with collision (continental-continental) — AP asks which plate boundary creates which feature

lessons.lessonTitle: The Rock Cycle and Soil Formation
topics: Igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic: formation and interconversion
Soil horizons: O, A, B, C layers and what each contains
Weathering (physical and chemical) as soil formation mechanism
lessons.examTip: Describing soil only by texture, not horizon — AP FRQ asks about which horizon is most fertile (A horizon) and why (accumulated organic matter from decomposition)

topics: Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere: properties of each
Troposphere contains weather; stratosphere contains ozone layer
Greenhouse gases: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, H₂O vapor — relative forcing
lessons.examTip: Treating ozone depletion and greenhouse effect as the same problem — ozone depletion is in the stratosphere from CFCs; greenhouse effect is in the troposphere from CO₂/CH₄; they're distinct

lessons.lessonTitle: Solar Radiation, Albedo, and Earth's Energy Budget
topics: Albedo: fraction of solar radiation reflected; ice-albedo feedback
Earth's energy budget: shortwave in, longwave out, greenhouse retention
Latitude effects on solar angle and energy intensity
lessons.examTip: Confusing albedo with emissivity — albedo is about incoming shortwave; greenhouse effect involves outgoing longwave; ice-albedo feedback links melting ice to more warming

lessons.lessonTitle: Global Wind Patterns and Ocean Currents
topics: Hadley, Ferrel, Polar cells: rising/falling air creating wind belts
Coriolis effect deflecting winds and ocean currents
Thermohaline circulation: density-driven global ocean conveyor
lessons.examTip: Not connecting wind patterns to precipitation — air rises at equator (wet) and descends at 30° (desert belt); AP gives a location's latitude and asks about likely climate

lessons.lessonTitle: El Niño/La Niña and Climate Variability
topics: El Niño: weakened trade winds, warm water moves east, drought in Australia/Indonesia
La Niña: strengthened trade winds, opposite effects of El Niño
ENSO impacts on global precipitation patterns
lessons.examTip: Confusing which region experiences drought vs. flooding — El Niño brings drought to western Pacific (Australia) and flooding to South America's west coast; AP tests specific regional effects

lessons.lessonTitle: Water Systems — Hydrological Cycle and Freshwater
topics: Hydrological cycle: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff, infiltration
Aquifers: confined vs. unconfined; groundwater depletion
Watershed concept: all water draining to a single outlet
lessons.examTip: Ignoring groundwater when discussing freshwater — aquifers hold 30x more freshwater than all surface water; AP tests Ogallala Aquifer depletion as a case study

topics: Earthquakes: Richter scale logarithmic nature, P and S waves
Volcanic eruptions: viscosity and silica content predicting explosiveness
Hurricanes: formation conditions (warm water, moisture, low wind shear)
lessons.examTip: Not applying logarithmic scale to earthquake magnitude — a magnitude 7 earthquake releases 31.6× more energy than magnitude 6; AP gives Richter data expecting this relationship

lessons.lessonTitle: Agriculture — Green Revolution and Its Consequences
topics: High-yield variety crops, synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, irrigation
Benefits: food production increase; costs: soil degradation, water use, chemical runoff
Subsistence vs. industrial agriculture tradeoffs
lessons.examTip: Treating the Green Revolution as purely positive — AP FRQ asks for both benefits AND environmental costs; must address nutrient runoff (eutrophication), soil salinization from irrigation

topics: Wind and water erosion: rates accelerated by tillage and removal of cover
Salinization from irrigation in arid regions: salt accumulation
Desertification: land degradation at dry-land margins from overuse
lessons.examTip: Confusing salinization (salt buildup from irrigation) with acidification (pH drop from industrial pollution or acid rain) — they have different causes and remediation strategies

topics: Contour plowing, terracing, windbreaks: physical erosion control
Cover crops, crop rotation, no-till: biological and chemical soil conservation
Integrated pest management (IPM): minimizing pesticide use
lessons.examTip: Listing conservation practices without explaining mechanisms — AP asks WHY contour plowing reduces erosion (water follows contour lines, slowing runoff rather than channeling downhill)

lessons.lessonTitle: Forestry — Logging Methods and Their Impacts
topics: Clear-cutting vs. selective cutting: extent of disturbance and recovery
Old-growth vs. second-growth forests: biodiversity and carbon storage differences
Deforestation drivers: agriculture, logging, urbanization
lessons.examTip: Treating selective cutting as environmentally neutral — still causes soil compaction, erosion, edge effects, and fragmentation; AP asks you to compare specific environmental impacts of each method

topics: Surface mining (strip, open-pit) vs. subsurface mining — impact comparison
Acid mine drainage: iron sulfide oxidation producing sulfuric acid
Reclamation requirements: legal standards for post-mining restoration
lessons.examTip: Describing mining impacts generally — AP expects specific chemistry: acid mine drainage involves FeS₂ + O₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ + Fe(OH)₃; must name the process and product

topics: Overfishing indicators: declining catch per unit effort, smaller fish
Bycatch: non-target species in commercial fishing nets
Aquaculture benefits and problems: disease, escaped species, nutrient pollution
lessons.examTip: Treating aquaculture as a sustainable solution without caveats — AP FRQ asks for problems with aquaculture (water pollution from waste, disease spread, escaped fish competing with wild stocks)

topics: Urban heat island effect: dark surfaces, reduced vegetation
Impervious surfaces: increased stormwater runoff and reduced groundwater recharge
Smart growth principles: density, transit, green space
lessons.examTip: Explaining urban heat islands only by human heat generation — dark surfaces absorbing more radiation and evapotranspiration loss (no vegetation) are the main mechanisms; human waste heat is secondary

lessons.lessonTitle: Water Use, Diversion, and Irrigation Issues
topics: Drip vs. flood irrigation: efficiency comparison
Aral Sea case study: diversion leading to ecosystem collapse
Water rights law: prior appropriation vs. riparian rights
lessons.examTip: Not quantifying water use differences — drip irrigation uses 30-50% less water than flood; AP gives efficiency data and asks to calculate water savings or evaluate policy options

lessons.lessonTitle: Fossil Fuels — Formation, Extraction, Environmental Costs
topics: Coal, oil, natural gas: relative carbon content and emissions per unit energy
Extraction: surface mining, fracking, deep-sea drilling — environmental risks of each
EROI (Energy Return on Energy Investment) declining for fossil fuels
lessons.examTip: Ranking fossil fuels only by CO₂ without considering other pollutants — coal produces most CO₂ AND SO₂/NOx/particulates; natural gas burns cleaner but has methane leakage issues

lessons.lessonTitle: Nuclear Energy — Fission, Waste, and Risk
topics: Fission chain reaction: U-235 splits releasing neutrons and energy
Radioactive waste: half-life and long-term storage challenges
Chernobyl/Fukushima: what went wrong and why containment matters
lessons.examTip: Treating nuclear as either zero-risk or too dangerous without nuance — AP FRQ asks for specific advantages (no CO₂ emissions, high energy density) AND disadvantages (waste storage, accident risk)

lessons.lessonTitle: Solar Energy — Photovoltaic and Passive Systems
topics: PV cells: semiconductor converting photons to electrons
Passive solar design: orientation, thermal mass, glazing
Intermittency problem and storage solutions
lessons.examTip: Ignoring lifecycle environmental costs of solar — manufacturing solar panels requires mining rare earth elements and produces toxic waste; AP tests full lifecycle analysis

topics: Wind: capacity factor (~30%), bird/bat mortality, visual impact
Hydroelectric: reliable but habitat disruption, altered sediment flow
Geothermal: limited to tectonically active regions, H₂S emissions
lessons.examTip: Treating all renewables as equally applicable everywhere — hydroelectric requires significant elevation drop and water flow; geothermal requires volcanic activity; AP tests location-specific feasibility

topics: First generation (food crops) vs. second generation (cellulosic) biofuels
Net energy calculation: EROI for corn ethanol is near 1
Land use conflicts: food vs. fuel vs. forest
lessons.examTip: Assuming biofuels are carbon-neutral — only if regrowth absorbs all CO₂ emitted; corn ethanol lifecycle often produces more GHG than gasoline when land use change is included

topics: First law (quantity) vs. second law (quality) efficiency losses
Cogeneration (CHP): using waste heat to increase overall efficiency
Building energy use: insulation, HVAC, lighting efficiency improvements
lessons.examTip: Confusing efficiency with conservation — efficiency means getting more output per unit energy input; conservation means using less total energy; AP asks for both strategies

lessons.lessonTitle: The Energy Mix — Global and US Patterns
topics: Percentage contributions of fossil fuels, nuclear, renewables globally and in US
Electricity grid vs. transportation sector energy sources
Energy security and geopolitical implications of fossil fuel dependence
lessons.examTip: Giving outdated energy mix percentages — AP provides current data tables; must read the given data rather than relying on memorized percentages from different years

lessons.lessonTitle: Energy Policy — Economics, Subsidies, and Incentives
topics: Carbon tax vs. cap-and-trade: mechanisms and tradeoffs
Fossil fuel subsidies vs. renewable energy incentives
Cost-benefit analysis of energy transition
lessons.examTip: Describing policy without mechanism — AP FRQ asks HOW a carbon tax reduces emissions (raises price → reduces demand/shifts to alternatives), not just that it does

topics: Primary: emitted directly (SO₂, NOx, CO, particulates, VOCs)
Secondary: formed in atmosphere (ozone, PAN, H₂SO₄, HNO₃)
EPA six criteria pollutants and their health effects
lessons.examTip: Confusing ground-level ozone (bad, tropospheric pollutant) with stratospheric ozone (good, UV shield) — AP explicitly tests this distinction; the same molecule has opposite effects at different altitudes

topics: NOx + VOCs + sunlight → ozone + PAN (photochemical smog)
Temperature inversion trapping pollutants near surface
Los Angeles conditions: cars + sunlight + topography creating smog
lessons.examTip: Confusing photochemical smog (ozone-based, sunny cities) with industrial/London smog (sulfurous, foggy, cold) — different chemistry, different conditions, different health effects

lessons.lessonTitle: Acid Deposition — Chemistry and Ecological Damage
topics: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ → H₂SO₄; NOx + H₂O → HNO₃
pH effects on aquatic ecosystems: aluminum mobilization at pH < 5
Long-range transport: acid rain affecting regions far from sources
lessons.examTip: Treating acid rain as only a local problem — emissions in Ohio create acid rain in New England due to prevailing westerly winds; AP tests transboundary pollution and international policy

topics: CFC catalytic destruction: Cl + O₃ → ClO + O₂; ClO + O → Cl + O₂ (Cl regenerated)
Antarctic ozone hole: polar stratospheric clouds concentrating Cl
Montreal Protocol as policy success story
lessons.examTip: Saying CFCs 'destroy' ozone as a one-time reaction — each Cl atom catalytically destroys ~100,000 ozone molecules before being removed; the catalytic cycle is the critical AP concept

topics: Radon: natural radioactive gas from uranium decay, lung cancer risk
VOCs from building materials and cleaning products
Developing world indoor air pollution from biomass combustion
lessons.examTip: Overlooking indoor air quality as an AP topic — AP specifically tests radon (enter through foundation cracks, accumulates in basements) and its mechanism of harm (alpha particle emission in lungs)

lessons.lessonTitle: The Clean Air Act and Pollution Reduction
topics: NAAQS standards for six criteria pollutants
Best available control technology (BACT) requirements
Cap-and-trade for SO₂ under 1990 CAA Amendments
lessons.examTip: Treating regulation as binary (yes/no) — AP tests HOW regulations work; cap-and-trade sets total emissions cap, issues permits, allows trading so cheapest reductions happen first

topics: Noise pollution effects on wildlife: disrupted communication, navigation, reproduction
Light pollution: disrupted circadian rhythms, sea turtle disorientation
Solutions: shielding lights, reducing unnecessary illumination
lessons.examTip: Treating noise/light pollution as trivial AP topics — they appear in FRQ expecting mechanistic explanations; sea turtles navigate by moon over ocean, artificial lights cause disorientation

lessons.lessonTitle: Climate Change and Atmospheric Pollution Linkages
topics: Black carbon (soot) both absorbs radiation AND causes health problems
Ozone as both pollutant (troposphere) and greenhouse gas
Co-benefits of pollution reduction: improving air quality AND reducing warming
lessons.examTip: Separating air pollution from climate policy — methane reduction prevents climate change AND reduces ground-level ozone; AP tests these co-benefits

lessons.lessonTitle: Water Pollution — Point vs. Nonpoint Sources
topics: Point source: specific location (pipe, drain) — easier to regulate
Nonpoint source: diffuse (agricultural runoff, urban stormwater) — harder to control
Clean Water Act: discharge permits for point sources
lessons.examTip: Applying point source regulations to nonpoint problems — a farmer's field has no single discharge point; AP tests why nonpoint source pollution is harder to regulate and what strategies address it

topics: Nitrogen and phosphorus runoff → algal bloom → decomposition → oxygen depletion
Hypoxic dead zones: Gulf of Mexico as primary AP case study
Limiting nutrient concept: adding phosphorus to freshwater triggers growth
lessons.examTip: Confusing which nutrient limits which system — phosphorus usually limits freshwater systems; nitrogen usually limits marine/coastal systems; AP asks about the specific system in the scenario

topics: Biomagnification: concentration increases at higher trophic levels
PCBs, DDT, mercury: fat-soluble or non-metabolizable, concentrate in fatty tissue
Bioaccumulation in individual organisms vs. biomagnification across food web
lessons.examTip: Confusing bioaccumulation (within one organism over time) with biomagnification (increasing concentration across trophic levels) — AP explicitly distinguishes these two processes
