topics: Municipal solid waste composition: food (most by weight), paper, plastics
Landfill anatomy: liner, leachate collection, methane capture
Waste hierarchy: reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose
lessons.examTip: Treating recycling as the top priority — the waste hierarchy puts REDUCTION first; AP FRQ asks to rank strategies and explain why source reduction is more effective than recycling

topics: RCRA characterizing hazardous waste: ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity, toxicity
Superfund (CERCLA): polluter-pays principle, National Priorities List
Brownfields: contaminated industrial sites and redevelopment challenges
lessons.examTip: Assuming all industrial waste is regulated the same — RCRA governs current hazardous waste; CERCLA (Superfund) addresses historical abandoned sites; AP tests which law applies to which scenario

topics: Physical effects: coating seabirds, smothering benthic organisms
Chemical toxicity: PAH compounds affecting fish reproduction
Bioremediation: hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria as cleanup tool
lessons.examTip: Focusing only on visible oil effects — long-term chronic effects from PAH compounds and dispersant toxicity persist for decades; AP tests both acute and long-term impacts of spills

topics: Heavy metal contamination: lead, arsenic, cadmium from mining/industry
Phytoremediation: plants (hyperaccumulators) extracting metals from soil
In-situ vs. ex-situ remediation tradeoffs
lessons.examTip: Describing phytoremediation without mechanism — plants must be harvested AND disposed of properly to actually remove metals from the site; if left to decompose, metals return to soil

topics: Disproportionate pollution exposure in low-income and minority communities
Locally unwanted land uses (LULUs) and siting decisions
EJ movement and EPA environmental justice policies
lessons.examTip: Treating environmental justice as separate from environmental science — AP FRQ integrates EJ with pollution topics; must connect which communities bear the greatest burden from specific pollutants

lessons.lessonTitle: The Greenhouse Effect and Climate Science
topics: Mechanism: shortwave in, longwave absorbed by GHGs, re-radiated toward Earth
CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, H₂O as greenhouse gases — relative warming potential
Evidence: ice cores, temperature records, sea level rise, Arctic sea ice
lessons.examTip: Explaining climate change vaguely — AP FRQ requires molecular mechanism: greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared radiation because their bonds vibrate at IR frequencies

topics: Positive feedback: ice-albedo, water vapor amplification, permafrost methane
Negative feedback: blackbody radiation, cloud albedo effects
Tipping points: threshold beyond which feedbacks become self-sustaining
lessons.examTip: Calling all climate feedbacks positive (amplifying) — negative feedbacks also exist; AP tests that more outgoing radiation as temperature rises is a stabilizing (negative) feedback

lessons.lessonTitle: Climate Change Impacts — Ecological and Human
topics: Phenological shifts: earlier spring events disrupting predator-prey timing
Sea level rise: thermal expansion + ice melt; coastal flooding
Coral bleaching: thermal stress expelling zooxanthellae
lessons.examTip: Listing impacts without connecting to mechanism — coral bleaching: warmer water stresses zooxanthellae (symbiotic algae), coral expels them (bleaches), loses food source and may die if prolonged

topics: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻: chemistry of acidification
pH drop dissolving calcium carbonate shells of marine organisms
Pteropods, oysters, corals as most vulnerable organisms
lessons.examTip: Confusing ocean acidification with general ocean pollution — caused specifically by dissolved CO₂ from atmosphere; pH has dropped from 8.2 to 8.1 (30% more acidic); AP tests the chemistry

topics: Renewable energy transition, electrification of transportation
Carbon capture and storage (CCS): geological sequestration
Carbon offsets: reforestation, soil carbon, methane capture from landfills
lessons.examTip: Treating mitigation as only energy-sector solutions — AP tests agriculture (methane, N₂O from fertilizer), land use change, and waste sector contributions to total GHG inventory

lessons.lessonTitle: Adaptation Strategies — Living With Climate Change
topics: Sea walls, managed retreat, living shorelines for coastal flooding
Heat-resilient crops and shifting agricultural zones
Early warning systems and disaster preparedness
lessons.examTip: Confusing mitigation (preventing emissions) with adaptation (adjusting to changes) — AP FRQ distinguishes and asks which strategy addresses a specific scenario

lessons.lessonTitle: International Climate Policy — UNFCCC, Paris Agreement
topics: Paris Agreement: NDCs, 1.5°C and 2°C targets, review mechanism
Common but differentiated responsibilities: developed vs. developing nations
Carbon markets and international emissions trading
lessons.examTip: Treating the Paris Agreement as legally binding — it's a voluntary pledge system (NDCs); lack of enforcement mechanism is a key weakness; AP asks about both structure and limitations

lessons.lessonTitle: Ozone Recovery and Environmental Policy Lessons
topics: Montreal Protocol: phaseout of CFCs leading to measurable ozone recovery
Using Montreal Protocol as model for climate policy discussions
Substitutes for CFCs: HCFCs → HFCs (some still potent GHGs)
lessons.examTip: Treating ozone recovery as complete — the ozone hole still forms annually but is smaller than peak; full recovery projected for 2060s; AP tests that HFC replacements became a new climate problem

lessons.lessonTitle: Position, Velocity, and Acceleration — Vectors vs. Scalars
topics: Displacement vs. distance; velocity vs. speed — vector vs. scalar distinction
Instantaneous vs. average velocity from position-time graphs
Acceleration as rate of change of velocity, not speed
lessons.examTip: Confusing negative velocity with deceleration — an object with negative velocity and negative acceleration is speeding up; AP explicitly tests the sign relationship

topics: Four kinematic equations and which variable each solves for
Identifying known and unknown variables before choosing equation
Free fall as special case: a = -g = -9.8 m/s²
lessons.examTip: Using kinematic equations when acceleration is not constant — equations only apply to CONSTANT acceleration; for variable acceleration must use graphs or calculus

topics: Slope of x-t graph = velocity; slope of v-t graph = acceleration
Area under v-t graph = displacement
Interpreting curved vs. straight segments on each graph type
lessons.examTip: Confusing area under x-t graph (not meaningful) with area under v-t graph (displacement) — AP experiments regularly use motion sensor graphs requiring correct graph interpretation

topics: Horizontal: constant velocity; vertical: constant acceleration (g)
Independence of horizontal and vertical motion
Range, maximum height, and time of flight calculations
lessons.examTip: Mixing horizontal and vertical components — horizontal velocity never changes in projectile motion (no air resistance); using g in horizontal equations is the most common AP error

topics: Velocity addition: v_AB = v_AC + v_CB
Choosing reference frames to simplify problems
Relative velocity in 2D: perpendicular and parallel components
lessons.examTip: Forgetting that reference frame choice is arbitrary — AP riverboat/airplane problems require vector addition; students often add magnitudes instead of doing vector math

topics: Period, frequency, angular velocity relationship: ω = 2π/T
Centripetal acceleration: ac = v²/r = ω²r
Linear vs. angular velocity for different points on a rotating object
lessons.examTip: Thinking centripetal acceleration points in the direction of motion — centripetal acceleration always points toward the center (inward), perpendicular to velocity

topics: Angular position, angular velocity, angular acceleration analogs to linear
Rotational kinematic equations (same structure as linear)
Relating linear and angular quantities: v = ωr, a_tangential = αr
lessons.examTip: Using linear kinematic equations for rotating objects — must use rotational equations with θ, ω, α; or use v=ωr to convert, but mixing the two systems creates errors

lessons.lessonTitle: Calculus Connections — Derivatives and Integrals in Motion
topics: Velocity as derivative of position; acceleration as derivative of velocity
Position as integral of velocity; velocity as integral of acceleration
Using area under graphs as integration (non-calculus approach)
lessons.examTip: Treating AP Physics 1 as requiring calculus — it doesn't; all calculus concepts are tested graphically; slope = derivative, area = integral; must interpret graphs, not compute derivatives

lessons.lessonTitle: Newton's First and Third Laws — The Underestimated Laws
topics: Inertia: objects maintain state without net force
Newton's 3rd Law pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, different objects
Identifying true Newton's 3rd Law pairs vs. different forces on same object
lessons.examTip: Treating Newton's 3rd Law pairs as canceling — they act on DIFFERENT objects so they never cancel; a horse-cart tension and cart-horse tension are 3rd law pairs but don't affect net force on either

lessons.lessonTitle: Free Body Diagrams and Newton's Second Law
topics: Identifying all forces: gravity, normal, tension, friction, applied
ΣF = ma applied to x and y components separately
Choosing coordinate system aligned with acceleration direction
lessons.examTip: Including velocity or acceleration as forces in FBDs — FBDs show only forces (interactions with other objects), never velocity vectors or acceleration arrows as forces

lessons.lessonTitle: Friction — Static, Kinetic, and Its Limits
topics: Static friction: variable, up to maximum fs,max = μsN
Kinetic friction: constant once sliding, fk = μkN < fs,max
Friction direction always opposing relative motion or tendency of motion
lessons.examTip: Using μN for static friction in all situations — static friction only equals μsN at the moment of impending slip; before that, it's whatever value is needed to prevent motion

topics: Centripetal force is the NET inward force — not a separate force
Banking, friction, gravity, tension providing centripetal force in different contexts
Critical speed at the top of a loop: N = 0 minimum condition
lessons.examTip: Drawing centripetal force as a separate arrow on the FBD — it's the result of the NET force inward, not an additional force; AP deducts for adding 'centripetal force' as a separate FBD element

topics: F = Gm₁m₂/r²: force proportional to product of masses, inverse square with distance
Orbital velocity from setting gravitational force equal to centripetal
Why g = 9.8 m/s² at Earth's surface but less at altitude
lessons.examTip: Confusing orbital speed with escape speed — orbital speed keeps an object in circular orbit; escape speed (√2 times orbital) breaks the gravitational bond entirely

topics: F = -kx: restoring force proportional to displacement, opposes displacement
Elastic potential energy: PE = ½kx²
Spring combinations: series vs. parallel effective spring constants
lessons.examTip: Forgetting the negative sign in Hooke's Law means restoring — the spring force always opposes displacement direction; AP gives displacement direction and asks for force direction

topics: Torque = rFsinθ: only the perpendicular component of force matters
Conditions for rotational equilibrium: Στ = 0
Lever arm: perpendicular distance from pivot to force line of action
lessons.examTip: Using the total distance to force rather than perpendicular distance (lever arm) — torque uses the perpendicular component; for angled forces must multiply by sinθ

topics: Treating connected objects as a system vs. analyzing each separately
Tension is the same throughout a massless string
Pulley problems: direction of acceleration from net force on system
lessons.examTip: Drawing separate FBDs then getting tension wrong — in an Atwood machine, the tension in the rope is the SAME on both sides (massless rope); treating them as different is the #1 system error

lessons.lessonTitle: Work — The Physics Definition vs. Everyday Meaning
topics: W = Fd cosθ: only force component parallel to displacement does work
Work done by friction: always negative (opposes displacement)
Net work = change in kinetic energy (work-energy theorem)
lessons.examTip: Calculating work using the full force magnitude when force is angled — must use Fcosθ (component along displacement); holding a heavy box while walking does zero work

topics: KE = ½mv²; GPE = mgh; spring PE = ½kx²
Reference level for GPE is arbitrary — only changes in PE matter
Conservative vs. non-conservative forces and energy path dependence
lessons.examTip: Choosing an inconvenient zero-PE reference and getting confused — AP rewards choosing reference at the lowest point or starting point to simplify numbers

lessons.lessonTitle: Conservation of Energy — When and How to Apply
topics: Mechanical energy conserved only when no non-conservative forces do work
Energy bar charts as visual bookkeeping tools
When to use energy conservation vs. kinematics: energy is usually faster
lessons.examTip: Applying conservation of mechanical energy when friction is present — friction converts mechanical to thermal energy; total energy still conserved, but mechanical energy is not

topics: P = W/t = Fv: power as rate of doing work or instantaneous force × velocity
Distinguishing high power (fast work) from high energy (lots of work total)
Efficiency = useful power output / total power input
lessons.examTip: Confusing total work done with power — two motors that do the same work have the same energy output; the one that does it faster has more power; AP tests this distinction with data

lessons.lessonTitle: The Work-Energy Theorem — Net Work Equals ΔKE
topics: Wnet = ΔKE regardless of the path taken
Applying work-energy theorem when multiple forces act
Connecting to Newton's laws: both describe the same physics differently
lessons.examTip: Applying work-energy theorem using only one force when multiple exist — must sum all work done by all forces to get net work; or calculate net force × displacement

topics: Total energy constant in SHM: PE + KE = constant
Maximum KE at equilibrium; maximum PE at amplitude
Period of spring-mass: T = 2π√(m/k); independent of amplitude
lessons.examTip: Thinking larger amplitude means higher frequency in SHM — amplitude does NOT affect period for ideal springs or pendulums; AP tests this counterintuitive result

lessons.lessonTitle: Rotational Kinetic Energy and Moment of Inertia
topics: KE_rot = ½Iω²: analog of translational KE
Moment of inertia depends on both mass AND distribution: I = Σmr²
Rolling without slipping: both translational and rotational KE
lessons.examTip: Forgetting rotational KE when calculating total energy for rolling objects — a rolling ball has both ½mv² and ½Iω²; using only ½mv² gives the wrong speed after rolling down a ramp

lessons.lessonTitle: Energy Methods vs. Force Methods — Choosing the Right Tool
topics: When energy methods are easier: curved paths, variable forces
When force methods are needed: finding forces at specific points
Combining methods: use energy to find speed, then Newton's 2nd for force
lessons.examTip: Always defaulting to Newton's laws — many AP problems are much easier with energy; a block released from height h, what speed at bottom? Energy is 3 steps; F=ma with kinematics is 8 steps

units.unitTitle: Systems of Particles and Linear Momentum

topics: p = mv (vector); impulse J = FΔt = Δp
Impulse-momentum theorem connecting force, time, and momentum change
Impulse from area under F-t graph
lessons.examTip: Confusing impulse (change in momentum) with force — a large force applied briefly can equal a small force applied for longer; AP gives F-t graphs and asks for Δp (area)

lessons.lessonTitle: Conservation of Momentum — When It Applies
topics: Momentum conserved when net external force = 0
Isolated systems in collisions (even when energy is not conserved)
Center of mass velocity constant when no external forces act
lessons.examTip: Applying momentum conservation when external forces are present — friction or gravity can change total momentum; must confirm the system is isolated or treat the impulse carefully

topics: Elastic: both momentum AND kinetic energy conserved
Perfectly inelastic: maximum KE loss, objects stick together
Coefficient of restitution: relative speed after / before collision
lessons.examTip: Assuming all collisions conserve kinetic energy — only elastic collisions do; in perfectly inelastic collisions, some KE converts to thermal/deformation energy; AP asks to prove elasticity using data

topics: Momentum components conserved independently in x and y
Glancing collisions: solving two equations (px and py conservation)
Finding angle of deflection from vector components
lessons.examTip: Adding momentum magnitudes instead of using vector components — momentum is a vector; x and y components must be conserved separately; can't add speeds directly

lessons.lessonTitle: Center of Mass — Location and Motion
topics: x_cm = Σm_i x_i / Σm_i for discrete masses
Center of mass velocity: v_cm = Σm_i v_i / Σm_i
System center of mass motion determined by external forces only
lessons.examTip: Treating center of mass as always between objects — for objects of different masses, CM is closer to the heavier object; AP gives masses and positions and expects CM calculation

topics: L = Iω = mvr (for point mass in circular orbit)
Angular momentum conserved when net external torque = 0
Spinning skater: reducing r increases ω to conserve L
lessons.examTip: Confusing angular momentum conservation with energy conservation — when a skater pulls arms in, KE INCREASES (because I decreases and ω increases more); angular momentum is conserved, not energy

topics: Internal forces cause momentum change of parts but not the system
Momentum of system conserved even as KE increases
Recoil problems: rifle/bullet, rocket propulsion
lessons.examTip: Thinking explosions must violate momentum conservation — they don't; if system starts at rest, total momentum remains zero (rifle recoils backward when bullet goes forward)

lessons.lessonTitle: Rocket Propulsion and Varying Mass Systems
topics: Thrust from ejecting mass at high velocity — momentum change per time
Why rockets work in vacuum (no air to push against)
Staging: dropping empty fuel tanks to reduce inert mass
lessons.examTip: Thinking rockets push against air — they push against ejected exhaust gas; Newton's 3rd law pairs are rocket and exhaust, not rocket and air; works in space with no atmosphere

lessons.lessonTitle: Rotational Dynamics — Torque and Angular Acceleration
topics: Στ = Iα: rotational analog of Newton's second law
Net torque about any pivot determines angular acceleration
Sign convention: counterclockwise positive (usually)
lessons.examTip: Not specifying the pivot point when calculating torque — the same force has different torques about different pivots; AP always specifies or asks you to choose a convenient pivot

lessons.lessonTitle: Moment of Inertia — Why Mass Distribution Matters
topics: I = Σmr² for point masses; table formulas for solid objects
Parallel axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md²
Larger I means more torque needed for same angular acceleration
lessons.examTip: Using I = mr² for any rotating object — that formula only works for point masses or hollow rings; solid disk I = ½mr², solid sphere = 2/5mr²; AP provides formulas but you must apply the right one

topics: Constraint: v_cm = ωr, a_cm = αr for rolling without slipping
Static friction acts on rolling objects (enables rolling, does no work)
Total KE = ½mv² + ½Iω² for rolling objects
lessons.examTip: Applying kinetic friction to a rolling object — if rolling without slipping, static friction acts (no energy loss); kinetic friction only when slipping occurs

topics: L = Iω for rotating extended objects
Torque as rate of change of angular momentum: τ = dL/dt
Angular impulse: τΔt = ΔL
lessons.examTip: Applying point-mass angular momentum (L=mvr) to extended rotating objects — a disk has L=Iω; the mvr formula only applies to point masses or particles in circular orbits

lessons.lessonTitle: Static Equilibrium — Torques and Forces Balanced
topics: Two conditions: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0
Choosing pivot to eliminate unknowns from torque equation
Center of gravity vs. center of mass (same for uniform g)
lessons.examTip: Not using torque condition when forces are balanced — knowing ΣF=0 doesn't tell you where the object is supported; need Στ=0 to find the specific forces or positions

topics: Precession: torque perpendicular to L causes direction change of L
Gyroscopic stability: fast-spinning objects resist orientation change
Torque and angular momentum as vectors (right-hand rule)
lessons.examTip: Treating precession as simple rotation — precession occurs when torque is perpendicular to angular momentum; the axis of rotation itself rotates; AP may give a qualitative question about direction

topics: Work by torque: W = τΔθ (analog of W = Fd)
Power from rotation: P = τω
Energy stored in rotating flywheel: KE = ½Iω²
lessons.examTip: Forgetting rotational KE in energy conservation problems — a rotating pulley has kinetic energy; treating it as massless when it has significant mass gives wrong answers

topics: Objects can simultaneously translate and rotate
Newton's 2nd law for translation: ΣF = ma_cm
Newton's 2nd law for rotation about CM: Στ_cm = I_cm α
lessons.examTip: Using only the translational equation for a rolling object — must apply both F=ma AND τ=Iα simultaneously; friction provides the torque for rolling AND affects the translational acceleration

lessons.lessonTitle: Simple Harmonic Motion — Defining the Pattern
topics: SHM conditions: restoring force proportional to displacement (F = -kx)
x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ): amplitude, angular frequency, phase
Period, frequency, and angular frequency relationships
lessons.examTip: Assuming all oscillation is SHM — SHM requires F ∝ -x; large-angle pendulums and nonlinear springs don't qualify; AP tests whether conditions for SHM are met

topics: Spring: T = 2π√(m/k) — depends on mass and spring constant, not amplitude
Simple pendulum: T = 2π√(L/g) — depends on length and g, not mass or amplitude
Why pendulum on moon has longer period: lower g
lessons.examTip: Thinking period depends on amplitude — for ideal SHM (small angle for pendulum), amplitude does NOT affect period; AP exploits this misconception regularly

lessons.lessonTitle: Energy in SHM — Constant Total, Exchanged Continuously
topics: PE = ½kx²; KE = ½mv²; PE + KE = ½kA² (constant)
Maximum velocity at x=0; maximum acceleration at x=±A
Phase relationship: velocity leads position by 90°
lessons.examTip: Not recognizing that maximum acceleration occurs at maximum displacement — a in SHM is proportional to -x; at the amplitude (max x), acceleration is maximum, not zero

topics: Underdamping, critical damping, overdamping — different decay rates
Resonance: driving frequency matching natural frequency → amplitude grows
Real oscillators: energy lost to friction/air resistance each cycle
lessons.examTip: Thinking resonance is always harmful — AP asks about beneficial resonance (musical instruments, MRI) as well as destructive resonance (bridge vibration, earthquake damage)

lessons.lessonTitle: Waves From Oscillators — Connecting SHM to Wave Motion
topics: Wave as energy transport without matter transport
Transverse vs. longitudinal waves: particle motion relative to propagation
Wave parameters: wavelength, frequency, speed, period — relationships
lessons.examTip: Confusing particle motion with wave motion — particles in a transverse wave move perpendicular to wave travel; the particles don't travel with the wave

topics: v = fλ: fundamental wave equation
Wave speed determined by medium, not frequency
Changing frequency changes wavelength but not speed in same medium
lessons.examTip: Thinking higher frequency makes waves travel faster — speed is a property of the medium; higher frequency → shorter wavelength at the SAME speed; applies to sound, light, waves on strings

topics: Constructive interference: path difference = nλ; destructive: (n+½)λ
Standing waves: nodes and antinodes; fundamental frequency and harmonics
Resonance in strings and pipes: which end is node or antinode
lessons.examTip: Confusing open and closed pipe harmonics — closed pipe has node at closed end and only odd harmonics; open pipe has antinodes at both ends and all harmonics; AP gives pipe type and asks for harmonic frequencies

topics: Doppler effect: source and observer moving relative to each other changes observed frequency
f_observed increases when source approaches; decreases when receding
Applications: radar, medical ultrasound, redshift in astronomy
lessons.examTip: Applying Doppler symmetrically to source and observer motion — moving source compresses/expands wavelength; moving observer changes rate of wave encounters; they give different mathematical results

topics: F = Gm₁m₂/r²: inverse square law, both masses matter
Gravitational field g = GM/r²: at Earth's surface vs. at altitude
Shell theorem: uniform sphere attracts external objects as if mass at center
lessons.examTip: Using g = 9.8 m/s² at altitudes other than Earth's surface — g decreases with altitude as 1/r²; AP gives altitude and expects you to calculate the new g

topics: Setting gravitational force = centripetal force to find orbital speed
Orbital period from circumference / orbital speed
Higher orbits: slower speed, longer period, higher total energy
lessons.examTip: Thinking higher orbit means faster speed — higher orbit means SLOWER orbital speed (Fg is weaker, needs less centripetal force); v = √(GM/r) decreases with increasing r

topics: Kepler's 1st: orbits are ellipses with sun at one focus
Kepler's 2nd: equal areas in equal times — faster near perihelion
Kepler's 3rd: T² ∝ r³ (or semi-major axis cubed)
lessons.examTip: Applying T²=kr³ with wrong r — for elliptical orbits, r is the SEMI-MAJOR AXIS, not the closest or farthest approach distance; AP gives an elliptical orbit and asks for period

lessons.lessonTitle: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
topics: U = -GMm/r (negative, zero at infinity, most negative at surface)
Escape velocity: KE + PE = 0 at infinity → v = √(2GM/r)
Binding energy: energy required to escape to infinity from orbit
lessons.examTip: Using U = mgh for large distances from Earth — that formula only works near the surface; the exact formula U = -GMm/r applies for large distances where g varies

topics: Tidal force from differential gravity across extended object
Why Moon causes ocean bulge on both sides of Earth
Roche limit: tidal forces exceeding internal gravity shred satellites
lessons.examTip: Thinking ocean tidal bulge occurs only on Moon-facing side — Earth's far side also has a bulge because the Moon pulls the Earth more than the far ocean (differential acceleration)

topics: Total mechanical energy E = KE + U = -GMm/(2r) for circular orbit
Energy increases (less negative) for higher orbits despite slower speed
Adding energy to a satellite causes it to move to a higher, slower orbit
lessons.examTip: Confusing that adding energy to an orbit makes it faster — adding energy increases orbital radius; at the new higher orbit, the satellite is actually slower (v ∝ 1/√r)

topics: Gravitational field as vector field — direction toward mass
Superposition: add field vectors from multiple masses
Field inside spherical shell is zero; grows linearly inside solid sphere
lessons.examTip: Not applying shell theorem inside a sphere — inside a solid sphere, only the mass at smaller radius contributes to g; at the center, g=0; AP tests this radial variation

lessons.lessonTitle: Black Holes and General Relativity Concepts
topics: Schwarzschild radius: event horizon where escape velocity = c
Gravitational time dilation: clocks run slower in stronger gravitational fields
GPS satellites require GR corrections to maintain accuracy
lessons.examTip: Treating general relativity as optional AP content — AP Physics 1 requires conceptual understanding of gravitational time dilation and spacetime curvature; no mathematical GR is required

lessons.lessonTitle: Pressure in Fluids — Depth and Pascal's Law
topics: P = P₀ + ρgh: pressure increases linearly with depth
Pascal's Law: pressure applied to enclosed fluid transmitted equally
Hydraulic systems: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ force multiplication
lessons.examTip: Treating pressure as force — pressure is force per unit area; the same pressure can exert different forces on different areas; AP gives areas and asks for forces or vice versa

topics: Buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced (ρ_fluid × V_submerged × g)
Floating condition: weight = buoyant force → fraction submerged = ρ_object/ρ_fluid
Apparent weight: scale reads W_actual - F_buoyant
lessons.examTip: Using the object's volume instead of submerged volume — for partially submerged objects, buoyancy uses V_submerged only; for fully submerged objects they're equal

lessons.lessonTitle: Fluid Flow — Continuity and Bernoulli's Equation
topics: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ (for incompressible fluid)
Bernoulli's equation: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant along streamline
Venturi effect: narrowing increases velocity, decreases pressure
lessons.examTip: Applying Bernoulli without checking assumptions — Bernoulli requires steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow along a streamline; AP asks to identify when it applies or doesn't

topics: Viscosity as resistance to flow — molecular-level explanation
Poiseuille's Law: flow rate ∝ r⁴/length (radius dominates)
Reynolds number: predicting laminar vs. turbulent flow
lessons.examTip: Applying Bernoulli to viscous flow — Bernoulli ignores viscosity; real pipe flow loses pressure to viscous drag; AP asks to identify limitations of the ideal model

topics: Surface tension: cohesive forces at liquid surface minimizing area
Capillary action: adhesion to walls competing with gravity
Contact angle predicting whether liquid spreads or beads
lessons.examTip: Explaining capillary rise only as 'surface tension' without specifying adhesion/cohesion roles — water rises in glass because adhesion to glass > cohesion in water; mercury in glass does the opposite

lessons.lessonTitle: Applications of Fluid Statics — Dams, Blood Pressure, Atmospheres
topics: Gauge pressure vs. absolute pressure
Blood pressure: systolic/diastolic and hydrostatic effects with posture
Atmospheric pressure variation with altitude
lessons.examTip: Confusing gauge pressure (relative to atmosphere) with absolute pressure (total) — a tire gauge reads gauge pressure; blood pressure is gauge pressure above atmospheric; AP specifies which is asked

topics: Heart as pressure pump; circulatory system applying Bernoulli and continuity
Why arterial narrowing (plaque) increases blood velocity and drops pressure
Respiration: pressure gradients driving lung airflow
lessons.examTip: Not connecting physics to biology in context problems — AP Physics 2 regularly embeds physics in biological scenarios; must identify which fluid dynamics principle applies

lessons.lessonTitle: Plasma — The Fourth State of Matter
topics: Plasma as ionized gas behaving differently from neutral gas
Plasma in stars, lightning, and fusion reactors
Magnetic confinement: why plasma requires containment in fusion
lessons.examTip: Treating plasma as just hot gas — plasma's charged particles interact with electromagnetic fields in ways neutral gas doesn't; AP tests why magnetic confinement works

topics: Temperature as average kinetic energy; heat as energy transfer
Zeroth law: thermal equilibrium and temperature measurement
Specific heat capacity: q = mcΔT
lessons.examTip: Treating heat and temperature as the same — a larger mass at lower temperature can contain more thermal energy than a smaller mass at higher temperature; AP tests calorimetry calculations

lessons.lessonTitle: Ideal Gas Law and Kinetic Theory
topics: PV = nRT: what each variable represents and its units
Kinetic theory: pressure from molecular collisions with walls
rms speed: v_rms = √(3kT/m); heavier molecules are slower at same T
lessons.examTip: Using different unit systems in PV=nRT — R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) for SI units; must use Kelvin (not Celsius) for all gas law calculations

topics: Isothermal, isobaric, isochoric, adiabatic processes on P-V diagram
Work = area under P-V curve (positive for expansion)
Internal energy change: ΔU = Q - W (first law of thermodynamics)
lessons.examTip: Getting the sign of work wrong — work done BY the gas is positive when the gas expands (area under P-V curve, volume increases); work done ON the gas is negative for the gas

lessons.lessonTitle: Heat Engines and the Second Law
topics: Heat engine: Q_H absorbed, W done, Q_C rejected; efficiency e = W/Q_H
Carnot efficiency: e_max = 1 - T_C/T_H (temperatures in Kelvin)
Second law: no engine can be 100% efficient; entropy increases
lessons.examTip: Applying Carnot efficiency with Celsius temperatures — must convert to Kelvin; a 'Carnot engine operating between 200°C and 100°C' has e = 1 - 373/473, not 1 - 100/200

lessons.lessonTitle: Entropy and the Direction of Natural Processes
topics: Entropy as measure of disorder/microstates; ΔS = Q/T for reversible process
Second law: entropy of universe never decreases
Irreversibility: why heat flows from hot to cold, not cold to hot
lessons.examTip: Applying second law only to heat — AP tests entropy in all contexts: mixing, expansion of gases, phase changes; any irreversible process increases total entropy

topics: Conduction: P = kA(ΔT)/L; thermal conductivity and insulation
Convection: fluid motion driven by density differences
Radiation: P = εσAT⁴; Stefan-Boltzmann law
lessons.examTip: Treating all heat transfer as equivalent — vacuum prevents conduction and convection but not radiation; the Sun heats Earth by radiation only; AP tests which mechanism applies

topics: Latent heat of fusion and vaporization: Q = mL
Plateau regions on heating curves where temperature doesn't change
Why vaporization requires more energy than fusion
lessons.examTip: Forgetting latent heat calculations when crossing phase boundaries — AP heating/cooling curve problems require recognizing when temperature is constant (phase change) vs. rising (same phase)

lessons.lessonTitle: Refrigerators, Heat Pumps, and Real Cycles
topics: Refrigerator: work input moves heat from cold to hot reservoir
Coefficient of performance: COP = Q_C/W for refrigerator
Real vs. Carnot cycles: irreversibilities reduce efficiency
lessons.examTip: Confusing refrigerator COP with engine efficiency — COP can be greater than 1 (move more heat than work input); efficiency is always less than 1 (get less work than heat input)

topics: F = kq₁q₂/r²: same form as gravity but can repel
Superposition: vector sum of forces from multiple charges
Electric force vs. gravitational force: relative magnitudes
lessons.examTip: Adding force magnitudes instead of vector components — multiple charges exert forces in different directions; must add as vectors; AP gives charge configurations and expects vector sum

topics: E = F/q = kq/r²: field from point charge
Field lines: density represents magnitude, direction shows force on + charge
Uniform field between parallel plates: E = V/d
lessons.examTip: Confusing field direction with force direction on negative charges — field lines show force on POSITIVE test charges; force on negative charge is opposite to field direction

topics: V = kq/r: scalar potential from point charge
Potential difference: work per unit charge; W = qΔV
Equipotential surfaces: perpendicular to field lines, no work to move along them
lessons.examTip: Confusing potential (scalar) with field (vector) — potential is a scalar and can be added algebraically; field requires vector addition; AP gives both and tests which calculation method applies

topics: Charges on conductor surface only; field inside is zero at equilibrium
Charge concentrates at sharp points (highest surface charge density)
Faraday cage: external field cannot penetrate conducting shell
lessons.examTip: Putting charge inside a conductor — excess charge on conductor always moves to the outer surface at electrostatic equilibrium; the interior has zero field and zero net charge

topics: C = Q/V; C = ε₀A/d for parallel plate capacitor
Energy stored: U = ½QV = ½CV² = Q²/(2C)
Dielectric: increases capacitance by reducing E field between plates
lessons.examTip: Not accounting for what's held constant when dielectric is inserted — if battery stays connected, V is constant and Q increases; if disconnected, Q is constant and V decreases; AP tests both

lessons.lessonTitle: Electric Potential in Uniform and Non-Uniform Fields
topics: E = -dV/dx: field is negative gradient of potential
Equipotential maps and their relationship to field line maps
Potential energy diagrams for charged particles in fields
lessons.examTip: Treating potential like the field — potential is a scalar; the field magnitude is the potential's slope (gradient), not its value; AP gives V vs. position graph and asks for field

topics: Gauss's law: ΦE = Q_enclosed/ε₀
Choosing Gaussian surface to exploit symmetry
Applications: spherical, cylindrical, planar charge distributions
lessons.examTip: Choosing an arbitrary Gaussian surface — must choose surface where E is uniform and perpendicular (or parallel) so the flux integral simplifies to E × A

topics: Dipole moment p = qd: magnitude and direction (negative to positive)
Dipole in uniform field: torque tends to align with field, no net force
Dielectric polarization: aligned dipoles reduce net field inside material
lessons.examTip: Saying a dipole experiences a net force in a uniform field — in a uniform field there's only torque (rotation), not net force; net force requires a non-uniform field

topics: I = ΔQ/Δt: conventional current direction and electron flow direction
V = IR; resistivity ρ and R = ρL/A
Ohmic vs. non-ohmic devices: straight vs. curved I-V graph
lessons.examTip: Confusing conventional current (+ to -) with electron flow (- to +) — AP uses conventional current; when given electron flow, must reverse direction for conventional current

topics: Series: same current, voltages add, R_eq = ΣR
Parallel: same voltage, currents add, 1/R_eq = Σ1/R
Identifying series vs. parallel from circuit diagram
lessons.examTip: Misidentifying parallel vs. series when circuits are drawn non-standardly — parallel means connected between the SAME two nodes (same two endpoints); AP draws circuits in unusual orientations

topics: KCL: sum of currents entering a node = sum leaving (charge conservation)
KVL: sum of voltage changes around any loop = 0 (energy conservation)
Setting up and solving simultaneous equations
lessons.examTip: Getting KVL signs wrong — must be consistent about sign convention: crossing a resistor in the assumed current direction is a voltage drop; crossing a battery from - to + is a voltage gain

lessons.lessonTitle: Power in Circuits — Where Energy Goes
topics: P = IV = I²R = V²/R: three equivalent power expressions
Total power from source = sum of power dissipated in all components
Why parallel circuits draw more current and use more power
lessons.examTip: Using wrong power formula — P = IV always works; P = V²/R when voltage is known; P = I²R when current is known; mixing V and R from different branches gives wrong answers

lessons.lessonTitle: Capacitors in Circuits — Charging and Discharging
topics: RC circuits: exponential charging Q = Q_max(1 - e^(-t/RC))
Time constant τ = RC: 63% charged in one time constant
Fully charged capacitor: current = 0, acts like open circuit
lessons.examTip: Treating a fully charged capacitor as a regular resistor — at steady state, no current flows through capacitor; AP gives an RC circuit and asks for current after a long time (answer: only paths without capacitors carry current)

topics: Terminal voltage: V_terminal = EMF - Ir (drops under load)
Why battery heats up when current drawn: power dissipated in r
Short circuit: R_external → 0, maximum current, minimum terminal voltage
lessons.examTip: Treating battery EMF as terminal voltage — under load, terminal voltage is always less than EMF; AP gives EMF and current to find terminal voltage using V = EMF - Ir

topics: Ammeter: low resistance, in series; voltmeter: high resistance, in parallel
How meter insertion affects the circuit being measured
Wheatstone bridge: null condition for precise resistance measurement
lessons.examTip: Forgetting meters affect measurements — a voltmeter with finite resistance draws some current; an ammeter with nonzero resistance drops some voltage; AP asks how measurements differ from ideal

topics: N-type and P-type doping: extra electrons vs. holes
P-N junction: depletion region and built-in potential barrier
Diode: forward bias conducts, reverse bias blocks
lessons.examTip: Treating semiconductors as conductors or insulators — they're neither; conductivity depends on doping level and temperature; AP tests that current flows through a diode only one way

topics: Magnetic field from moving charges and current-carrying wires
Right-hand rule for B field direction around wire (curl rule)
Magnetic field of a solenoid: uniform inside, weak outside
lessons.examTip: Applying electric field rules to magnetic fields — magnetic field lines form closed loops (no magnetic monopoles); electric field lines start and end on charges

topics: F = qv × B: magnitude qvBsinθ; direction from right-hand rule (or left for electrons)
Circular motion of charges in magnetic field: r = mv/qB
Velocity selector: electric and magnetic forces balanced
lessons.examTip: Using the right-hand rule for negative charges — the right-hand rule gives force direction for positive charges; for electrons (negative), reverse the result; this is tested consistently on AP

topics: F = IL × B: force on wire depends on length, current, and field
Parallel wires attract (currents same direction) or repel (opposite)
Torque on current loop in magnetic field — motor principle
lessons.examTip: Forgetting force direction on antiparallel wires — parallel currents attract; antiparallel currents repel; AP tests this with a diagram where you apply the right-hand rule to each wire separately

topics: EMF = -dΦ/dt: changing flux induces EMF
Lenz's Law: induced current opposes the change causing it (energy conservation)
Sources of changing flux: changing B, changing area, relative motion
lessons.examTip: Not applying Lenz's Law direction correctly — the induced current creates a B field that OPPOSES the change in flux, not opposes the original B field; a decreasing flux induces current to maintain it

topics: Transformer ratio: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p; I_s/I_p = N_p/N_s
Energy conservation: power input = power output (ideal transformer)
Why transformers only work with AC, not DC
lessons.examTip: Thinking transformers work with DC — DC creates constant flux; no changing flux means no induction; transformers require AC to create changing flux; AP tests why DC doesn't work

topics: Inductor opposes changes in current through self-inductance
Energy stored in inductor: U = ½LI²
LR circuit behavior: current rises exponentially (time constant L/R)
lessons.examTip: Treating inductors like resistors at steady state — at steady state, inductor acts like a wire (zero resistance); the voltage across it is zero; AP tests inductor behavior at t=0 vs. t=∞

topics: Four laws: Gauss (E), Gauss (B), Faraday, Ampere-Maxwell
Displacement current: changing E field produces B field
Electromagnetic waves from Maxwell's equations
lessons.examTip: Treating Maxwell's equations as unrelated — each represents one fundamental aspect of electromagnetism; together they predict EM waves travel at c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀)

topics: EM wave: E and B fields oscillate perpendicular to each other and to propagation
All EM waves travel at c in vacuum; slower in material (v = c/n)
EM spectrum: radio through gamma, all governed by same wave equations
lessons.examTip: Thinking different EM waves have different speeds in vacuum — ALL EM waves travel at c = 3×10⁸ m/s in vacuum regardless of frequency or wavelength

topics: Law of reflection: θ_i = θ_r (angles from normal)
Snell's law: n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂
Total internal reflection when θ exceeds critical angle
lessons.examTip: Measuring angles from the surface instead of from the normal — all angles in optics are measured from the NORMAL to the surface; using surface angles gives wrong Snell's law results

lessons.lessonTitle: Lenses and Mirrors — Thin Lens Equation
topics: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i: thin lens/mirror equation
Sign conventions: real images positive, virtual images negative
Magnification m = -d_i/d_o; positive m = upright, negative = inverted
lessons.examTip: Getting sign conventions wrong — virtual images have negative image distance; for mirrors, objects and images on same side as incident light are positive; AP provides sign convention tables

topics: Three rays for converging lens: parallel→through F, through center→straight, through F→parallel
Virtual vs. real image location from ray diagram
Diverging lens/convex mirror always produce virtual, upright, reduced images
lessons.examTip: Using wrong principal ray rules for mirrors vs. lenses — the rules differ; for concave mirrors, parallel ray reflects through focal point; for convex mirrors it reflects as if coming from focal point behind mirror

topics: Young's double slit: constructive at d sinθ = mλ; destructive at (m+½)λ
Fringe spacing Δy = λL/d on screen at distance L
Coherent light requirement for stable interference pattern
lessons.examTip: Confusing slit width (d) with slit separation (d) — in double slit, d is the center-to-center separation; in single slit diffraction, a is the slit width; AP uses different variables for each

topics: Single slit minima: a sinθ = mλ (m = ±1, ±2...)
Rayleigh criterion: minimum angular resolution = 1.22λ/D
Why smaller apertures produce wider diffraction patterns
lessons.examTip: Applying double-slit formula to single-slit — they look similar but differ; single slit has minima where double slit has maxima for the same equation form; AP explicitly tests which formula applies

topics: Phase shift of π (half wavelength) on reflection from higher-n medium
Constructive vs. destructive thin film conditions depend on number of phase shifts
Soap bubbles and oil slicks: color patterns from thin film interference
lessons.examTip: Forgetting phase shift on reflection — if light reflects from one higher-n surface, there's one phase shift; the constructive condition flips; AP gives a thin film scenario and asks for constructive thickness

topics: Polarization by reflection: Brewster's angle
Malus's Law: I = I₀cos²θ for intensity through polarizer
Birefringence and optical rotation in biological molecules
lessons.examTip: Thinking only reflected light gets polarized — transmitted light is also partially polarized at Brewster's angle; and scattering (blue sky) also produces polarization; AP tests all mechanisms

topics: Compound microscope: objective forms real image; eyepiece magnifies it
Refracting telescope: objective lens + eyepiece for distant objects
Angular magnification vs. linear magnification
lessons.examTip: Treating all optical instruments the same — a telescope magnifies angular size (brings distant objects closer); a microscope magnifies linear size (makes small objects bigger); AP tests the distinction

topics: E = hf: photon energy proportional to frequency, not intensity
Work function: minimum energy to eject electron from metal
Threshold frequency: below this, no electrons ejected regardless of intensity
lessons.examTip: Thinking brighter light ejects faster electrons — intensity affects NUMBER of electrons ejected; frequency affects MAXIMUM kinetic energy; above threshold, KE_max = hf - φ

lessons.lessonTitle: Matter Waves and de Broglie Wavelength
topics: λ = h/p = h/(mv): matter waves for particles with momentum
Electron diffraction as evidence for matter waves
Heisenberg uncertainty principle: ΔxΔp ≥ ℏ/2
lessons.examTip: Applying de Broglie only to electrons — ANY particle with momentum has a de Broglie wavelength; protons, neutrons, even baseballs have wavelengths (just unmeasurably small)

topics: Bohr model: electrons in quantized orbits, photon emitted/absorbed at transitions
E_photon = E_upper - E_lower = hf
Emission vs. absorption spectra: same lines, different direction of light
lessons.examTip: Thinking emission and absorption happen at different wavelengths for the same transition — they're identical; hydrogen absorbs and emits at exactly the same frequencies; AP tests this symmetry

topics: Atomic number Z, mass number A, neutron number N = A-Z
Strong nuclear force vs. electrostatic repulsion: stability balance
Band of stability: N/Z ratio predicting stable nuclides
lessons.examTip: Treating all isotopes as equivalent in stability — neutron-rich nuclides undergo beta-minus decay; proton-rich undergo beta-plus; AP gives nuclide location on N-Z chart and asks decay mode

topics: Alpha: ⁴₂He emitted; Z-2, A-4
Beta-minus: neutron → proton + e⁻ + antineutrino; Z+1, same A
Gamma: no change in Z or A; high-energy photon from nuclear excitation
lessons.examTip: Writing beta decay without the antineutrino — AP requires complete decay equations; missing the neutrino/antineutrino in beta decay loses credit on FRQ

topics: Half-life: N = N₀(½)^(t/t½); exponential decay law
Carbon-14 dating: ¹⁴C/¹²C ratio in dead organisms decays at known rate
Appropriate dating method depends on age range and t½
lessons.examTip: Using carbon-14 for objects older than ~50,000 years — after 10 half-lives only 1/1024 remains; too little to measure accurately; AP asks which isotope is appropriate for geological timescales

topics: E = mc²: mass defect converted to energy
Nuclear binding energy: energy to separate all nucleons
Fission: heavy nucleus splitting releases energy; fusion: light nuclei joining
lessons.examTip: Confusing which releases more energy per gram: fission vs. fusion — fusion releases more energy per unit mass; fission releases more energy per reaction but involves heavier nuclei

lessons.lessonTitle: Wave-Particle Duality and Quantum Mechanics Overview
topics: Double slit with single electrons: interference pattern builds up one electron at a time
Quantum superposition: particle exists in multiple states until measured
Copenhagen interpretation vs. other interpretations of QM
lessons.examTip: Treating quantum uncertainty as just measurement error — Heisenberg uncertainty is not about imprecise instruments; it's fundamental to nature; a particle genuinely has no definite position and momentum simultaneously

topics: v(t) = dx/dt; a(t) = dv/dt — deriving motion functions
Integrating acceleration to find velocity; velocity to find position
Polynomial and trigonometric position functions
lessons.examTip: Treating derivatives as approximations — in Physics C, calculus is exact; AP gives a(t) and expects you to integrate (with initial conditions) to find x(t)

topics: Separating x and y equations of motion with integration
Finding trajectory equation y(x) by eliminating t
Range maximization using calculus
lessons.examTip: Using kinematic equations for non-constant acceleration — Physics C problems may give variable a(t); must integrate rather than use v = v₀ + at

lessons.lessonTitle: Relative Motion and Non-Inertial Reference Frames
topics: Relative acceleration: fictitious forces in accelerating frames
Coriolis and centrifugal forces in rotating frames
Solving problems from different reference frames
lessons.examTip: Not identifying pseudoforces in non-inertial frames — AP C asks you to analyze motion from both inertial and accelerating frames; must add fictitious force in non-inertial frame

topics: Angular velocity and acceleration as derivatives: ω = dθ/dt, α = dω/dt
Centripetal and tangential acceleration components
Non-uniform circular motion: both centripetal and tangential acceleration present
lessons.examTip: Using only centripetal acceleration when angular speed is changing — non-uniform circular motion requires both a_c = v²/r AND a_t = r(dω/dt); AP C tests the full vector acceleration

topics: Constraint equations relating accelerations in Atwood/pulley systems
String/rope constraints: how acceleration relates across components
Solving multi-body systems using system approach + internal forces
lessons.examTip: Setting up wrong constraint — if rope goes over a pulley, the magnitudes of acceleration are equal but directions differ; AP C often has compound pulley systems requiring multiple constraint equations

topics: Given F(t), F(x), or F(v) — choosing the right form of Newton's 2nd law
Separation of variables: m(dv/dt) = F(v) → m dv/F(v) = dt
Terminal velocity from F_net = 0 condition
lessons.examTip: Trying to use kinematic equations when force is velocity-dependent — drag force F = -bv requires differential equation solution; AP C free response regularly tests this

topics: Vector differential equations for 2D motion
Numerical/graphical solutions when analytical integration is difficult
Phase space (v vs. x) for analyzing motion
lessons.examTip: Solving x and y components independently when forces are coupled — some 2D problems have forces that mix components; must check if equations are truly separable before separating

topics: Position as vector function r(t) = x(t)î + y(t)ĵ
Arc length and path length calculations
Curvature of trajectory and its relation to centripetal acceleration
lessons.examTip: Confusing speed (|v|) with velocity (vector) — speed = √(vx² + vy²); AP C gives component functions and asks for speed at specific time or minimum speed

lessons.lessonTitle: Newton's Laws with Calculus — Variable Forces
topics: F = m(dv/dt) as a differential equation
Solving F(t) = m(dv/dt) by direct integration
Impulse as integral of F(t)dt
lessons.examTip: Using average force for variable-force impulse — must integrate F(t) for exact impulse; AP C gives F(t) function and expects ∫F dt, not F_avg × Δt

lessons.lessonTitle: Free Body Diagrams for Complex Systems
topics: Multiple connected objects with different constraints
Normal force at maximum compression/minimum support points
Tension variation in non-massless ropes
lessons.examTip: Assuming rope is massless when the problem specifies mass — a massive rope has different tension at each point; AP C sometimes gives rope linear mass density and expects integration

topics: Friction as constraint force responding to other applied forces
Maximum static friction angle and incline problems
Minimum force to start motion at various angles
lessons.examTip: Optimizing force direction for minimum effort — to move a box with minimum force, optimal angle θ = arctan(μk); AP C may ask to derive this using calculus minimization

lessons.lessonTitle: Circular Motion — Vertical and Banked Turns
topics: Normal force at top/bottom of vertical circle — different values
Banking angle without friction: tanθ = v²/(rg)
Maximum and minimum speed for no slipping on banked curve with friction
lessons.examTip: Using the same equation for normal force at top and bottom of a loop — at the top N + mg = mv²/r; at the bottom N - mg = mv²/r; signs differ based on net centripetal direction

topics: Linear drag: F_d = bv → differential equation m(dv/dt) = mg - bv
Solution: v(t) = v_T(1 - e^(-bt/m)); terminal velocity v_T = mg/b
Quadratic drag: F_d = cv² (more realistic, harder to solve)
lessons.examTip: Giving terminal velocity without solving the DE — must show v_T from dv/dt = 0 (net force = 0); AP C FRQ walks through deriving v(t) and requires showing the exponential approach to terminal velocity

topics: Solving m(d²x/dt²) = -kx to get x(t) = Acos(ωt + φ)
Identifying ω = √(k/m) as the coefficient in the DE solution
Initial conditions determining A and φ
lessons.examTip: Memorizing x = Acos(ωt) without justifying ω = √(k/m) — AP C FRQ asks to set up and solve the differential equation, not just use the formula

topics: Centrifugal force: mω²r outward in rotating frame
Coriolis force: 2m(v × ω) for moving objects in rotating frame
Analyzing pendulum deflection on rotating Earth
lessons.examTip: Treating centrifugal force as real in an inertial frame — it only exists in the rotating frame as a pseudoforce; from an inertial frame, only the centripetal force is needed

topics: Euler method: x(t+Δt) ≈ x(t) + v(t)Δt
Error accumulation and step size reduction
When analytical solutions don't exist and numerical methods are needed
lessons.examTip: Not recognizing when to use numerical methods — AP C doesn't usually require numerical computation, but may ask conceptually why a given F(x) requires numerical integration

topics: W = ∫F·dr for non-constant forces
Work from F(x) graph as area under curve
Path independence of conservative forces
lessons.examTip: Using W = Fd only for constant forces — when F varies with position, must integrate; AP C gives F(x) = bx² and expects W = ∫₀ˣ bx'² dx'

topics: U(x) = -∫F dx: deriving PE function from force
F = -dU/dx: finding force from potential energy curve
Equilibrium points: F = 0 where U has extrema
lessons.examTip: Not identifying stable vs. unstable equilibrium from U(x) — minimum of U is stable equilibrium (like valley); maximum is unstable (like hilltop); AP C gives U(x) and asks equilibrium type

topics: Conservative: work independent of path; F = -∇U
Test for conservative force: ∂Fy/∂x = ∂Fx/∂y
Non-conservative forces don't have potential energy functions
lessons.examTip: Assuming any force that 'stores energy' is conservative — spring force is conservative; friction is not (dissipates energy); AP C tests this distinction in multi-force problems

lessons.lessonTitle: Power and Efficiency with Variable Forces
topics: P(t) = F(t)·v(t): instantaneous power
Average power from total work / total time
Power output of engine under variable load
lessons.examTip: Using average force × average velocity for average power — correct only if F and v are proportional; in general, P_avg = W_total/Δt requires integrating

topics: Energy conservation with multiple bodies and spring systems
Spring energy stored at different compression/extension values
Work-energy theorem for systems with internal energy changes
lessons.examTip: Applying energy conservation when internal friction converts energy — total mechanical energy is not conserved; must track all energy transformations; AP C may give a friction coefficient AND a spring

topics: U = -GMm/r vs. U = mgh: when each applies
Escape velocity derivation: KE + U = 0
Energy in elliptical orbits: E = -GMm/(2a)
lessons.examTip: Using U = mgh for orbital calculations — the linear approximation fails beyond a few hundred km altitude; AP C orbital problems require U = -GMm/r

topics: Normal modes of coupled oscillators: in-phase and out-of-phase
Energy exchange between coupled pendulums
Resonance and energy transfer in driven systems
lessons.examTip: Treating coupled oscillators as two independent simple oscillators — coupling changes the normal mode frequencies; AP C may give the equations of motion and ask for normal mode frequencies

topics: Turning points where KE=0 from U(x) graph
Allowed and forbidden regions based on total energy E
Bound vs. unbound motion depending on E vs. U_max
lessons.examTip: Not using U(x) graphs to find turning points — wherever E (horizontal line) intersects U(x) curve, the particle turns around; AP C gives U(x) function and total energy for analysis

units.unitTitle: Systems of Particles and Linear Momentum

lessons.lessonTitle: Center of Mass with Calculus — Continuous Distributions
topics: x_cm = (1/M)∫x dm for continuous mass distributions
Choosing dm in terms of dx, dy, or polar coordinates
Center of mass of semicircular wire, triangular plate, etc.
lessons.examTip: Not matching dm to the geometry — for a thin rod, dm = ρ dx; for a disk, dm = σ(2πr)dr; getting dm wrong makes the whole integral wrong; AP C tests this setup carefully

topics: Rocket equation: M(dv/dt) = -v_e(dM/dt) — thrust force
Deriving Δv = v_e ln(M₀/M_f) for ideal rocket
Collisions with embedded projectiles: before/after momentum analysis
lessons.examTip: Treating rocket mass as constant — the whole point of the rocket equation is that M decreases with time; must use the variable-mass DE, not F=ma with constant m

topics: Two equations (p and KE conservation) for two unknowns (v₁', v₂')
Special case: equal masses exchange velocities completely
Center of mass frame simplifying collision analysis
lessons.examTip: Solving elastic collisions by only conserving momentum — must use both conservation laws; AP C gives both equations and expects you to solve the resulting system algebraically

topics: L = r × p for point particles; L = Iω for rigid bodies
Total L of system = orbital + spin angular momenta
Conservation of angular momentum and its conditions
lessons.examTip: Not distinguishing orbital angular momentum (r × mv) from spin (Iω) — a rolling ball has both; AP C asks for total L of a system containing both types

topics: J = ∫F dt: exact impulse for variable forces
Graphical: impulse = area under F-t curve
Connecting impulse to momentum change for known initial and final states
lessons.examTip: Using average force when force varies — must integrate for exact result; AP C gives F(t) = F₀ sin(πt/T) and asks for impulse over half period

lessons.lessonTitle: Collision Analysis in 2D with Calculus Methods
topics: Vector equations for momentum components in oblique collisions
Solving two-equation systems for velocities after 2D collision
Off-center elastic collisions: using energy + vector momentum
lessons.examTip: Neglecting one of the three conservation equations available in elastic 2D — have 3 equations (px, py, KE) and 4 unknowns for two final velocities; need one additional constraint (like coefficient of restitution)

topics: Wave equation derivation from Newton's 2nd law applied to string segment
Speed of wave on string: v = √(T/μ)
Power transported by a wave
lessons.examTip: Memorizing wave speed formulas without the derivation — AP C expects you to show how wave speed follows from the string's equation of motion; the derivation tests calculus and Newton's laws simultaneously

topics: Energy converted to deformation/thermal energy in inelastic collision
Maximum deformation in collision: using COM frame analysis
Collision time and average force from impulse-momentum theorem
lessons.examTip: Assuming maximum compression is at the end of the collision — maximum deformation occurs when both objects have the SAME velocity (center of mass velocity); not at the final state for partially inelastic collisions

topics: I = ∫r² dm for continuous distributions
Setting up integral for rod, disk, sphere, hollow cylinder
Parallel axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md²
lessons.examTip: Using wrong dm expression for the geometry — for a solid disk, dm = ρ(2πr dr)h; AP C expects you to set up and evaluate the integral from scratch, not just recall the result

lessons.lessonTitle: Torque and Angular Acceleration with Calculus
topics: τ = dL/dt in general; τ = Iα only for constant I
Newton's 2nd law for rotation: Στ = Iα + ω(dI/dt) when I changes
Angular impulse: ∫τ dt = ΔL
lessons.examTip: Using Στ = Iα when moment of inertia is changing — if mass is redistributed (ice skater pulling arms in), the full form τ = dL/dt must be used

topics: Rolling without slipping: a_cm = αR as the kinematic constraint
Friction force magnitude and direction for rolling on incline
Static vs. kinetic friction determining whether rolling persists
lessons.examTip: Not solving rolling problems with both translational AND rotational Newton's 2nd law simultaneously — one equation isn't enough; need F_net = ma AND Στ = Iα with the rolling constraint linking them

lessons.lessonTitle: Angular Momentum — Vector Form and Conservation
topics: L = r × p for particle; direction from right-hand rule
τ = dL/dt in vector form; torque changes direction of L
Conservation when external torque = 0; precession when τ ≠ 0
lessons.examTip: Applying scalar angular momentum where vector treatment is needed — if the axis of rotation can change, must use vector L; AP C gyroscope problems require cross product reasoning

topics: W_rot = ∫τ dθ; P_rot = τω
Rotational KE = ½Iω²; conservation of energy with rotation
Energy stored in and released by rotating flywheels
lessons.examTip: Forgetting to include rotational KE in energy conservation — a solid sphere rolling from height h reaches bottom at v = √(10gh/7), not √(2gh); the ½Iω² term makes a significant difference

topics: Precession: Ω_precession = τ/L = Mgr/(Iω)
Direction of precession from τ = dL/dt (cross product)
Nutation: superimposed wobble on precession
lessons.examTip: Using torque magnitude without direction for precession — must use τ = dL/dt as vectors; the precession direction is perpendicular to BOTH the torque and the angular momentum vectors

topics: Generalized coordinates and constraints
Lagrangian L = T - V; Euler-Lagrange equations
Applying Lagrangian to pendulum, spring, and constrained systems
lessons.examTip: Treating Lagrangian mechanics as optional — AP C Mechanics FRQ has included Lagrangian-style problems; knowing L = T - V and how to derive equations of motion is testable

lessons.lessonTitle: Precession, Nutation, and Stability of Rotating Bodies
topics: Stability of spinning top: fast spin stabilizes against gravity
Earth's precession: 26,000-year cycle from solar/lunar torques
Gyroscopic stabilization in navigation and engineering
lessons.examTip: Not connecting gyroscopic stability to angular momentum — a fast-spinning gyroscope resists reorientation because any torque changes L direction (precesses) rather than knocking it over

lessons.lessonTitle: Deriving SHM from the Differential Equation
topics: m(d²x/dt²) = -kx → general solution x = Acos(ωt) + Bsin(ωt)
Identifying ω² = k/m from the equation structure
Applying initial conditions to find A and B (or amplitude and phase)
lessons.examTip: Not showing the DE derivation — AP C FRQ expects you to write Newton's 2nd law, identify it as a harmonic oscillator equation, and state the solution form with justification

topics: E = ½kA² = ½mv_max² = constant
v(x) = ω√(A² - x²) from energy conservation
Phase relationships: position, velocity, acceleration sinusoids
lessons.examTip: Deriving v(x) using kinematics instead of energy — energy method v = ω√(A²-x²) is faster and more general; AP C often asks for velocity at a non-equilibrium position

topics: Underdamped: x = Ae^(-bt/2m)cos(ω't + φ); reduced frequency
Quality factor Q = ω₀/γ measuring sharpness of resonance
Resonance amplitude: driven at natural frequency, maximum response
lessons.examTip: Using undamped frequency in damped oscillator solutions — damped angular frequency ω' = √(ω₀² - (b/2m)²) is slightly less than ω₀; AP C tests whether you use the correct ω'

topics: Physical pendulum: τ = -Mgd sinθ ≈ -Mgdθ for small angles → T = 2π√(I/Mgd)
Torsional oscillator: τ = -κθ → T = 2π√(I/κ)
Compound pendulum finding pivot for minimum period
lessons.examTip: Using simple pendulum formula for extended objects — the physical pendulum uses moment of inertia I (about pivot), not just mass; AP C gives a rod or disk pendulum requiring I calculation

topics: Two coupled oscillators have two normal modes
Symmetric mode: same frequency as uncoupled; antisymmetric: higher frequency
Beating: superposition of two close frequencies
lessons.examTip: Treating coupled oscillators as two independent ones — coupling introduces two normal mode frequencies; if started in a non-normal-mode state, energy oscillates between the two oscillators

topics: Large-angle pendulum: period increases with amplitude (not SHM)
Period of large-angle pendulum: elliptic integral or series expansion
Bifurcation and chaos in driven, damped oscillators
lessons.examTip: Assuming pendulum period is always 2π√(L/g) — this is the small-angle approximation; AP C may give a large-angle problem and ask to explain why the actual period is longer than predicted

topics: Wave equation: ∂²y/∂x² = (1/v²)∂²y/∂t²
Standing waves as superposition of traveling waves
Normal modes of strings: f_n = nv/(2L)
lessons.examTip: Memorizing standing wave formulas without connection to the wave equation — AP C expects derivation of allowed frequencies from boundary conditions, not just formula recall

topics: Anharmonic potential: U = ½kx² + bx³ + cx⁴
First-order perturbation: small correction to SHM period
Thermal expansion from anharmonicity
lessons.examTip: Treating any restoring force as SHM — SHM requires STRICTLY linear restoring force; for anharmonic potential the period is amplitude-dependent; AP C tests when linear approximation breaks down

lessons.lessonTitle: Gravitational Field as Vector Field — Calculus Treatment
topics: g(r) = GM/r² for external; g(r) = GMr/R³ inside uniform sphere
Superposition of fields from multiple mass distributions
Shell theorem derivation using integration
lessons.examTip: Using constant g inside a sphere — inside a uniform sphere, g increases linearly from 0 at center to g_surface at surface; AP C tests this radial dependence with integration

topics: V = -GM/r (scalar field); U = mV = -GMm/r
Potential of continuous distributions by integration
Potential well visualization and escape energy
lessons.examTip: Confusing gravitational field (vector) with potential (scalar) — potential is integrated from field; V = -∫g·dr; AP C gives a mass distribution and expects both g and V derivations

topics: Kepler's laws derived from Newton's law + calculus
Vis-viva equation: v² = GM(2/r - 1/a)
Orbital transfer (Hohmann transfer): minimum energy path between orbits
lessons.examTip: Using kinematic intuition for orbital transfers — to go from low to high orbit, thrust in the direction of motion (counterintuitively slows down at the destination); AP C tests vis-viva equation application

lessons.lessonTitle: Extended Mass Distributions and Tidal Forces
topics: Gravitational force on extended body from non-uniform field
Tidal force: differential acceleration across body of finite size
Tidal locking: synchronous rotation from tidal torques
lessons.examTip: Treating tidal force as just 'differential gravity' without calculating — AP C may ask to express tidal force mathematically as dF/dr × Δr = 2GMmΔr/r³

topics: E = -GMm/(2r) for circular orbit (half the potential energy)
E > 0: hyperbolic orbit (unbound); E < 0: elliptical (bound); E = 0: parabolic (escape)
Transfer energy: how much energy to change orbits
lessons.examTip: Thinking that giving energy to a satellite speeds it up — the total energy becomes less negative (higher), but at the new orbit the speed is lower; AP C tests this orbital mechanics paradox

topics: Gravitational field of infinite rod, infinite plane, ring
Using integration for ring mass distribution
Comparison with electric field analogies
lessons.examTip: Forgetting direction when integrating non-symmetric distributions — for a ring, horizontal components cancel; only axial components add; AP C sets up this integral and expects correct component analysis

topics: General relativity: gravity as spacetime curvature
Gravitational time dilation and redshift
Precession of Mercury's perihelion as GR evidence
lessons.examTip: Not connecting GR to observable predictions — AP C may ask about gravitational time dilation quantitatively using Δt = Δt₀/√(1-2GM/rc²) or qualitatively about GPS corrections

lessons.lessonTitle: Three-Body Problem and Chaos in Orbital Mechanics
topics: Why three-body problem has no closed-form solution in general
Lagrange points: L1-L5 stability positions in two-body system
Resonances and orbital stability in planetary systems
lessons.examTip: Treating Lagrange points as simple orbital mechanics — the L4 and L5 points are stable due to Coriolis force in the rotating frame; AP C may ask to explain stability qualitatively using effective potential

courses.courseName: AP Physics C: Electricity and Magnetism

lessons.lessonTitle: Coulomb's Law and Superposition — Vector Calculus
topics: Electric force as vector; superposition principle
Force on charge from continuous distribution by integration
Electric field E = F/q₀ as a vector field
lessons.examTip: Adding force magnitudes without considering direction — must resolve into components and add; AP C gives charge distributions and expects component integration

lessons.lessonTitle: Electric Field from Continuous Charge Distributions
topics: dE = k dq/r² r̂: building field from infinitesimal elements
Linear (λ), surface (σ), volume (ρ) charge densities
Field of infinite line charge, ring, disk by integration
lessons.examTip: Not exploiting symmetry to simplify integrations — for a ring of charge, perpendicular components cancel; only axial component survives; setting up dE correctly then identifying cancellations is key

topics: Φ_E = Q_enc/ε₀: Gauss's law and its derivation
Applying to spherical, cylindrical, planar symmetry
Field inside and outside conductor; field between plates
lessons.examTip: Choosing non-symmetric Gaussian surfaces — Gauss's law always holds, but only simplifies when E is uniform and perpendicular on the surface; AP C tests whether you choose the right surface shape

topics: V = -∫E·dr from reference point (usually infinity)
Potential of continuous distributions: V = k∫dq/r (scalar, easier than field)
E = -∇V: finding field from potential gradient
lessons.examTip: Integrating E to get V in the wrong direction — must go from the field point to infinity (or chosen reference), not along field lines; AP C gives a charge distribution and expects both E and V derivations

topics: E = 0 inside conductor; charges on outer surface only
Induced charges on conductor in external field
Charge distribution on non-spherical conductors — surface charge density proportional to curvature
lessons.examTip: Not accounting for induced charges on nearby conductors — when a charge is brought near a grounded conductor, induced surface charges redistribute; AP C FRQ often includes this induced-charge scenario

topics: C = Q/V; C = ε₀A/d; C = 4πε₀R for isolated sphere
Energy U = ½CV² = Q²/2C; energy density u = ½ε₀E²
Capacitors in series and parallel; dielectric effects
lessons.examTip: Forgetting to recalculate V or Q when connecting capacitors — AP C gives charged and uncharged capacitors connected; must conserve total charge, then find new V across the combined capacitance

topics: Dielectric constant κ: C_new = κC₀; E reduced to E₀/κ inside
Molecular polarization mechanism: why κ > 1
Bound surface charges from polarization
lessons.examTip: Confusing the effect of dielectric when battery-connected vs. disconnected — with battery (V constant): C increases, Q increases, U increases; without battery (Q constant): V decreases, C increases, U decreases

lessons.lessonTitle: Electrostatic Boundary Conditions and Uniqueness Theorem
topics: Boundary conditions for E: tangential component continuous, normal component has discontinuity
Uniqueness theorem: solution determined by boundary conditions alone
Method of images: equivalent charge configurations
lessons.examTip: Not applying boundary conditions when solving for charge distributions — AP C FRQ may give a partially specified system and ask to find surface charge using boundary condition E_above - E_below = σ/ε₀

lessons.lessonTitle: Resistance and Ohm's Law from Microscopic View
topics: J = σE (current density); R = ρL/A from microscopic Ohm's law
Drift velocity and its relation to current: I = nqv_d A
Resistivity temperature dependence: ρ = ρ₀(1 + αΔT)
lessons.examTip: Not distinguishing conductivity (σ) from resistivity (ρ) — σ = 1/ρ; higher conductivity means lower resistivity; AP C FRQ may ask you to derive R from σ and geometry

topics: Kirchhoff's loop: ε - IR - Q/C = 0; differentiate to get dI/dt equation
Solution: Q(t) = Qmax(1 - e^(-t/RC)); I(t) = I₀e^(-t/RC)
Energy budget: half of battery energy stored in C, half dissipated in R
lessons.examTip: Not deriving the exponential from the DE — AP C FRQ requires setting up the DE from KVL, separating variables, and integrating to get the exponential; just stating Q = Qmax(1-e^(-t/RC)) without derivation loses credit

topics: Series/parallel combinations and equivalent capacitance
Energy distribution among capacitors in a network
Partial discharge when capacitors are reconnected
lessons.examTip: Not tracking which capacitors share the same charge or voltage — in series, all capacitors have the same charge; in parallel, all have the same voltage; AP C gives complex networks requiring careful identification

lessons.lessonTitle: Steady-State and Transient Behavior in RC Circuits
topics: Initial state (t=0): capacitor acts as wire (V=0, max current)
Steady state (t→∞): capacitor acts as open circuit (no current)
Complete transient analysis between these extremes
lessons.examTip: Not correctly identifying initial and final states — at t=0 the capacitor voltage = 0 (for uncharged) or its initial value; AP C asks for current and voltage at specific times requiring knowledge of both limits

topics: u_E = ½ε₀E²: energy per unit volume in electric field
Total energy in capacitor = ∫u_E dV over all space
Comparing energy in capacitor vs. energy in resistor
lessons.examTip: Treating electrical energy as located in the circuit components rather than the field — energy is stored in the FIELD throughout space; AP C may ask to calculate field energy from E(r) distribution

topics: Matrix method for solving large resistor networks
Node voltage method vs. mesh current method
Thevenin and Norton equivalent circuits
lessons.examTip: Only using KVL without KCL at nodes — complex circuits require both; at each node, sum of incoming currents = sum of outgoing; missing this equation leaves the system underdetermined

topics: Diode I-V characteristic: exponential in forward bias
Transistor as current-controlled current source
Load line analysis for nonlinear elements
lessons.examTip: Applying Ohm's law to nonlinear elements — diodes don't have constant resistance; AP C may give an I-V curve and ask for the operating point (intersection of I-V curve and load line)

topics: Capacitor in timing circuit: how RC sets a time scale
Dielectric breakdown: maximum field before dielectric fails
Electrolytic capacitors: polarity requirement and large capacitance
lessons.examTip: Ignoring breakdown voltage in AP C problems — a capacitor can store more charge with a dielectric, but the dielectric limits the maximum field; real capacitor design involves this tradeoff

topics: Superposition theorem for multiple sources
Thevenin/Norton equivalents simplifying complex networks
Maximum power transfer theorem: R_load = R_Thevenin
lessons.examTip: Not using superposition correctly — each source acts alone; all others zeroed (voltage sources = short, current sources = open); then superimpose results; AP C tests this for two-source networks

lessons.lessonTitle: Charge and Current Conservation in Complex Circuits
topics: KCL at every node; KVL around every independent loop
Counting independent equations: branch currents = nodes + loops - 1
Matrix formulation and solution
lessons.examTip: Writing too many KVL equations — for n nodes and b branches, need b-(n-1) independent KVL equations; extra equations are redundant; AP C expects you to identify the minimum set

topics: Power delivered by source vs. dissipated in resistors
Maximum power transfer condition
Efficiency of power delivery
