lessons.examTip: Confusing power delivered to load vs. total power from source — total power = ε × I; power to load = I²R_load; efficiency = R_load/(R_load + R_internal); AP C tests all three quantities

topics: Impedance: Z_R = R, Z_C = 1/(jωC), Z_L = jωL
Phasor diagrams for phase relationships
Series RLC resonance: Z minimum at ω₀ = 1/√(LC)
lessons.examTip: Using DC methods for AC circuits — capacitors and inductors have frequency-dependent impedance; at DC (ω=0), capacitor is open and inductor is short; AP C expects phasor analysis

topics: LC oscillation: energy oscillates between L and C
Natural frequency ω₀ = 1/√(LC); Q oscillates sinusoidally
Analogy: LC circuit ↔ mass-spring system
lessons.examTip: Not setting up the DE for LC circuit — must write KVL: L(dI/dt) + Q/C = 0 → d²Q/dt² = -Q/(LC); AP C FRQ expects the DE derivation and solution identification

topics: Low-pass RC filter: attenuates high frequencies
High-pass RC filter: attenuates low frequencies
Frequency response and -3dB cutoff frequency
lessons.examTip: Not recognizing filter behavior from circuit topology — capacitor to ground = low-pass (at high frequency, C shorts the output to ground); AP C may give a circuit and ask to identify filter type and cutoff

lessons.lessonTitle: Grounding, Shielding, and Practical Circuit Issues
topics: Grounding as voltage reference; chassis ground vs. earth ground
Faraday cage shielding magnetic vs. electric fields
Noise coupling and electromagnetic interference
lessons.examTip: Thinking a Faraday cage blocks magnetic fields — it blocks ELECTRIC fields (conductor redistributes charges); static magnetic fields penetrate; AP C tests this distinction

lessons.lessonTitle: Measuring Instruments and Their Effect on Circuits
topics: Oscilloscope: high-impedance voltage probe
Ammeter insertion resistance changing current
Bridge circuit for precision measurements
lessons.examTip: Ignoring instrument loading effects — an ideal ammeter has zero resistance; a real one doesn't; AP C may give ammeter resistance and ask how much the measurement differs from true current

lessons.lessonTitle: Biot-Savart Law — Magnetic Field from Current
topics: dB = (μ₀/4π)(I dl × r̂)/r²: field from current element
Applying to long wire, circular loop, solenoid
Superposition of magnetic fields from multiple sources
lessons.examTip: Not correctly identifying dl × r̂ direction — must use right-hand rule for each current element; for a wire, dl is along current direction; AP C expects the cross product setup

lessons.lessonTitle: Ampere's Law — Using Symmetry for B
topics: ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enc: Ampere's law
Applying to infinite wire, solenoid, toroid
B inside a solenoid: B = μ₀nI (uniform)
lessons.examTip: Choosing an Amperian loop where B is not uniform or not along the loop — must choose loop where B is constant and parallel to dl; the symmetric Amperian loop is always the key choice on AP C

lessons.lessonTitle: Magnetic Force on Moving Charges — Cyclotron Motion
topics: F = qv × B; circular motion when v ⊥ B: r = mv/(qB)
Helical motion when v has component parallel to B
Cyclotron frequency f = qB/(2πm): mass spectrometer principle
lessons.examTip: Forgetting that magnetic force does no work — the magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity; it changes direction but not speed; AP C tests that KE is constant in purely magnetic deflection

topics: dF = I dl × B; F = IL × B for straight wire in uniform B
Torque on current loop: τ = NIAB sinθ = m × B
Magnetic dipole moment m = NIA
lessons.examTip: Not using the full vector cross product for force on a current segment — must identify the angle between current direction and field; AP C gives a current loop at an angle and expects torque calculation

topics: Diamagnetic, paramagnetic, ferromagnetic: mechanisms and characteristics
Magnetic permeability μ = κ_m μ₀; B = μH inside material
Hysteresis in ferromagnets: remnant magnetization and coercive field
lessons.examTip: Treating all magnetic materials as equivalent — AP C distinguishes the three types; ferromagnets retain magnetization after field is removed (hysteresis); paramagnets don't

topics: Displacement current: I_d = ε₀(dΦ_E/dt)
Modified Ampere's law: ∮B·dl = μ₀(I_enc + I_d)
Why changing electric field produces magnetic field — EM wave implication
lessons.examTip: Thinking real current is always needed to create B — changing electric flux (displacement current) also creates B; this is the key symmetry that leads to EM waves; AP C tests this in capacitor problems

lessons.lessonTitle: Hall Effect and Charge Carrier Identification
topics: Hall voltage from charge buildup in conductor in magnetic field
Sign of Hall voltage tells sign of charge carriers
Hall coefficient R_H = 1/(nq): measuring carrier density
lessons.examTip: Getting Hall voltage polarity wrong for holes vs. electrons — both deflect to the same side initially, but holes accumulate on the deflection side creating + voltage; electrons on the same side create - voltage; AP C tests this sign

lessons.lessonTitle: Magnetic Flux and Its Role in Induction
topics: Φ_B = ∫B·dA: magnetic flux calculation over surface
Motional EMF: ε = ∫(v × B)·dl
Flux through circuits in non-uniform fields
lessons.examTip: Calculating flux as B × A without checking angle — must use Φ = BAcosθ where θ is between B and the surface normal; AP C gives tilted loops and non-uniform fields requiring careful flux calculation

lessons.lessonTitle: Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law — Full Formulation
topics: ε = -dΦ_B/dt: EMF from changing flux (in any loop)
Lenz's law gives the sign: induced EMF opposes change
Three sources of changing flux: changing B, moving loop, changing orientation
lessons.examTip: Not using Lenz's law to determine current direction — AP C FRQ regularly asks for direction of induced current; must state which way the induced B opposes the change and use right-hand rule for current

topics: Self-inductance L: Φ = LI; ε = -L(dI/dt)
Inductance of solenoid: L = μ₀n²Al
Mutual inductance M: EMF in secondary from changing current in primary
lessons.examTip: Not deriving inductance from first principles — AP C FRQ may ask to calculate L for a solenoid; must use Φ = μ₀nI × Al and L = NΦ/I = μ₀n²Al to get the formula

lessons.lessonTitle: RL Circuits — Differential Equation and Solution
topics: KVL: ε - IR - L(dI/dt) = 0 → I(t) = (ε/R)(1-e^(-Rt/L))
Time constant τ = L/R; half the final current at t = τln2
Energy stored: U_L = ½LI²; energy density u_B = B²/(2μ₀)
lessons.examTip: Not deriving the RL response from the DE — AP C FRQ follows same pattern as RC: write KVL, identify DE, separate variables, integrate; must show each step

topics: LC circuit oscillates between electric (½CV²) and magnetic (½LI²) energy
Frequency ω₀ = 1/√(LC); Q(t) = Q₀cos(ω₀t + φ)
Analogy to mechanical oscillator: L↔m, 1/C↔k, Q↔x, I↔v
lessons.examTip: Not using the mechanical analogy to set up the DE — L d²Q/dt² + Q/C = 0 maps directly to mx'' + kx = 0; AP C tests this analogy explicitly

topics: Underdamped: ω' = √(ω₀² - (R/2L)²); critical damping at R = 2√(L/C)
Energy loss rate in RLC: P = I²R
Quality factor Q = ω₀L/R = ω₀/(2γ)
lessons.examTip: Using undamped frequency for damped RLC — actual oscillation frequency ω' < ω₀; for heavily damped circuit, oscillations die out quickly; AP C tests whether you identify the correct solution form

topics: All four Maxwell's equations in integral and differential form
Gauss's law for E and B, Faraday's law, Ampere-Maxwell law
How the equations predict electromagnetic wave propagation
lessons.examTip: Not connecting displacement current to EM wave prediction — without the ε₀(dΦ_E/dt) term, Maxwell's equations wouldn't predict EM waves; AP C tests that this term is essential for c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀)

topics: Wave equation for E and B from Faraday and Ampere-Maxwell
Speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) = 3×10⁸ m/s from wave equation
Energy transport: Poynting vector S = (1/μ₀)(E × B)
lessons.examTip: Not knowing how to derive the wave equation — AP C FRQ may ask to show that E satisfies the wave equation by differentiating Maxwell's equations; requires taking curl of curl of E

lessons.lessonTitle: Electromagnetic Induction Applications — Generators and Motors
topics: AC generator: rotating coil in field → sinusoidal EMF
Back-EMF in motors opposing applied voltage
Eddy currents: induced currents in bulk conductors opposing motion
lessons.examTip: Not including back-EMF when analyzing motor circuits — at startup, back-EMF = 0, so current is highest; at full speed, back-EMF reduces current; AP C tests the transient motor startup behavior

topics: Intuitive limit: behavior of f(x) as x→a (regardless of f(a))
One-sided limits: left and right must agree for limit to exist
Limit notation and evaluation by tables and graphs
lessons.examTip: Thinking f(a) determines the limit — limit is about approach, not arrival; f(a) could be undefined while lim f(x) exists; AP tests this distinction constantly

topics: Direct substitution, factoring, rationalizing, conjugate method
Limits of rational functions: factor and cancel common factors
L'Hôpital's rule for 0/0 and ∞/∞ indeterminate forms
lessons.examTip: Applying L'Hôpital's rule without verifying the indeterminate form — must first confirm 0/0 or ∞/∞; applying to determinate forms gives wrong answers

lessons.lessonTitle: Limits at Infinity and Asymptotic Behavior
topics: Horizontal asymptotes: comparing degree of numerator vs. denominator
Vertical asymptotes where denominator = 0 (and numerator ≠ 0)
End behavior of polynomials, rationals, and transcendentals
lessons.examTip: Calling every denominator-zero a vertical asymptote — if numerator also = 0 at the same point, it might be a hole (removable discontinuity) after factoring; AP tests removable vs. non-removable

lessons.lessonTitle: Squeeze Theorem and Special Trig Limits
topics: lim(sinx/x) = 1 as x→0; lim((1-cosx)/x) = 0
Squeeze theorem: bounding an unknown limit between two known limits
Using special limits with substitution for more complex expressions
lessons.examTip: Applying lim(sinx/x)=1 when x is not the argument of both sin and denominator — lim(sin(2x)/x) = 2, not 1; must identify the matching structure; AP tests variations of this limit

topics: Three conditions: f(a) defined, lim exists, limit = function value
Types of discontinuity: removable, jump, infinite
Intermediate Value Theorem: continuous function takes all intermediate values
lessons.examTip: Forgetting to check all three conditions — saying 'lim exists so it's continuous' misses checking f(a) is defined AND equals the limit; AP FRQ asks you to verify or justify continuity

topics: Formal definition: for every ε>0, there exists δ>0 such that |f(x)-L|<ε when 0<|x-a|<δ
Verifying limit claims with delta-epsilon proof
Why this definition captures the intuitive notion
lessons.examTip: Treating epsilon-delta as optional for AP — while not heavily tested, AP may ask conceptual questions about what the definition guarantees; understanding the logic is more important than formal proofs

topics: Computing one-sided limits for piecewise functions separately
Checking continuity at breakpoints using three conditions
Creating piecewise functions that are/are not continuous at a point
lessons.examTip: Not matching the correct piece of a piecewise function — at x=a, left limit uses the piece defined for x<a; right limit uses piece for x>a; AP gives piecewise functions and asks about continuity at breakpoints

lessons.lessonTitle: Intermediate Value Theorem and Extreme Value Theorem
topics: IVT: continuous on [a,b] → takes every value between f(a) and f(b)
EVT: continuous on closed interval → absolute max and min exist
Using IVT to prove existence of zeros
lessons.examTip: Using IVT on open intervals or discontinuous functions — IVT requires closed interval AND continuity; AP gives a function and asks to justify existence of a root; must cite both conditions

lessons.lessonTitle: Derivative as a Limit — The Formal Definition
topics: f'(a) = lim[(f(a+h)-f(a))/h] as h→0
Geometric meaning: slope of tangent line
Differentiability implies continuity (but not vice versa)
lessons.examTip: Confusing the difference quotient with the derivative — the difference quotient [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h gives average rate of change; the derivative is the limit as h→0; AP tests both interpretations

lessons.lessonTitle: Power Rule, Constant Multiple, Sum/Difference Rules
topics: d/dx[xⁿ] = nxⁿ⁻¹ for all real n
Linearity of differentiation: (cf)' = cf', (f+g)' = f'+g'
Differentiating polynomials and simple rational functions
lessons.examTip: Applying power rule to non-power functions — e^x, ln(x), sin(x) are NOT power functions; AP tests recognizing which rule applies to each function type

topics: d/dx[sinx] = cosx; d/dx[cosx] = -sinx; d/dx[tanx] = sec²x
Derivatives of all six trig functions and how to derive reciprocal function derivatives
Higher-order derivatives and their patterns for sine/cosine
lessons.examTip: Getting the sign wrong for d/dx[cosx] = -sinx (negative!) — AP constantly tests this; also d/dx[cotx] = -csc²x and d/dx[cscx] = -cscxcotx all have negatives

topics: Product rule: (fg)' = f'g + fg'
Quotient rule: (f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g²
When each rule applies and common simplification pitfalls
lessons.examTip: Using the quotient rule when product rule with a negative exponent is simpler — d/dx[x/sinx] can use quotient rule or product rule on x·(sinx)⁻¹; AP accepts either but tests both

lessons.lessonTitle: Derivatives of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
topics: d/dx[eˣ] = eˣ; d/dx[ln x] = 1/x
d/dx[aˣ] = aˣ ln a; d/dx[log_a x] = 1/(x ln a)
Logarithmic differentiation for complicated products/powers
lessons.examTip: Forgetting the ln a factor in d/dx[aˣ] = aˣ ln a — this only equals eˣ when a=e; AP gives base-2 or base-10 exponentials requiring the ln a factor

lessons.lessonTitle: Rates of Change and the Derivative's Meaning
topics: Instantaneous rate of change = derivative value at a point
Velocity as derivative of position; acceleration as derivative of velocity
Units of derivatives in applied contexts
lessons.examTip: Confusing average rate of change (secant slope) with instantaneous (tangent slope) — AP gives both a function and an interval and asks which calculation gives which; must distinguish Δf/Δx vs. f'(x)

lessons.lessonTitle: Differentiability at a Point — When Derivatives Fail
topics: Corners, cusps, vertical tangents — not differentiable but may be continuous
Checking differentiability of piecewise functions: both derivative one-sided limits must agree
Absolute value function and its non-differentiability at x=0
lessons.examTip: Assuming continuity implies differentiability — |x| is continuous but not differentiable at x=0; AP gives piecewise functions and asks to determine where both conditions hold

topics: L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a): tangent line as linear approximation
Differential dy = f'(x)dx and its use in estimation
Error in linear approximation from concavity (overestimate/underestimate)
lessons.examTip: Not identifying whether approximation is over or underestimate — if f is concave up, tangent line is below f (underestimate); if concave down, tangent is above (overestimate); AP tests this consistently

units.unitTitle: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit, and Inverse Functions

lessons.lessonTitle: Chain Rule — The Most Used Rule
topics: d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x): 'outside derivative times inside derivative'
Identifying outer and inner function in compositions
Multiple chain rule applications for nested compositions
lessons.examTip: Forgetting to multiply by the derivative of the inside — d/dx[sin(x²)] = cos(x²)·2x, not just cos(x²); AP has multiple-layer compositions where missing any chain factor loses points

topics: Differentiating both sides with respect to x; dy/dx appears when differentiating y
Chain rule applied to y terms: d/dx[y²] = 2y(dy/dx)
Finding slope of implicit curves at specific points
lessons.examTip: Not applying chain rule to y terms — d/dx[y³] = 3y²(dy/dx), not 3y²; AP implicit differentiation problems are entirely about correctly applying the chain rule to y expressions

topics: If g = f⁻¹, then g'(x) = 1/f'(g(x)): inverse function derivative
Derivatives of arcsin, arccos, arctan, arcsec
Using the inverse derivative formula when the inverse isn't explicitly given
lessons.examTip: Memorizing inverse trig derivatives without understanding the derivation — AP may give a non-standard function and its derivative, then ask for derivative of the inverse; must use g'(x) = 1/f'(g(x))

topics: Identifying related variables and differentiating an equation with respect to time
Chain rule gives rates: dV/dt = (dV/dr)(dr/dt)
Drawing a diagram to identify geometric relationships before differentiating
lessons.examTip: Plugging in fixed values before differentiating — must differentiate first, THEN substitute the given values; substituting first loses the rate terms and gives wrong equations

topics: Taking ln of both sides to simplify products and powers
Differentiating ln(f(x)) = ln(numerator) - ln(denominator)
y = x^x: logarithmic differentiation for variable base and exponent
lessons.examTip: Differentiating y = x^x directly as a power rule or exponential — neither works alone; must use logarithmic differentiation (take ln, differentiate implicitly); AP tests this function type

topics: Second derivative f'': concavity and acceleration
Third derivative and beyond: interpretation in context
Notation: f'', f''', f^(n), d²y/dx², d³y/dx³
lessons.examTip: Thinking higher derivatives follow the same pattern as the first — the pattern repeats with period 4 for sin/cos; polynomial derivatives eventually reach zero; AP asks for specific higher-order derivatives of trig functions

lessons.lessonTitle: Parametric Differentiation — dy/dx from x(t) and y(t)
topics: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt): dividing the rates
Second derivative: d²y/dx² = [d/dt(dy/dx)]/(dx/dt)
Tangent lines and horizontal/vertical tangents in parametric form
lessons.examTip: Computing d²y/dx² as (d²y/dt²)/(d²x/dt²) — WRONG; must differentiate dy/dx with respect to t, then divide by dx/dt; AP tests this exact misconception

lessons.lessonTitle: Implicit Curves — Tangent Lines and Second Derivatives
topics: Finding tangent line to implicit curve using implicit differentiation
Second derivative from implicit differentiation (substituting dy/dx expression)
Identifying horizontal and vertical tangents on implicit curves
lessons.examTip: Not simplifying dy/dx before finding d²y/dx² implicitly — AP gives y² = x³ and asks for second derivative; must differentiate dy/dx = 3x²/(2y) again implicitly, substituting dy/dx in the result

topics: Speed = |v(t)|; object moving right when v>0, left when v<0
Total distance vs. displacement: integrate |v(t)| vs. v(t)
lessons.examTip: Confusing total distance with displacement — displacement = ∫v(t)dt (can cancel); distance = ∫|v(t)|dt (always positive); AP repeatedly tests this distinction

lessons.lessonTitle: Rates of Change in Applied Contexts
topics: Interpreting derivative units in applied problems (e.g., gallons/minute)
Rate of change of a rate: second derivative in context
Average rate vs. instantaneous rate in word problems
lessons.examTip: Not including units in derivative interpretations — if f(t) is gallons and t is minutes, f'(t) is gallons per minute; AP FRQ deducts for missing units in contextual interpretations

topics: Differentiating geometric formulas implicitly with respect to time
Setting up: identify all variables, write the geometric relation, differentiate
Common setups: cone, sphere, triangle, Pythagorean
lessons.examTip: Not drawing and labeling the geometric figure before setting up — without a diagram it's easy to use the wrong relationship; AP FRQ partial credit includes the setup even if the arithmetic is wrong

lessons.lessonTitle: L'Hôpital's Rule — When and How to Use It
topics: Required: 0/0 or ∞/∞ form; differentiate numerator and denominator separately
Applying repeatedly when result is still indeterminate
Other indeterminate forms (0·∞, ∞-∞, 1^∞) requiring algebraic conversion
lessons.examTip: Applying L'Hôpital's to non-indeterminate forms — must verify 0/0 or ∞/∞ first; applying to a determinate limit gives a completely wrong answer; AP provides limits where checking first reveals it's not needed

topics: Tangent line as best linear approximation near a point
Estimating f(1.02) using L(x) = f(1) + f'(1)(x-1)
Relative and percentage error in approximations
lessons.examTip: Not stating whether the linear approximation is an overestimate or underestimate — AP FRQ always asks for justification; must state concavity and connect it to whether the tangent line is above/below the curve

lessons.lessonTitle: Tangent Lines and Normal Lines to Curves
topics: Tangent line: slope = f'(a); normal line: slope = -1/f'(a)
Finding x-intercept of tangent line for Newton's method concept
Tangent to parametric and implicit curves
lessons.examTip: Using the wrong slope for normal line — normal slope is the NEGATIVE RECIPROCAL of tangent slope; AP gives a curve and asks for both lines at a point; negative reciprocal is the key step

topics: Exponential growth/decay: dP/dt = kP → P(t) = P₀eᵏᵗ
Doubling time and half-life from k
Logistic model: dP/dt = kP(1 - P/M)
lessons.examTip: Solving exponential growth with separation of variables algebraically but making ln errors — dP/P = k dt → ln|P| = kt + C → P = Aeᵏᵗ; sign of k determines growth vs. decay; AP tests whether k is positive or negative in context

lessons.lessonTitle: Implicit and Related Rate Problems — Advanced Setups
topics: Multi-step related rates with trigonometry or Pythagorean theorem
When to use implicit differentiation vs. explicit solving
Verifying reasonableness of related rate answers
lessons.examTip: Getting the sign of a rate wrong — if a shadow is getting longer, its rate should be positive; if a distance is decreasing, its rate is negative; AP tests rate sign interpretation in context

lessons.lessonTitle: Mean Value Theorem — The Central Theorem
topics: MVT: if f continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then f'(c) = [f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a) for some c
Geometric interpretation: tangent line parallel to secant somewhere
Using MVT to justify existence of certain derivative values
lessons.examTip: Stating MVT conclusion without verifying its hypotheses — must first confirm continuity on closed interval AND differentiability on open interval; AP FRQ requires citing both conditions

lessons.lessonTitle: Extreme Values — Finding Absolute Max and Min
topics: Closed interval method: check critical points AND endpoints
Critical points: f'(x) = 0 or f'(x) undefined
Absolute vs. local extrema: local can't be absolute if endpoint is higher/lower
lessons.examTip: Forgetting to check endpoints when finding absolute extrema on closed intervals — the absolute max/min might be at an endpoint, not a critical point; AP closed-interval problems always require endpoint check

lessons.lessonTitle: First Derivative Test for Local Extrema
topics: Sign chart for f': positive→negative = local max; negative→positive = local min
f'(x) not changing sign at critical point = neither max nor min (inflection)
Connecting sign of f' to increasing/decreasing behavior
lessons.examTip: Forgetting to check sign CHANGES, not just the sign of f' at the critical point — must check sign on BOTH sides; AP gives complicated f'(x) and expects correct sign analysis in each interval

topics: f'' > 0: concave up; f'' < 0: concave down
Second derivative test: f'(c)=0 and f''(c)>0 → local min; f''(c)<0 → local max
Inflection points where concavity changes (f'' changes sign)
lessons.examTip: Calling every zero of f'' an inflection point — f'' must CHANGE SIGN; f'' = 0 at a point where it doesn't change sign is NOT an inflection point; AP tests this with f'' = x⁴ at x=0

topics: Connecting f, f', f'' behaviors: reading one graph to infer others
Identifying intervals of increase/decrease, concavity, and extrema
Sketching f when given f' graph (and vice versa)
lessons.examTip: Confusing f and f' on a graph — when given f' graph, positive f' means f is increasing (not that f is positive); AP regularly gives f' graph and asks for properties of f

topics: Write objective function and constraint; substitute constraint to get single-variable function
Find critical points of objective function; check second derivative or sign chart
Verify the answer makes contextual sense
lessons.examTip: Not verifying the critical point is a minimum/maximum in context — finding f'(c)=0 is not enough; must show it's the type (max or min) the problem asks for; AP FRQ requires justification

lessons.lessonTitle: Rolle's Theorem and Mean Value Theorem Applications
topics: Rolle's theorem: special case of MVT when f(a)=f(b) → f'(c)=0
Using MVT to bound function values
Applying MVT to differential equations and existence arguments
lessons.examTip: Using Rolle's theorem when f(a) ≠ f(b) — Rolle's requires equal values at endpoints; if they differ, use the full MVT instead; AP may give a function and ask which theorem applies

lessons.lessonTitle: Particle Motion — Using Derivatives to Analyze
topics: When particle changes direction: v(t) changes sign (zero crossing with sign change)
Total distance traveled: sum of |displacement| in each interval
Acceleration and speed: speeding up when a and v have same sign
lessons.examTip: Confusing 'changes direction' with 'v=0' — the particle changes direction when v changes SIGN at zero; if v just touches zero without changing sign, the particle doesn't change direction

topics: ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C: antiderivative notation and constant of integration
Basic antiderivative rules: power, trig, exponential
Initial conditions determining the specific antiderivative
lessons.examTip: Forgetting +C in indefinite integrals — AP always deducts for missing constant; also, C must be determined from given initial conditions, not just written as an unknown

lessons.lessonTitle: Definite Integrals as Area and Accumulation
topics: Riemann sums: left, right, midpoint as approximations
∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx as signed area: negative for portions below x-axis
Properties: linearity, reversal of limits, splitting interval
lessons.examTip: Adding all areas as positive when function dips below axis — definite integral counts area below x-axis as negative; for total area, integrate |f(x)|; AP tests whether you're asked for integral or area

lessons.lessonTitle: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus — Both Parts
topics: FTC Part 1: d/dx[∫ₐˣ f(t)dt] = f(x)
FTC Part 2: ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b) - F(a)
Connecting differentiation and integration as inverse processes
lessons.examTip: Not applying chain rule with FTC Part 1 when the upper limit is a function — d/dx[∫ₐᵍ⁽ˣ⁾ f(t)dt] = f(g(x))·g'(x); AP tests this with g(x) = x², 2x, sin(x)

topics: Identifying u = g(x) and du = g'(x)dx to simplify integrand
Adjusting limits of integration for definite integral substitution
Recognizing when substitution applies: look for a function and its derivative
lessons.examTip: Forgetting to change the limits of integration when using u-sub on a definite integral — either change limits to u-values OR substitute back to x before evaluating; AP accepts either method if executed correctly

topics: Net change = ∫rate dt: fundamental applied interpretation
Displacement = ∫v dt; total distance = ∫|v| dt
Accumulation function F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t)dt and its properties
lessons.examTip: Not interpreting the integral as accumulated net change — AP gives a rate function and asks for total amount; answer is ∫rate dt PLUS initial amount; forgetting the initial value loses points

topics: ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C; ∫1/x dx = ln|x| + C (absolute value matters!)
∫sinx dx = -cosx + C; ∫cosx dx = sinx + C
∫sec²x dx = tanx + C; ∫1/(1+x²) dx = arctan(x) + C
lessons.examTip: Writing ∫1/x dx = ln(x) without absolute value — must write ln|x| + C; for a definite integral where x stays positive, |x|=x, but on AP FRQ the general antiderivative requires absolute value

lessons.lessonTitle: Numerical Integration — Riemann Sums and Trapezoidal Rule
topics: Left, right, midpoint Riemann sums and their over/underestimate relationship to concavity
Trapezoidal rule: ½(f(a)+f(b))(b-a) for trapezoids
Error analysis: midpoint and trapezoidal rules have opposite concavity biases
lessons.examTip: Applying over/underestimate rules for Riemann sums without checking concavity — if f is increasing, left-sum underestimates; if f is concave up, trapezoidal overestimates; AP gives a function and asks which applies

topics: ∫ₐᵃ f dx = 0; ∫ₐᵇ f dx = -∫ᵦᵃ f dx
Even/odd function integrals on symmetric intervals
Combining integrals: splitting and combining with common limits
lessons.examTip: Not recognizing odd function symmetry — ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x)dx = 0 if f is odd; = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx if even; AP gives an integral with symmetric limits and expects you to identify the function parity

topics: Slope field: plotting f'=F(x,y) as slope segments at each point
Matching a DE to its slope field from pattern analysis
Sketching solution curves through initial conditions on slope fields
lessons.examTip: Drawing solution curves that cross slope segments instead of being tangent — solution curves must be tangent to the slope field at every point; AP gives a slope field and asks to sketch a specific solution

topics: Step size h and its effect on accuracy
Error accumulation: Euler's method overestimates/underestimates based on concavity
lessons.examTip: Using the new x value in the slope calculation for a given step — Euler's method uses the CURRENT point's slope to advance; AP gives a DE with initial condition and asks for Euler approximation at a specific x

topics: Separating dy/dx = f(x)g(y) into (1/g(y))dy = f(x)dx then integrating both sides
Applying initial conditions to find C (the specific solution)
Verifying solutions satisfy the original DE
lessons.examTip: Forgetting to include the constant C on BOTH sides when separating — when integrating both sides, C can be combined into one constant on one side; AP FRQ expects the full solution process shown step by step

topics: dP/dt = kP → P(t) = P₀eᵏᵗ: the canonical separable DE
k>0: growth; k<0: decay; half-life = -ln2/k
Newton's law of cooling: dT/dt = k(T - T_ambient)
lessons.examTip: Applying exponential model to non-proportional growth — dP/dt = k means LINEAR growth, not exponential; dP/dt = kP means exponential; AP tests whether you correctly identify the model from the DE

topics: dP/dt = kP(1-P/M): logistic DE; M is carrying capacity
Solution approaches M as t→∞; fastest growth when P = M/2
Inflection point at P = M/2 on logistic curve
lessons.examTip: Not connecting the inflection point to M/2 — the logistic curve has its inflection (fastest growth) when P = M/2; AP gives M and asks when growth is maximum

topics: Checking y = f(x) satisfies dy/dx = F(x,y) by substitution
Initial condition verification
General solution (with C) vs. particular solution (specific C)
lessons.examTip: Verifying only the initial condition and not the DE — must substitute y into the DE AND check f(x₀) = y₀; AP FRQ explicitly asks to 'verify' or 'show' which requires both steps

lessons.lessonTitle: Accumulation and Net Change from Rate Functions
topics: Total amount = initial + ∫rate dt (net change theorem)
When rate is negative, the accumulated quantity decreases
Multiple processes: net rate = inflow rate - outflow rate
lessons.examTip: Treating ∫rate dt as the total quantity rather than the CHANGE — if tank starts with 100 gallons and ∫(inflow-outflow)dt = 30, final amount is 130; AP gives an initial value that must be added

topics: Predator-prey system: coupled DEs
Equilibrium solutions and stability
Phase plane analysis: solution curves in y₁-y₂ space
lessons.examTip: Solving coupled systems as two independent DEs — they're coupled; changing y₁ affects dy₂/dt and vice versa; AP Physics C and advanced AP Calc may present coupled systems at a conceptual level

topics: A = ∫[top-bottom] dx for vertical slices; = ∫[right-left] dy for horizontal slices
Finding intersection points to determine limits of integration
Choosing the correct orientation when curves intersect multiple times
lessons.examTip: Not checking which function is on top throughout the interval — if curves intersect, the top function may switch; must split the integral at intersection points and take [top-bottom] in each sub-interval

lessons.lessonTitle: Volumes by Disk and Washer Methods
topics: Disk: V = π∫[f(x)]² dx (rotation around x-axis)
Washer: V = π∫([f(x)]² - [g(x)]²) dx (hole in the middle)
Rotation around y-axis or other axes: change integration variable
lessons.examTip: Using disk instead of washer when there's a gap between the curve and the axis — if the region doesn't touch the axis of rotation, there's a hole and the washer method is required

topics: V = 2π∫x·f(x) dx for rotation around y-axis with vertical slices
Shell radius and shell height for horizontal and vertical shells
Choosing disk/washer vs. shell based on ease of setup
lessons.examTip: Confusing which axis requires which method — rotating around the y-axis with vertical slices uses shells (2πx); using horizontal slices (dy) uses washers; AP accepts either if set up correctly

lessons.lessonTitle: Volumes of Solids with Known Cross Sections
topics: V = ∫A(x) dx where A(x) is cross-sectional area perpendicular to x-axis
Common cross sections: squares, semicircles, equilateral triangles
Identifying the function that gives the side/diameter of each cross section
lessons.examTip: Using the function value as the area directly — if cross section is a square with side = f(x), area = [f(x)]²; AP gives a specific cross section type and expects the correct area formula

topics: Arc length: L = ∫√(1 + [f'(x)]²) dx
Surface area of revolution: SA = 2π∫f(x)√(1+[f'(x)]²) dx
Parametric arc length: L = ∫√([x'(t)]² + [y'(t)]²) dt
lessons.examTip: Forgetting to include the radical factor in surface area — adding the 2πf(x) factor without √(1+[f']²) gives circumference × height, which undercounts the actual surface area of a curved surface

topics: f_avg = (1/(b-a))∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx
Mean Value Theorem for integrals: f(c) = f_avg for some c in [a,b]
Interpreting average value in context (e.g., average temperature, average velocity)
lessons.examTip: Confusing average value (1/(b-a)∫f dx) with average rate of change ([f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a)) — they're completely different; AP gives a function and an interval and specifies which average

lessons.lessonTitle: Integration in Motion Problems — Total Distance
topics: Displacement = ∫v(t) dt; total distance = ∫|v(t)| dt
Net change = ∫rate dt + initial value for final position
When particle is moving in different directions in different intervals
lessons.examTip: Computing ∫v dt for total distance — this gives NET displacement (positive and negative cancel); for total distance, must integrate |v(t)| by splitting at zeros where v changes sign

topics: Rate in minus rate out = net rate; final = initial + ∫net rate dt
Traffic flow, tank filling/draining, population changes
Finding when accumulated amount reaches a specific value
lessons.examTip: Not adding the initial value to the integral — the integral gives CHANGE, not total amount; AP scenarios start with a given initial condition that must be included; final = initial + ∫(net rate)dt

lessons.lessonTitle: Limits Review and L'Hôpital's Rule — BC Depth
topics: Indeterminate forms beyond 0/0: 0·∞, ∞-∞, 1^∞, 0^0, ∞^0
Converting all to 0/0 or ∞/∞ before applying L'Hôpital's
Limits involving e^x and ln x at infinity
lessons.examTip: Applying L'Hôpital's to 0·∞ directly — must rewrite as 0/0 or ∞/∞ first; AP BC tests the conversion step explicitly

lessons.lessonTitle: Continuity on Closed Intervals and IVT Applications
topics: IVT to prove existence of solutions
Uniform continuity concept
Lipschitz conditions for uniqueness of ODE solutions
lessons.examTip: Not citing both IVT hypotheses (continuity + closed interval) when proving root existence — AP FRQ requires explicit justification, not just 'by IVT'

lessons.lessonTitle: Differentiation Rules — BC Speed and Fluency
topics: Chain, product, quotient rules in rapid succession
Derivatives of all six trig and inverse trig functions
Implicit differentiation for complex relations
lessons.examTip: Slow chain rule execution on multi-layer compositions — BC exam is time-pressured; must recognize and differentiate sin²(e^(x²)) in one pass without step-by-step rewriting

topics: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt); d²y/dx² = [d/dt(dy/dx)]/(dx/dt)
Concavity of parametric curves from second derivative sign
Arc length in parametric form: ∫√(x'² + y'²) dt
lessons.examTip: Computing d²y/dx² as (y'')/(x'') — wrong; must differentiate dy/dx with respect to t, then divide by dx/dt

topics: Differentiating complex implicit relations with product and chain rules
Finding d²y/dx² implicitly by differentiating dy/dx again
Tangent lines at multiple points on the same curve
lessons.examTip: Not substituting dy/dx expression when computing second implicit derivative — AP BC gives y²= x³-x and asks for d²y/dx²; must substitute the first derivative result into the second derivative expression

topics: dy/dx for polar: (dr/dθ · sinθ + r·cosθ)/(dr/dθ · cosθ - r·sinθ)
Horizontal tangents: dy/dθ = 0; vertical tangents: dx/dθ = 0
Rate of change of r with respect to θ
lessons.examTip: Finding horizontal tangent by setting dr/dθ = 0 instead of dy/dθ = 0 — horizontal tangent requires y'(θ) = 0 in polar form, not dr/dθ = 0 (that's only tangent to r itself)

topics: Indeterminate forms in limits from physical models
Applying L'Hôpital's multiple times when needed
Connection to Taylor series as alternative to L'Hôpital
lessons.examTip: Not recognizing when Taylor series is faster than L'Hôpital — for lim (sinx - x)/x³, Taylor expansion is far cleaner; AP BC often rewards either approach but Taylor is less error-prone

lessons.lessonTitle: Optimization and Related Rates — BC Complexity
topics: Multi-constraint optimization requiring Lagrange multipliers concept
Related rates with implicit geometric relations
Newton's method and iterative root-finding
lessons.examTip: Not verifying which critical point is the global optimum in multi-variable setups — AP BC gives scenarios with multiple critical points; must test all and compare values

lessons.lessonTitle: Graphical Analysis — f, f', f'' Across BC Contexts
topics: Reading and constructing graphs of f from graphs of f'
Inflection points from sign changes of f''
MVT and Rolle's theorem application in proofs
lessons.examTip: Identifying local max/min from f' without confirming sign change — AP BC gives graphs of f' with zero crossings; must confirm the sign changes, not just identify zeros

lessons.lessonTitle: Extreme Values in Parametric and Polar Forms
topics: Finding extrema of r(θ) in polar form
Finding extrema of arc length or area in parametric
Second derivative test for parametric curves
lessons.examTip: Finding critical θ values from r'(θ) = 0 when looking for max/min of the curve's position — AP BC may ask for the maximum distance from origin, which requires r'(θ)=0, not dy/dθ=0

lessons.lessonTitle: Integration by Parts — When and How
topics: ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du; LIATE for choosing u
Tabular integration for repeated integration by parts
Definite integrals using integration by parts with limits
lessons.examTip: Choosing u as the function that gets more complicated when differentiated — LIATE: Logarithm, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential; the first applicable type is u

topics: Decomposing A/(x-r)(x-s) into partial fractions
Integrating 1/(x-a) = ln|x-a| + C from partial fractions
Long division first when degree of numerator ≥ denominator
lessons.examTip: Skipping long division when numerator degree ≥ denominator degree — partial fraction decomposition only works for proper fractions; must divide first to get proper rational + polynomial

lessons.lessonTitle: Improper Integrals — Infinite Limits and Discontinuities
topics: Type I: infinite limits → ∫ₐ^∞ f dx = lim_{b→∞} ∫ₐᵇ f dx
Type II: discontinuous integrand → limit at point of discontinuity
Convergence/divergence: p-integral ∫₁^∞ 1/xᵖ dx converges iff p>1
lessons.examTip: Evaluating improper integrals without converting to a limit — must write lim and take it explicitly; AP FRQ requires showing the limit notation, not just plugging in ∞

topics: Trig substitution for √(a²-x²), √(a²+x²), √(x²-a²)
Completing the square to prepare for trig substitution or arctan form
Choosing the right substitution from the form of the integrand
lessons.examTip: Using trig substitution without restricting the range of the substitution variable — for x = asinθ, need θ ∈ [-π/2, π/2]; AP BC expects you to show the restriction and convert back correctly

lessons.lessonTitle: Integration of Parametric and Polar Functions
topics: Area under parametric curve: A = ∫y dx = ∫y(t)x'(t)dt
Area in polar: A = ½∫r² dθ
Arc length for polar: L = ∫√(r² + (dr/dθ)²) dθ
lessons.examTip: Forgetting the factor of ½ in polar area formula — A = ½∫r² dθ (not ∫r² dθ); AP consistently tests this factor; also must correctly identify limits θ₁ and θ₂ from the curve description

lessons.lessonTitle: Separable DEs and Logistic Growth — BC Depth
topics: Solving logistic DE by partial fractions and integration
Equilibrium stability analysis from sign of dP/dt
Approximating logistic behavior at early (exponential) and late (plateau) stages
lessons.examTip: Not solving the logistic DE fully — AP BC FRQ asks for the explicit solution P(t); must use partial fractions to integrate 1/[P(M-P)] and solve for P

lessons.lessonTitle: Euler's Method and Numerical Error Analysis
topics: Comparing Euler's method accuracy at different step sizes
Error direction from concavity of solution curve
Improved Euler (Heun's) method concept
lessons.examTip: Not connecting Euler error direction to concavity — Euler overestimates when concave down, underestimates when concave up; AP BC asks to justify whether the approximation is an over or underestimate

lessons.lessonTitle: Area and Volume — BC Integration Methods
topics: Area between polar curves: A = ½∫(r_outer² - r_inner²)dθ
Volume from parametric curves
Shell, disk, washer for all rotation axes
lessons.examTip: Using incorrect limits for area between polar curves — find intersections by setting r₁(θ)=r₂(θ); the limits must correctly capture the region; AP BC gives two polar curves and expects the correct setup

lessons.lessonTitle: Arc Length in Multiple Coordinate Systems
topics: Cartesian: L = ∫√(1+[f'(x)]²)dx
Parametric: L = ∫√(x'²+y'²)dt
Polar: L = ∫√(r²+(dr/dθ)²)dθ
lessons.examTip: Mixing up which arc length formula applies — AP BC gives a curve in one of three forms; must identify the form and apply the corresponding formula; polar arc length is the most commonly confused

units.unitTitle: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates, and Vector-Valued Functions

topics: Eliminating parameter to find Cartesian form
dy/dx and d²y/dx² for parametric curves
Speed = √(x'² + y'²); distance traveled = ∫speed dt
lessons.examTip: Computing distance as displacement (∫velocity components separately) — total distance traveled requires integrating speed = √(x'²+y'²), not integrating x'(t) and y'(t) separately

topics: Converting between polar (r,θ) and Cartesian (x,y)
Graphing common polar curves: rose curves, limaçons, cardioids, spirals
Symmetry tests in polar: replacing θ with -θ, π-θ
lessons.examTip: Not identifying the type of polar curve before graphing — AP BC gives r = 2+3cosθ (limaçon with inner loop) and expects you to sketch it; recognizing curve type from the equation form is essential

lessons.lessonTitle: Area and Arc Length in Polar
topics: A = ½∫ₐᵇ r² dθ: area swept by radius vector
Area between polar curves using outer minus inner
Finding intersection points of polar curves (including pole)
lessons.examTip: Missing intersections at the pole — two curves can both pass through the origin at DIFFERENT θ values; AP BC tests whether you find ALL intersections, including the pole as a special case

topics: r(t) = x(t)î + y(t)ĵ; r'(t) = velocity vector
Speed, displacement, total distance from vector functions
Unit tangent vector T = r'/|r'|
lessons.examTip: Confusing velocity vector with speed — velocity is r'(t) (a vector with direction); speed is |r'(t)| (a scalar); AP BC tests that displacement uses ∫r'(t)dt while total distance uses ∫|r'(t)|dt

topics: Position from velocity by integration with initial condition
Acceleration vector and its decomposition into tangential and normal components
Curvature κ = |r' × r''|/|r'|³
lessons.examTip: Not using vector integration correctly — ∫r'(t)dt + r(0) gives position; must integrate EACH component and add the initial position vector component-by-component

topics: Monotone convergence theorem: bounded + monotone → converges
L'Hôpital for sequence limits involving ∞/∞ or 0/0
Squeeze theorem for sequences
lessons.examTip: Confusing sequence convergence with series convergence — a sequence {aₙ} can converge even if the series Σaₙ diverges (e.g., aₙ = 1/n converges to 0 but Σ1/n diverges); AP BC tests this distinction

lessons.lessonTitle: Series Convergence Tests — The Full Toolkit
topics: Geometric series: Σarⁿ converges iff |r|<1, sum = a/(1-r)
p-series: Σ1/nᵖ converges iff p>1
Comparison, limit comparison, ratio, root, integral tests
lessons.examTip: Using the ratio test for p-series or geometric series — ratio test gives inconclusive result (L=1) for p-series; use p-series test directly; AP BC tests choosing the right convergence test for the given series

topics: Alternating series test: alternating signs, decreasing |aₙ|→0
Alternating series error bound: |error| ≤ first omitted term
Absolute vs. conditional convergence distinction
lessons.examTip: Thinking alternating series always converge — must verify terms are decreasing AND approach 0; if |aₙ| doesn't approach 0, even an alternating series diverges; AP tests this necessary condition

lessons.lessonTitle: Power Series — Radius and Interval of Convergence
topics: Ratio test to find radius of convergence R
Testing endpoints separately (ratio test gives inconclusive at endpoints)
Interval of convergence vs. radius of convergence
lessons.examTip: Forgetting to test endpoints after finding the radius — the interval of convergence requires checking both endpoints by substitution; each may converge or diverge and must be tested separately

lessons.lessonTitle: Taylor and Maclaurin Series — Building Polynomial Approximations
topics: Taylor series centered at a: Σ[f^(n)(a)/n!](x-a)ⁿ
Common Maclaurin series: eˣ, sinx, cosx, 1/(1-x), ln(1+x)
Building new series from known ones by substitution and differentiation
lessons.examTip: Not using known Maclaurin series to build new ones — AP BC gives sin(x²) and expects substitution into the sinx series, not re-deriving; building from known series is faster and less error-prone

topics: Lagrange error bound: |error| ≤ M|x-a|^(n+1)/(n+1)! where M = max|f^(n+1)|
Using error bound to determine degree needed for given accuracy
Comparing Taylor error to alternating series error bound
lessons.examTip: Finding M as the derivative value at c instead of the maximum value on the interval — M must be the MAXIMUM of |f^(n+1)| on the entire interval from a to x; AP asks for the error bound, requiring correct M identification

topics: Differentiating and integrating power series term-by-term (valid within ROC)
Multiplying power series for products like eˣsinx
Using ∫power series to compute ∫(sinx/x)dx type integrals
lessons.examTip: Differentiating/integrating power series and forgetting to adjust the constant C and the shifted index — AP BC asks to use the series for 1/(1-x) to find a series for ln(1-x) by integrating; must include +C

lessons.lessonTitle: Series in Applied Problems — Using Taylor Polynomials
topics: Approximating function values with degree-n Taylor polynomial
Using series to evaluate difficult limits (better than L'Hôpital for some)
Error analysis: when is a Taylor approximation 'good enough'?
lessons.examTip: Not using Taylor series to simplify limit problems — lim(1-cosx)/x² is easy with Taylor (cosx ≈ 1 - x²/2 + ...) but tedious with L'Hôpital applied twice; AP BC rewards recognizing the more efficient approach

lessons.lessonTitle: Rates of Change and Average vs. Instantaneous Rate
topics: Average rate of change = (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a) as slope of secant
Instantaneous rate of change as limit of average rates
Concavity: positive second differences indicate concave up
lessons.examTip: Confusing average rate over interval with instantaneous rate at a point — AP Precalc specifically tests interpreting rate of change from tables and graphs; the slope of secant vs. tangent distinction is core

topics: End behavior from leading term: degree and sign of leading coefficient
Zeros: multiplicity determines whether graph crosses or touches x-axis
Factor theorem and polynomial division
lessons.examTip: Saying 'even multiplicity bounces' without explaining why — the factored form (x-r)² creates a local minimum or maximum AT r because the factor can't change sign; AP asks to justify the behavior

lessons.lessonTitle: Complex Numbers and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
topics: Complex roots come in conjugate pairs for real polynomials
Factoring over ℂ vs. over ℝ: all polynomials factor completely over ℂ
Degree of polynomial = number of complex zeros (counting multiplicity)
lessons.examTip: Counting only real zeros — a degree-4 polynomial has 4 zeros total (real or complex); if it has 2 real zeros, it must have 2 complex zeros forming a conjugate pair

topics: Vertical asymptote where denominator = 0 and numerator ≠ 0
Hole (removable discontinuity) where both numerator and denominator = 0 after factoring
Horizontal asymptote from degree comparison of numerator and denominator
lessons.examTip: Calling every zero of denominator a vertical asymptote — first factor and cancel; if the zero cancels, it's a hole; AP gives expressions requiring you to identify whether holes or asymptotes appear at specific x-values

topics: Sign chart method: test values in intervals between zeros
Solving f(x) > 0 from factored form
Using graphs to identify solution sets for inequalities
lessons.examTip: Not checking all intervals when solving polynomial inequalities — must test ONE value in each interval between zeros; AP gives a degree-4 polynomial inequality and expects the complete interval solution

topics: Parent function 1/x and its transformations: shifts, stretches, reflections
Oblique asymptote when degree of numerator = degree of denominator + 1
Complete rational function graph: zeros, holes, asymptotes, intercepts
lessons.examTip: Missing oblique asymptotes — when numerator degree exceeds denominator degree by 1, there's an oblique (slant) asymptote; AP Precalc tests identifying it from long division

topics: (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)): domain restriction from inside function
Inverse function: reflecting over y=x; f⁻¹(f(x)) = x
Finding inverse algebraically: swap x and y, solve for y
lessons.examTip: Confusing f(g(x)) domain with f's domain — must first restrict g's range to fit f's domain; AP gives f and g and asks for domain of f∘g, which may be more restricted than either domain alone

lessons.lessonTitle: Modeling with Polynomial and Rational Functions
topics: Choosing appropriate function type from data pattern
Regression: recognizing polynomial vs. rational behavior
Contextual interpretation of function parameters
lessons.examTip: Fitting any model without verifying residuals or reasonableness — AP Precalc may give a data table and ask which function type fits; must identify the pattern (constant differences vs. constant ratios)

lessons.lessonTitle: Exponential Growth vs. Decay — The Constant Ratio Property
topics: Exponential function: f(x) = abˣ; constant percent change per unit x
Growth factor b > 1 vs. decay factor 0 < b < 1
Percent change = (b-1) × 100% per unit time
lessons.examTip: Confusing the growth factor with the percent change — if b=1.05, growth is 5% per period, not 105%; AP Precalc tests the conversion between b and percent change

topics: e as the base where the function equals its own derivative rate
Continuous growth: A = Peʳᵗ vs. periodic: A = P(1+r/n)^(nt)
Converting between base-b and base-e forms
lessons.examTip: Confusing effective annual rate with continuous rate — A=Pe^(0.05t) does NOT give 5% annual growth; the effective annual rate = e^0.05 - 1 ≈ 5.13%; AP tests this comparison

topics: log_b(xy) = log_b x + log_b y; log_b(xʸ) = y log_b x
Change of base formula: log_b x = ln x / ln b
Solving exponential equations by taking logarithms of both sides
lessons.examTip: Applying log properties in reverse: log(x+y) ≠ log(x) + log(y) — the sum rule applies to products inside the log; AP tests these common misconceptions with trick problems

lessons.lessonTitle: Inverse Relationship Between Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
topics: f(x) = bˣ and g(x) = log_b x are inverses: f(g(x)) = x
Graph of logarithm as reflection of exponential over y=x
Domain and range: exponential (all x) → logarithmic (x > 0 only)
lessons.examTip: Taking log of negative numbers — ln(x) only exists for x > 0; AP gives equations where after solving, a negative solution must be rejected as extraneous

topics: Vertical/horizontal shifts and stretches of y = bˣ and y = log_b x
Effect of transformation on asymptote location
Matching transformed function to its graph
lessons.examTip: Shifting the asymptote incorrectly — y=2^(x-3)+4 has horizontal asymptote y=4 (not y=0); AP tests reading asymptote shifts from transformed forms

topics: Linearizing exponential data with semi-log plot: log(y) vs. x gives straight line
Log-log plot linearizes power functions: log(y) vs. log(x) gives straight line
Finding a and b from the linearized graph
lessons.examTip: Not connecting the linearized plot slope to the original parameters — on a semi-log plot, slope = log(b) for y=abˣ; must convert back to find b = 10^(slope); AP Precalc specifically tests this

lessons.lessonTitle: Modeling with Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
topics: Fitting exponential models to data: using two points to find a and b
Logarithmic regression for bounded growth models
Exponential vs. linear model selection from constant vs. percent change
lessons.examTip: Using an exponential model when differences are constant (linear) — if the data shows constant ABSOLUTE change per period, the model is linear; if PERCENT change is constant, it's exponential; AP gives data and asks which applies

topics: pH, Richter, decibel scales as logarithmic
Interpretation: each unit on a log scale represents a multiplicative factor
Solving problems comparing two measurements on log scales
lessons.examTip: Adding pH values instead of converting — pH 5 is 10× more acidic than pH 6, not twice as acidic; AP gives two pH values and asks for the ratio of hydrogen ion concentrations, requiring the exponential back-conversion

lessons.lessonTitle: The Unit Circle and Radian Measure
topics: Radian definition: arc length / radius; conversion factor π/180
Unit circle coordinates at key angles: 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, and quadrantal
sinθ and cosθ as y and x coordinates on unit circle
lessons.examTip: Using degree mode in calculator for radian problems — AP Precalc problems specify units; when radians are given, must use radian mode; not specifying units or using wrong mode is the most common calculator error

lessons.lessonTitle: Sine and Cosine Functions — Properties and Graphs
topics: Period, amplitude, midline, phase shift from y = Asin(B(x-C)) + D
Finding parameters from graph: period = 2π/B, amplitude = |A|, midline = D
Transformations and their effect on each parameter independently
lessons.examTip: Confusing B with period — period = 2π/B, not B; if B=2, period = π; AP gives a graph and asks for the equation, requiring you to calculate B from the observed period

topics: Graphs of all six trig functions: asymptotes, period, range
tanθ = sinθ/cosθ; asymptotes where cosθ = 0
Cotangent period is π (same as tangent); secant/cosecant period is 2π
lessons.examTip: Using wrong period for tangent — period of tan and cot is π, not 2π; AP tests this by asking for the period of y = tan(3x)

lessons.lessonTitle: Inverse Trig Functions — Domain, Range, Notation
topics: arcsin, arccos, arctan ranges: [-π/2,π/2], [0,π], (-π/2,π/2)
Evaluating: arcsin(√2/2) = π/4, not 3π/4 (range restriction)
Composition: sin(arcsin x) = x; arcsin(sin x) = x only in range
lessons.examTip: Giving all angles where sin = 0.5 instead of the principal value — arcsin returns ONLY the principal value; arcsin(0.5) = π/6, not also 5π/6; AP tests this range restriction

topics: Pythagorean identities: sin²+cos²=1, tan²+1=sec², 1+cot²=csc²
Sum/difference, double angle, half angle formulas
Using identities to rewrite expressions in equivalent form
lessons.examTip: Trying to solve a trig identity by treating it like an equation — to prove an identity, manipulate ONE side to match the other; never move terms across the equals sign

topics: General solution: sine and cosine have period 2π, tangent has period π
Using inverse trig to find reference angle, then all solutions in given interval
Factoring trig equations: 2sin²x - sinx - 1 = 0 style
lessons.examTip: Giving only one solution to a trig equation — most have multiple solutions in [0, 2π); AP asks for ALL solutions in a given interval; must identify the reference angle and use symmetry to find others

topics: Converting (r,θ) ↔ (x,y): x=rcosθ, y=rsinθ, r²=x²+y²
Graphing cardioids, rose curves, limaçons, circles, spirals
Symmetry tests in polar coordinates
lessons.examTip: Not understanding that polar curves can pass through the same point with different (r,θ) representations — the pole is at r=0 for any θ; two curves can intersect at the pole even if they don't have the same θ

topics: Fitting a sinusoidal model to data: finding A, B, C, D from max/min
Midline = (max+min)/2; Amplitude = (max-min)/2; Period from data
Interpreting sinusoidal model parameters in context
lessons.examTip: Finding phase shift by trial and error instead of calculation — C can be found by identifying when the function hits the midline going upward and reading that as x = C; AP gives a data scenario and expects a justified model

units.unitTitle: Functions Involving Parameters, Vectors, and Matrices

topics: Plotting parametric curve from (x(t), y(t)) tables
Eliminating parameter to identify Cartesian form
Direction of travel: arrow showing t increasing
lessons.examTip: Eliminating the parameter without specifying the valid range — the parametric form may only trace part of the Cartesian curve; must state the domain of t to correctly restrict the curve

topics: Vector components: v = ⟨a,b⟩; magnitude |v| = √(a²+b²)
Unit vectors: v̂ = v/|v|; direction angle θ = arctan(b/a)
Addition, scalar multiplication, dot product
lessons.examTip: Confusing direction angle with slope — direction angle is arctan(vy/vx); slope is vy/vx; AP Precalc asks for the angle (in degrees or radians), not the slope of the vector

lessons.lessonTitle: Vectors in Applied Contexts — Force, Velocity, Navigation
topics: Resultant force/velocity from vector addition
Component form from magnitude and direction
Relative velocity problems with moving reference frames
lessons.examTip: Not converting direction to standard angle before computing components — 'N 30° E' means 60° from positive x-axis, not 30°; AP gives compass bearings requiring careful angle conversion

topics: Matrix multiplication: dimensions must match; AB ≠ BA in general
Determinant and its meaning for 2×2 and 3×3 matrices
Inverse matrix: A⁻¹ exists iff det(A) ≠ 0
lessons.examTip: Multiplying matrices by multiplying corresponding elements (Hadamard vs. standard multiplication) — matrix multiplication is row-by-column, not element-by-element; AP tests a 2×3 times 3×2 multiplication

topics: Augmented matrix and row reduction (Gaussian elimination)
Cramer's rule for 2×2 and 3×3 systems
Classifying systems: unique solution, no solution, infinitely many solutions
lessons.examTip: Applying Cramer's rule when det(A) = 0 — Cramer's rule only works when det ≠ 0; if det = 0, the system is either inconsistent or dependent; AP tests recognizing which case applies

lessons.lessonTitle: Sequences and Series — Arithmetic and Geometric
topics: Arithmetic sequence: aₙ = a₁ + (n-1)d; sum Sₙ = n(a₁+aₙ)/2
Geometric sequence: aₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹; sum Sₙ = a₁(1-rⁿ)/(1-r)
Infinite geometric series: S = a₁/(1-r) for |r|<1
lessons.examTip: Using the geometric sum formula when |r|≥1 — infinite geometric series only converges for |r|<1; AP gives r=1.2 and asks if the series converges; answer is no

lessons.lessonTitle: Conic Sections — Circles, Ellipses, Parabolas, Hyperbolas
topics: Standard forms: center, vertices, foci for each conic
Eccentricity: e=0 (circle), 0<e<1 (ellipse), e=1 (parabola), e>1 (hyperbola)
Converting from general form to standard form by completing the square
lessons.examTip: Not completing the square correctly when converting conics — groups of x and y terms must each be completed separately; AP gives a general equation and expects standard form identification of the conic

topics: Normal distribution and the empirical rule (68-95-99.7)
Conditional probability and independence
Interpreting statistical plots in algebraic function contexts
lessons.examTip: Applying the empirical rule to non-normal distributions — the 68-95-99.7 rule ONLY applies to normal distributions; AP may give a skewed distribution and test whether these percentages apply

topics: Categorical vs. quantitative; discrete vs. continuous
Observational study vs. experiment: why experiments can show causation
Voluntary response bias and why such samples are unreliable
lessons.examTip: Confusing association with causation from observational data — correlation from an observational study cannot establish causation; AP FRQ expects 'association' not 'cause' language for non-experimental data

lessons.lessonTitle: Displaying Data — Graphs and Their Interpretation
topics: Dotplots, histograms, stemplots: when each is appropriate
Describing distributions: SOCS (shape, outliers, center, spread)
Comparing two distributions on the same scale
lessons.examTip: Describing histograms without all four SOCS components — AP FRQ always requires shape, center, spread, AND outliers; missing any component loses partial credit

lessons.lessonTitle: Measures of Center — Mean vs. Median
topics: Mean: sensitive to outliers; median: resistant to outliers
Skewed distributions: mean pulled toward tail, median stays near center
When to prefer each measure of center in context
lessons.examTip: Using mean to describe a skewed distribution — for skewed income data, the median is more representative; AP asks to choose AND justify which measure is more appropriate given the shape

lessons.lessonTitle: Measures of Spread — Standard Deviation and IQR
topics: IQR = Q3 - Q1: resistant to outliers; used with median
Standard deviation: sensitive to outliers; used with mean
1.5×IQR rule for identifying outliers
lessons.examTip: Applying the standard deviation outlier rule instead of 1.5×IQR — for box plots and five-number summaries, the 1.5×IQR rule applies; standard deviation-based rules are for normal distributions; AP tests which is appropriate

lessons.lessonTitle: Normal Distribution and the Empirical Rule
topics: 68-95-99.7 rule for normal distributions
Standardizing: z = (x-μ)/σ; z-score interpretation
Using z-table to find proportions and percentiles
lessons.examTip: Applying the empirical rule without confirming normality — the 68-95-99.7 rule ONLY applies to normal distributions; AP gives a distribution and may not confirm normality; must check before applying

topics: Converting between x-values and z-scores
Finding probability P(a < X < b) from z-table
Inverse normal: finding x given a percentile
lessons.examTip: Using the z-score formula with sample mean (x̄) instead of population mean (μ) when finding individual observation probabilities — z = (x-μ)/σ for individual values; z = (x̄-μ)/(σ/√n) for sample means

topics: Minimum, Q1, Median, Q3, Maximum and how to compute each
Modified boxplot: outliers displayed as individual points
Comparing distributions using side-by-side boxplots
lessons.examTip: Plotting suspected outliers in the box or whisker instead of as separate dots — AP specifically requires identifying and plotting outliers (beyond 1.5×IQR from quartiles) as individual points in modified boxplots

lessons.lessonTitle: Density Curves and the Area-as-Probability Convention
topics: Density curve: area under curve = probability; total area = 1
Uniform distribution: flat density curve, equal areas for equal intervals
Normal density curve properties and connection to probability
lessons.examTip: Treating the height of a density curve as probability — height is density (probability per unit interval), not probability; only AREA gives probability; AP tests this with uniform distributions where height > 1 is possible

topics: Describing scatterplot: direction, form, strength, outliers
Pearson r: measures linear association only, ranges from -1 to +1
Correlation does not imply causation — lurking variables
lessons.examTip: Using r to describe non-linear associations — r only measures linear strength; a strong curved relationship can have r ≈ 0; AP gives a curved scatterplot and tests whether r is an appropriate summary

topics: ŷ = a + bx; slope b = r(sy/sx); intercept a = ȳ - bx̄
Interpreting slope: predicted change in y per unit increase in x
Interpreting intercept in context (often not meaningful)
lessons.examTip: Describing slope without 'predicted' — in regression, the slope gives the PREDICTED (or average) change; for one specific observation the change may differ; AP FRQ deducts for missing 'predicted' or 'average'

topics: Residual = observed - predicted = y - ŷ
Residual plot: random scatter indicates good linear fit
Patterns in residual plot (curves, fans) indicate model problems
lessons.examTip: Calling a residual plot 'random' without looking for patterns — a curve in residuals means linear model is wrong; a funnel means non-constant variance; AP gives a residual plot and asks to interpret adequacy of the model

topics: R² = proportion of variation in y explained by linear relationship with x
R² ranges from 0 to 1; larger = better fit
Connection between r and R²: R² = r² for simple linear regression
lessons.examTip: Interpreting r² as 'r squared percent' — must say 'r² of the variation in y is explained by the linear relationship with x'; AP FRQ requires the full contextual interpretation with units/variables named

topics: Outlier in residuals: large |residual|, poor fit to line
High-leverage point: extreme x value, may not have large residual
Influential point: removal substantially changes the regression line
lessons.examTip: Confusing outlier (large residual) with influential point (changes the line when removed) — a high-leverage point on the regression line has small residual but is still influential; AP tests these as distinct concepts

topics: Log or square root transformation to linearize curved data
Power model: log(y) vs. log(x); exponential model: log(y) vs. x
Identifying which transformation achieves linearity from residual plots
lessons.examTip: Applying a transformation without verifying it achieves linearity — AP gives a residual plot after transformation and expects confirmation that the pattern is now random; linearization must be verified, not assumed

lessons.lessonTitle: Two-Way Tables and Association in Categorical Data
topics: Marginal, joint, and conditional distributions from two-way tables
Identifying association: conditional distributions differ across categories
Simpson's paradox: direction of association reverses when data is combined
lessons.examTip: Using marginal frequencies instead of conditional frequencies to assess association — must compare conditional distributions (row or column percentages); AP gives a two-way table and asks whether variables are associated

topics: Three explanations for association: causation, common cause, coincidence
Confounding variable: associated with both X and Y
Why randomized experiments can establish causation but observational studies can't
lessons.examTip: Describing a confounding variable as one that 'affects the outcome' — it must also be associated with the explanatory variable; AP FRQ asks to 'identify and explain' a potential confounding variable, requiring both parts

lessons.lessonTitle: Sampling Methods — Which to Use and Why
topics: SRS: every individual equally likely to be chosen
Stratified: divide into strata, SRS within each
Cluster: divide into groups, randomly select entire groups; systematic sampling
lessons.examTip: Confusing stratified with cluster sampling — stratified takes a few from EACH group; cluster sampling takes ALL from SOME groups; AP gives a sampling description and asks to identify the method

topics: Undercoverage, nonresponse, response bias: mechanisms of each
Voluntary response: self-selected samples overrepresent extreme opinions
Wording effects in survey questions
lessons.examTip: Calling any sampling error 'bias' — bias is SYSTEMATIC error in one direction; random sampling error is expected and decreases with sample size; AP tests whether a described error is bias or random variation

topics: Randomization, replication, control: why each is necessary
Control group vs. placebo group (not the same)
Blinding: single-blind and double-blind designs
lessons.examTip: Confusing control group with placebo group — control group receives no treatment; placebo group receives an inert treatment; both are controls, but AP distinguishes why placebos are used (to account for psychological effects)

topics: Block design: grouping similar experimental units before randomization
Matched pairs: simplest block design (pairing individuals or before/after)
Why blocking reduces variability and increases sensitivity to treatment effects
lessons.examTip: Describing blocking as 'randomly dividing into groups' — blocking is NOT random; you group similar units first, then randomize within blocks; AP asks to identify what constitutes an appropriate blocking variable

topics: Random assignment allows causal conclusions (unlike random sampling)
Scope of inference: random sample allows generalization; random assignment allows causation
Four conditions for establishing causation
lessons.examTip: Claiming random sampling establishes causation — random SAMPLING allows generalization to the population; random ASSIGNMENT allows causal conclusions; AP tests this two-condition distinction for scope of inference

topics: Informed consent, anonymity vs. confidentiality, IRB oversight
Ethical issues in observational vs. experimental research
Data privacy and protection
lessons.examTip: Confusing anonymity (researcher doesn't know identity) with confidentiality (researcher knows but won't disclose) — AP occasionally tests these distinctions and why they matter for bias and participant protection

topics: Designing a simulation to model a probability problem
Assigning digits/outcomes to represent probabilities
Running repetitions and computing empirical probability from results
lessons.examTip: Assigning multiple digits to the same outcome without justifying the proportion — if P(success) = 0.3, must assign exactly 30 of 100 equally-likely outcomes; AP FRQ asks to describe simulation design clearly and precisely

topics: Loaded questions, leading questions, and double-barreled questions
Order effects in survey items
Pilot testing and question validation
lessons.examTip: Not identifying the specific type of bias in a survey question — AP asks to identify AND explain the source; saying 'it's biased' without naming the mechanism (e.g., response bias from question wording) loses points

units.unitTitle: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions

topics: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B); simplifies if mutually exclusive
P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B|A); simplifies if independent
Complement rule: P(Aᶜ) = 1 - P(A)
lessons.examTip: Applying the simplified multiplication rule P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B) without checking independence — must first verify independence; AP gives probabilities and tests whether events are independent before using the product rule

topics: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B): conditional probability formula
Independence: P(A|B) = P(A); knowing B doesn't change probability of A
Testing independence from a two-way table
lessons.examTip: Confusing mutually exclusive with independent — mutually exclusive events (P(A and B)=0) are NOT independent (unless P(A)=0); if two events can't occur together, knowing one occurred tells you something about the other

lessons.lessonTitle: Discrete Random Variables — Expected Value and Variance
topics: E(X) = Σ[x·P(X=x)]: probability-weighted average
Var(X) = Σ[(x-μ)²·P(X=x)]; SD(X) = √Var(X)
Transformations: E(aX+b) = aE(X)+b; Var(aX+b) = a²Var(X)
lessons.examTip: Adding standard deviations instead of variances — Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) for independent X, Y; SD(X+Y) ≠ SD(X) + SD(Y); must add variances first, then take square root

topics: Four binomial conditions: BINS (Binary, Independent, fixed N, same p)
P(X=k) = C(n,k)pᵏ(1-p)^(n-k)
μ = np; σ = √(np(1-p)); normal approximation when np≥10 and n(1-p)≥10
lessons.examTip: Using binomial when independence assumption is violated — sampling without replacement from small populations violates independence; must check whether n is less than 10% of population for independence to hold approximately

topics: P(X=k) = (1-p)^(k-1)·p: number of trials until first success
E(X) = 1/p; Var(X) = (1-p)/p²
Geometric vs. binomial: geometric has no fixed n
lessons.examTip: Confusing binomial (count of successes in fixed n trials) with geometric (number of trials until first success) — AP gives a scenario and tests which distribution applies; the presence or absence of a fixed number of trials is the key distinction

topics: P(X=a) = 0 for continuous distributions; only intervals have nonzero probability
Uniform distribution: f(x) = 1/(b-a) on [a,b]
CDF: F(x) = P(X≤x) = cumulative area
lessons.examTip: Computing P(X=2.5) as nonzero for a continuous distribution — for continuous distributions, single values have probability zero; must compute P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = area; AP gives an interval and expects area calculation

topics: Standardizing to Z and using z-table or calculator normalcdf
Finding values from percentiles using invNorm
Combining normal random variables: X+Y still normal if X, Y normal
lessons.examTip: Not recognizing that a sum of normal random variables is also normal — AP gives the means and variances of two normal RVs and asks for probabilities about their sum; must compute new mean = μ₁+μ₂ and variance = σ₁²+σ₂² first

lessons.lessonTitle: Law of Large Numbers and Simulation
topics: LLN: sample proportion approaches true probability as n grows
Gambler's fallacy: past outcomes don't change future probabilities in independent trials
Using simulation to estimate probabilities empirically
lessons.examTip: Confusing LLN (proportion converges) with the gambler's fallacy (each trial has changed probability to 'balance out') — individual trials are independent; LLN is about long-run averages, not any specific next outcome

topics: p̂ is the sample proportion; its sampling distribution is approximately normal for large n
Center: μ_p̂ = p; spread: σ_p̂ = √(p(1-p)/n)
Large sample condition: np ≥ 10 and n(1-p) ≥ 10 for normality
lessons.examTip: Using the formula σ_p̂ = √(p̂(1-p̂)/n) with the observed p̂ instead of the true p — when the true p is known (null hypothesis), use p; only substitute p̂ when p is unknown (confidence intervals)

topics: μ_x̄ = μ; σ_x̄ = σ/√n (standard error)
Central Limit Theorem: x̄ is approximately normal for n ≥ 30 regardless of population shape
Population must be normal OR n large for x̄ to be normal
lessons.examTip: Applying CLT to small samples from skewed populations — CLT requires n ≥ 30 (approximately) for non-normal populations; if n=10 and population is skewed, x̄ is NOT approximately normal

lessons.lessonTitle: Central Limit Theorem — The Key Insight
topics: Why the CLT works: averaging many random values concentrates the distribution
CLT applies to means, not individual observations
Population distribution vs. sampling distribution of x̄
lessons.examTip: Applying CLT to individual observations — CLT describes the distribution of SAMPLE MEANS, not individual data values; P(X > 5) for one randomly chosen value uses the original distribution, not the normal approximation

topics: p̂₁ - p̂₂: center = p₁-p₂; variance = p₁(1-p₁)/n₁ + p₂(1-p₂)/n₂
x̄₁ - x̄₂: center = μ₁-μ₂; variance = σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂
Independence assumption required between samples
lessons.examTip: Adding standard errors instead of variances when combining two sampling distributions — must add VARIANCES and then take the square root; SE(x̄₁ - x̄₂) = √(σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂)

topics: Unbiasedness: E(estimator) = parameter
Variability: smaller standard error = more precise estimator
Bias-variance tradeoff in statistical estimation
lessons.examTip: Confusing bias (systematic error) with variability (precision) — an estimator can be unbiased but imprecise (high variance) or precise but biased; AP asks to describe an estimator in terms of BOTH properties

lessons.lessonTitle: Effect of Sample Size on Sampling Distributions
topics: Larger n: smaller standard error (SE = σ/√n)
Doubling n reduces SE by factor of √2, not 2
Sampling distribution narrowing as n increases visualized
lessons.examTip: Saying 'larger sample gives smaller standard deviation' — larger sample reduces the STANDARD ERROR (of the mean), not the population standard deviation or individual observation variability; AP tests this language precision

topics: t-distribution: heavier tails, used when σ unknown; degrees of freedom = n-1
t* vs. z*: t* > z* for same confidence level (heavier tails require wider interval)
t-distribution approaches z as degrees of freedom → ∞
lessons.examTip: Using z* instead of t* when σ is unknown — whenever population standard deviation is unknown (almost always in practice), must use t*; AP tests when each distribution is appropriate

lessons.lessonTitle: Conditions for Inference — The Three Checks
topics: Random condition: data from random sample or randomized experiment
Normal/Large Sample condition: n≥30 or normal population or no strong skew
Independence condition: population ≥ 10n (10% condition)
lessons.examTip: Skipping condition checks and going straight to calculations — AP FRQ requires explicitly stating, checking, and verifying all three conditions; missing any condition check typically costs 1 point on the scoring rubric

topics: CI: p̂ ± z*(√(p̂(1-p̂)/n)); using p̂ (not p) in SE for CI
Interpreting CI: 'We are 95% confident the true proportion is in...'
Margin of error, confidence level, sample size relationships
lessons.examTip: Saying 'there is a 95% probability the true proportion is in this interval' — the true proportion is FIXED (not random); the interval either contains it or not; correct language is 'we are 95% confident'

topics: H₀: p = p₀ vs. Hₐ: p ≠ p₀ (two-sided) or one-sided
Test statistic: z = (p̂ - p₀)/√(p₀(1-p₀)/n); using p₀ in SE for tests
P-value interpretation: probability of getting this result or more extreme IF H₀ true
