lessons.examTip: Students write Keq including solid and liquid concentrations — pure solids and pure liquids have CONSTANT concentrations (activity = 1) and are excluded from the expression; water in aqueous reactions is excluded

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Predict Which Way a Reaction Will Shift
topics: Le Chatelier's principle: stress and response
Q vs. K comparison to predict shift direction
Effect of temperature on Keq value (not just shift)
lessons.examTip: Students say adding a catalyst shifts equilibrium — a catalyst speeds up BOTH forward and reverse reactions equally; it reaches equilibrium faster but does NOT shift the equilibrium position or change Keq

lessons.lessonTitle: Acid-Base Equilibrium: What pH Really Measures
topics: Ka and Kb expressions
pH = −log[H⁺], pOH, and Kw = 10⁻¹⁴
Strong vs. weak acids: complete vs. partial dissociation
lessons.examTip: Students set up weak acid ICE tables then forget to check if the approximation (x << [HA]₀) is valid — if x/[HA]₀ > 5%, the quadratic must be solved; blindly using the approximation when invalid gives wrong pH

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Assign and Track Electron Bookkeeping (Oxidation States)
topics: Oxidation state rules: O = −2, H = +1, sum rules
Identifying oxidation vs. reduction (OIL RIG)
Oxidizing agent vs. reducing agent — which is which
lessons.examTip: Students confuse the oxidizing agent with the species being oxidized — the OXIDIZING AGENT causes oxidation in another species but is ITSELF REDUCED; the reducing agent is oxidized; always identify both the agent and what happens to it

lessons.lessonTitle: How Galvanic Cells Convert Chemistry to Electricity
topics: Anode (oxidation) and cathode (reduction)
Salt bridge function: maintaining charge neutrality
Cell notation: anode | solution || solution | cathode
lessons.examTip: Students reverse anode and cathode in galvanic cells — in galvanic (voltaic) cells, ANODE is negative and CATHODE is positive (opposite of electrolytic cells); mnemonic: Red Cat / An Ox (reduction at cathode, oxidation at anode)

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Calculate Cell Voltage and Spontaneity
topics: Standard reduction potentials (E°red)
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode
Relationship between E°cell, ΔG°, and Keq
lessons.examTip: Students multiply E° values by stoichiometric coefficients — standard reduction potentials are INTENSIVE properties (they don't scale with moles); only ΔG° and Keq scale; E°cell stays the same regardless of how many electrons are transferred

lessons.lessonTitle: How Electrolytic Cells Force Non-Spontaneous Reactions
topics: Electrolysis vs. galvanic cells
Faraday's law: moles of electrons and product mass
Applications: electroplating and water electrolysis
lessons.examTip: Students forget to convert coulombs to moles of electrons in Faraday's law problems — moles of e⁻ = charge(C) / 96,485 (C/mol); then use stoichiometry of the half-reaction; skipping the conversion to moles is the most common error

lessons.lessonTitle: The Difference Between How Fast and How Much (Speed vs. Velocity)
topics: Scalar vs. vector quantities
Distance vs. displacement
Average vs. instantaneous velocity
lessons.examTip: Students calculate average speed as (v₁ + v₂)/2 — this only works if acceleration is constant; average velocity = total displacement / total time, which is always correct; these give different answers for non-uniform motion

lessons.lessonTitle: What Constant Acceleration Really Looks Like
topics: Kinematic equations: v = v₀ + at, x = v₀t + ½at², v² = v₀² + 2ax
Graphs: slope of x-t is v, slope of v-t is a
Free fall: a = −9.8 m/s² always downward
lessons.examTip: Students use g = +9.8 m/s² and then wonder why answers are wrong — pick a consistent positive direction; if upward is positive, acceleration due to gravity is −9.8 m/s²; sign errors on g cause wrong answers on every free-fall problem

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Horizontal and Vertical Motion Are Independent
topics: Projectile motion: ax = 0, ay = −g
Range, max height, and time of flight equations
Launch angle optimization: 45° maximizes range on level ground
lessons.examTip: Students think a horizontally launched projectile falls slower because it moves forward — horizontal velocity has NO effect on vertical fall; both a dropped ball and a horizontally thrown ball hit the ground at the same time from the same height

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Add Vectors That Aren't in a Straight Line
topics: Vector components: Ax = A cos θ, Ay = A sin θ
Adding vectors by components
Resultant magnitude and direction
lessons.examTip: Students use the angle measured from the wrong reference axis — always specify the angle as measured from the x-axis (or explicitly state from which axis); θ in Ax = A cos θ is measured from the POSITIVE x-axis, not the vertical

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Objects Don't Naturally Stop Moving
topics: Newton's First Law: inertia and reference frames
Identifying inertial vs. non-inertial frames
Friction as an external force, not a natural tendency
lessons.examTip: Students say objects slow down because 'they run out of force' — Newton's 1st Law says objects in motion STAY in motion unless acted on by a net external force; friction is the external force causing deceleration, not nature

lessons.lessonTitle: How Force, Mass, and Acceleration Are Exactly Connected
topics: Newton's Second Law: Fnet = ma
Free body diagrams: all forces on ONE object
Normal force and tension as constraint forces
lessons.examTip: Students draw forces on multiple objects in one free body diagram — FBDs must show forces on ONE object only; the normal force on a block on a ramp is perpendicular to the ramp surface, NOT straight up

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Action-Reaction Pairs Never Cancel Each Other
topics: Newton's Third Law: equal and opposite force pairs
Why Newton's 3rd law pairs act on DIFFERENT objects
Identifying correct action-reaction pairs
lessons.examTip: Students say the book on a table is in equilibrium because 'gravity equals normal force — they're action-reaction pairs' — the normal force and gravity are NOT a Newton's 3rd law pair (they act on the same object); the N3 pair of gravity on book is gravity on Earth from book

lessons.lessonTitle: How Friction Works — and When to Use Which Equation
topics: Static vs. kinetic friction: fs ≤ μsN, fk = μkN
Why μs > μk
Friction on inclined planes
lessons.examTip: Students apply kinetic friction to a stationary object — use STATIC friction (up to maximum fs = μsN) when the object is not moving; kinetic friction applies only WHILE sliding; the maximum static friction is GREATER than kinetic

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Objects Moving in Circles Must Have Inward Force
topics: Centripetal acceleration: ac = v²/r toward center
Centripetal force as net inward force (not a new force)
Why 'centrifugal force' is not real in inertial frames
lessons.examTip: Students add centrifugal force to their free body diagrams — centrifugal force does NOT exist in inertial frames; centripetal force is the NET result of REAL forces (tension, gravity, normal) pointing inward; never draw it as a separate force

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Work Is Not the Same as Effort
topics: Work: W = Fd cos θ
Zero work: perpendicular force, no displacement
Work-energy theorem: Wnet = ΔKE
lessons.examTip: Students say gravity does no work on a pendulum — gravity does positive work on the downswing (force and displacement both downward) and negative work on the upswing; only centripetal force does ZERO work (always perpendicular to motion)

lessons.lessonTitle: How Energy Is Stored and Released in Conservative Systems
topics: Gravitational PE = mgh, Spring PE = ½kx²
Conservation of mechanical energy (no friction)
Energy bar charts and accounting
lessons.examTip: Students use h = 0 inconsistently in the same problem — choose a reference height and KEEP IT; if you set the lowest point as h = 0, then use that same h = 0 for both sides of the energy equation

lessons.lessonTitle: Where Does Energy Go When Friction Is Present?
topics: Thermal energy generated by friction: Eth = fk × d
Energy conservation with nonconservative forces
Power: P = W/t = Fv
lessons.examTip: Students forget that the distance in Eth = fkd is the SLIDING distance between surfaces — for a block pulled up a ramp, it's the length of the ramp, not the vertical height; these are different and using the wrong one gives wrong answers

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Momentum Is Harder to Change Than Speed
topics: Impulse-momentum theorem: FΔt = Δp
Conservation of momentum in collisions
Elastic vs. inelastic collisions
lessons.examTip: Students think kinetic energy is conserved in all collisions — KE is conserved ONLY in elastic collisions; in inelastic collisions, KE is converted to internal energy (heat, deformation); momentum is ALWAYS conserved if no external forces act

lessons.lessonTitle: What Actually Moves in a Wave (It's Not the Medium)
topics: Transverse vs. longitudinal waves
Wave parameters: amplitude, wavelength, frequency, speed
v = fλ relationship
lessons.examTip: Students say 'the water moves forward in a water wave' — water molecules in a transverse wave move PERPENDICULAR to wave propagation, not forward; a floating duck bobs up and down, not horizontally toward shore

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Waves Interfere and What the Patterns Mean
topics: Superposition principle: constructive and destructive interference
Path difference and phase difference
Standing waves: nodes and antinodes
lessons.examTip: Students think destructive interference destroys energy — energy is REDISTRIBUTED, not destroyed; where destructive interference occurs, the energy reappears at other locations (nodes have zero displacement but the energy is at antinodes)

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Strings and Pipes Produce Only Certain Frequencies
topics: Standing waves in strings: fn = nv/2L
Open and closed pipe harmonics
Why closed pipes only produce odd harmonics
lessons.examTip: Students apply the string formula to closed pipes — a closed pipe (one end open, one closed) has a NODE at the closed end and ANTINODE at the open end; fundamental = v/4L (not v/2L); only odd harmonics are present

lessons.lessonTitle: Why a Moving Source Changes the Pitch You Hear
topics: Doppler effect: source approaching vs. receding
Why the observer hears higher f as source approaches
Shock waves and sonic booms
lessons.examTip: Students flip the Doppler formula numerator and denominator — use f' = f × (v ± v_observer)/(v ∓ v_source); upper signs when approaching (increase), lower when receding (decrease); observer motion affects numerator, source motion affects denominator

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Like Charges Repel and What Controls the Force
topics: Coulomb's Law: F = kq₁q₂/r²
Electric field: E = F/q (force per unit charge)
Field lines: direction, density, and interpretation
lessons.examTip: Students double the force when charge is doubled and distance is also doubled — Coulomb's Law has r², so doubling r DECREASES force by 4×; doubling both charge and distance gives net change of 2/4 = ½ the original force

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Voltage and Energy Are Not the Same Thing
topics: Electric potential (V) vs. electric potential energy (PE = qV)
Equipotential lines and their relationship to field lines
Work done moving charge: W = qΔV
lessons.examTip: Students say 'higher voltage means more energy' without specifying the charge — electric potential energy = qV; a proton and an electron at the same potential have equal |PE| but the proton's is positive and the electron's is negative

lessons.lessonTitle: How Resistors Control Current in Circuits
topics: Ohm's Law: V = IR
Series and parallel resistor combinations
Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws
lessons.examTip: Students add resistors in parallel using the reciprocal formula but forget to take the final reciprocal — 1/Req = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ gives you 1/Req; you must take the reciprocal of that sum to get Req; the parallel combination is ALWAYS less than the smallest individual resistor

lessons.lessonTitle: How Moving Charges Create Magnetic Fields (and Vice Versa)
topics: Magnetic force on moving charge: F = qv × B (right-hand rule)
Force on current-carrying wire: F = IL × B
Magnetic field from long straight wire and solenoid
lessons.examTip: Students apply the right-hand rule without specifying the velocity direction of the charge — for negative charges, use the right-hand rule then REVERSE the direction; the magnetic force on an electron moving right in an upward B field points opposite to the force on a proton

lessons.lessonTitle: What It Means for a Relation to Be a Function
topics: Vertical line test
Domain, codomain, range distinction
Function notation: f(x) means output, not multiplication
lessons.examTip: Students write the range as all real numbers by default — the range is the set of ACTUAL OUTPUT values; always determine what y-values are actually achieved, not what's theoretically possible from the formula

lessons.lessonTitle: How Transformations Move and Reshape Graphs
topics: Vertical/horizontal shifts: f(x±h) and f(x)±k
Reflections: f(−x) and −f(x)
Stretches and compressions: af(x) and f(bx)
lessons.examTip: Students shift horizontally in the wrong direction — f(x − 3) shifts RIGHT 3 (not left); the sign inside the function is OPPOSITE to the direction of shift because you're replacing x with x−3, not adding 3 to x

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Inverse Functions Undo Each Other (And How to Find Them)
topics: Inverse function: swapping input and output
Horizontal line test for invertibility
Finding f⁻¹(x) algebraically: swap x and y, solve
lessons.examTip: Students confuse f⁻¹(x) with 1/f(x) — f⁻¹(x) is the INVERSE FUNCTION (swap x and y); 1/f(x) is the RECIPROCAL; these are completely different; f(x) = 2x has f⁻¹(x) = x/2 but 1/f(x) = 1/(2x)

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Combine Functions and What That Means
topics: Function operations: (f+g)(x), (f·g)(x)
Composition: (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x))
Domain restrictions in composed functions
lessons.examTip: Students evaluate f(g(x)) in the wrong order — (f∘g)(x) means apply g FIRST, then apply f to that result; they often compute g(f(x)) instead; always substitute the inner function result into the outer function

lessons.lessonTitle: Even, Odd, and Neither: Reading Symmetry Algebraically
topics: Even function: f(−x) = f(x) → y-axis symmetry
Odd function: f(−x) = −f(x) → origin symmetry
Testing algebraically, not just visually
lessons.examTip: Students test only one x-value to determine even/odd — a function must satisfy f(−x) = f(x) for ALL x in its domain to be even; one counterexample disproves it; always simplify f(−x) fully before concluding

lessons.lessonTitle: What the End Behavior of a Polynomial Tells You Before You Graph
topics: Leading term dominates for large |x|
Even/odd degree and positive/negative leading coefficient
Four end behavior cases
lessons.examTip: Students determine end behavior from the first term written, not the leading term — the leading term is the HIGHEST degree term; if a polynomial is written in non-standard form, identify the highest degree term first

lessons.lessonTitle: How Multiplicity of Zeros Controls Bouncing vs. Crossing
topics: Roots with odd multiplicity: graph crosses x-axis
Roots with even multiplicity: graph touches and bounces
Writing polynomial from given zeros
lessons.examTip: Students think double roots mean the graph barely crosses — a root with EVEN multiplicity means the graph TOUCHES but does not cross the x-axis; odd multiplicity means it CROSSES; multiplicity 1 = simple crossing

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Rational Functions Have Holes and Asymptotes (And Which Is Which)
topics: Vertical asymptotes vs. holes from factored form
Horizontal asymptote rules from degree comparison
Oblique asymptotes via polynomial division
lessons.examTip: Students make everything a vertical asymptote — a common factor that cancels creates a HOLE (removable discontinuity), not a vertical asymptote; the vertical asymptote comes from zeros of the denominator that DON'T cancel

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Divide Polynomials and Use the Remainder
topics: Polynomial long division
Synthetic division for (x − c) divisors
Remainder Theorem: f(c) = remainder
lessons.examTip: Students apply synthetic division to divisors like (x + 3) without changing the sign — synthetic division uses c where the divisor is (x − c); for (x + 3), c = −3, not +3; entering +3 gives completely wrong results

lessons.lessonTitle: Finding All Zeros: The Full Rational Root Strategy
topics: Rational Root Theorem: ±p/q candidates
Using synthetic division to test and deflate
Complex conjugate pairs and irreducible quadratics
lessons.examTip: Students stop after finding two real roots — the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra guarantees a degree-n polynomial has EXACTLY n roots (counting multiplicity) in the complex numbers; after finding real roots, check if remaining factor has complex roots

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Exponential Growth Eventually Beats Every Polynomial
topics: Exponential function f(x) = abˣ: base and growth/decay
Domain, range, and asymptote of exponential
Comparing linear, polynomial, and exponential growth rates
lessons.examTip: Students confuse exponential growth rate with percent increase — if b = 1.08, the growth rate is 8% PER PERIOD; the base directly encodes the growth factor, not the percent; b = 0.92 means 8% decay (1 − 0.92 = 0.08 = 8%)

lessons.lessonTitle: What a Logarithm Is Actually Asking
topics: log_b(x) = y means bʸ = x
Common log (base 10) and natural log (base e)
Graph of log as inverse of exponential
lessons.examTip: Students evaluate log_2(8) by calculating 2×8 or 8/2 — a logarithm asks 'what EXPONENT on the base gives this number?'; log_2(8) = 3 because 2³ = 8; always rewrite as the equivalent exponential equation to solve

lessons.lessonTitle: Logarithm Laws: Breaking Apart and Rebuilding Expressions
topics: Product: log(AB) = log A + log B
Quotient: log(A/B) = log A − log B
Power: log(Aⁿ) = n·log A
lessons.examTip: Students write log(A + B) = log A + log B — there is NO log law for the log of a sum; log(AB) = log A + log B (product rule applies to multiplication, NOT addition); this is the most common logarithm error

topics: Isolating the exponential, then taking log of both sides
Checking for extraneous solutions in log equations
Change of base formula
lessons.examTip: Students accept extraneous solutions in log equations — after solving, CHECK that the argument of EVERY log in the original equation is POSITIVE; log(negative number) is undefined, so solutions that make the argument ≤ 0 must be rejected

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Radians Are More Useful Than Degrees
topics: Radian definition: arc length / radius
Degree-radian conversions
Arc length and sector area formulas: s = rθ, A = ½r²θ
lessons.examTip: Students use degree measures in s = rθ — this formula REQUIRES θ in RADIANS; using degrees gives wrong answers; always convert to radians before applying arc length or sector area formulas

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Unit Circle Encodes All Trig Values
topics: Unit circle: (cos θ, sin θ) at angle θ
Reference angles and quadrant signs (ASTC)
Exact values at 0, π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2 and their multiples
lessons.examTip: Students memorize unit circle values without understanding reference angles — sin(5π/6) is not sin(5π/6) from scratch; 5π/6 is in Quadrant II with reference angle π/6; sin is positive in Q2, so sin(5π/6) = sin(π/6) = 1/2

lessons.lessonTitle: How Amplitude, Period, and Phase Shift Transform Trig Graphs
topics: y = A sin(Bx + C) + D: identifying each parameter
Period = 2π/|B|
Phase shift = −C/B (direction trap)
lessons.examTip: Students read phase shift as −C when it should be −C/B — for y = sin(2x − π), factor as sin(2(x − π/2)); phase shift is π/2 to the RIGHT, not π; always factor out B before reading the phase shift

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Inverse Trig Functions Have Restricted Ranges
topics: arcsin, arccos, arctan: restricted ranges
Why restrictions are necessary for invertibility
Solving trig equations on restricted vs. full domains
lessons.examTip: Students give all solutions when only the principal value is needed (or vice versa) — arcsin(x) returns ONE value in [−π/2, π/2]; when solving sin θ = 0.5 on [0, 2π], there are TWO solutions (π/6 and 5π/6); read the problem carefully for the domain

topics: Pythagorean identities: sin²+cos²=1 and derived forms
Sum and difference formulas
Double angle formulas: sin 2θ, cos 2θ
lessons.examTip: Students 'prove' identities by cross-multiplying both sides — proofs must be one-directional; transform ONE side only until it equals the other; never operate on both sides simultaneously as if it's an equation to solve

lessons.lessonTitle: What Makes a Sequence Arithmetic or Geometric
topics: Arithmetic: aₙ = a₁ + (n−1)d
Geometric: aₙ = a₁ · rⁿ⁻¹
Identifying from ratios vs. differences
lessons.examTip: Students apply arithmetic formula to geometric sequences — check: constant DIFFERENCE → arithmetic; constant RATIO → geometric; if successive terms multiply by the same factor, the sequence is geometric even if the terms grow rapidly

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Sum a Finite Arithmetic or Geometric Series
topics: Arithmetic series sum: Sₙ = n(a₁+aₙ)/2
Geometric series sum: Sₙ = a₁(1−rⁿ)/(1−r)
Setting up the formula: finding n, a₁, aₙ or r
lessons.examTip: Students confuse n (number of terms) with aₙ (the nth term value) — n is the COUNT of terms; if terms run from a₁ to a₁₀₀, n = 100; to find n when terms are listed as values, use the nth term formula first

lessons.lessonTitle: When an Infinite Geometric Series Has a Finite Sum
topics: Convergence condition: |r| < 1
Sum formula: S∞ = a₁/(1−r)
Why |r| ≥ 1 diverges
lessons.examTip: Students apply S∞ = a₁/(1−r) when |r| > 1 — this formula is only valid when |r| < 1 (series CONVERGES); for |r| ≥ 1, the series diverges (sum grows without bound); always check |r| before applying the formula

lessons.lessonTitle: What Makes an Argument Persuasive vs. Just Assertive
topics: Claim, evidence, warrant (Toulmin model)
Thesis that takes a genuine position
Why assertions without support are not arguments
lessons.examTip: Students write thesis statements that announce a topic rather than take a position — 'This essay will discuss climate change' is not a thesis; a thesis must be ARGUABLE ('Climate change policy fails because...'); evaluate every thesis: can a reasonable person disagree?

lessons.lessonTitle: How Logos, Ethos, and Pathos Work Together (Not in Isolation)
topics: Ethos: credibility through expertise, fairness, tone
Logos: logical structure and quality of evidence
Pathos: emotional connection to audience values
lessons.examTip: Students identify appeals as though they're separate — skilled arguments blend all three simultaneously; a statistic (logos) from a respected expert (ethos) that illustrates human suffering (pathos) does all three at once; label the dominant appeal but acknowledge blending

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Counterarguments Make Your Argument Stronger
topics: Concession-refutation structure
Steelmanning vs. straw man fallacy
Where to place counterargument for maximum effect
lessons.examTip: Students treat counterargument as admitting weakness — a well-handled counterargument INCREASES credibility (ethos) by showing the writer has considered other views; the key is to refute or qualify it, not just acknowledge it and move on

lessons.lessonTitle: Recognizing Logical Fallacies Before They Undermine Your Argument
topics: Ad hominem, false dichotomy, slippery slope
Hasty generalization and anecdotal evidence
Circular reasoning and appeal to authority
lessons.examTip: Students identify the fallacy name but can't explain WHY it undermines the argument — the explanation requires showing what VALID form of reasoning it violates; false dichotomy fails because it ignores the possibility of multiple solutions beyond the two presented

lessons.lessonTitle: Using Evidence Without Letting It Replace Your Voice
topics: Quote integration: framing, embedding, explaining
Paraphrase vs. summary vs. direct quote
Commentary as the writer's own analytical voice
lessons.examTip: Students drop quotes without analysis ('Quote sandwiching' without the bread) — every piece of evidence needs framing before (context) and analysis after (what it means for your argument); the analysis must advance your claim, not just re-describe the quote

lessons.lessonTitle: What Theme Is (and Why It's Not Just a Topic)
topics: Theme as a complete statement about human experience
How multiple elements work together to build theme
Distinguishing theme from moral or lesson
lessons.examTip: Students write theme as a single word ('loyalty') instead of a thematic statement — 'loyalty' is a topic; 'True loyalty sometimes requires betraying what others expect of you' is a theme; it must make a CLAIM about life

lessons.lessonTitle: How Authors Use Structure to Control Meaning
topics: Linear vs. non-linear narrative
In medias res, flashback, foreshadowing
How structure mirrors or ironizes content
lessons.examTip: Students describe structure without explaining its effect — saying 'the story uses flashback' earns no credit; you must explain WHAT the flashback reveals and HOW it changes the reader's understanding of the present-tense events

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Analyze a Character Beyond 'Describe Their Personality'
topics: Dynamic vs. static and round vs. flat characterization
Foil characters and what contrast reveals
Motivation, internal conflict, and character arc
lessons.examTip: Students confuse dynamic and round characters — a character can be ROUND (complex, many dimensions) but STATIC (doesn't change); a DYNAMIC character changes; these are independent axes; a flat character can be dynamic if they shift from one simple trait to another

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Point of View Is One of the Most Powerful Authorial Choices
topics: First person limitations vs. intimacy
Third person limited vs. omniscient tradeoffs
Unreliable narrator and dramatic irony
lessons.examTip: Students say 'first person is more relatable' without analyzing limitations — the key analytical move is explaining what the CHOSEN POV RESTRICTS as much as what it enables; first person limits information but creates intimacy; the restriction is often the point

lessons.lessonTitle: How Symbolism Works Without Being Heavy-Handed
topics: Building symbolic meaning through repetition and context
Conventional vs. contextual symbols
How to distinguish symbolism from coincidence in texts
lessons.examTip: Students assert a symbol without textual support — you must show how the TEXT builds the symbolic meaning through repetition, contrast, or explicit connection; 'the green light represents hope' requires tracing how Fitzgerald develops this meaning throughout, not just stating it

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Write a Literary Analysis That Makes a Real Argument
topics: Interpretive thesis vs. summary thesis
Close reading as primary evidence
Connecting textual evidence to the larger thematic argument
lessons.examTip: Students write plot summaries dressed up as analysis — every body paragraph must advance an ARGUMENT about meaning, not narrate events; the question to ask after each paragraph: 'So what? What does this prove about the author's message?'

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Evaluate Sources Before You Trust Them
topics: CRAAP test: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose
Primary vs. secondary sources
Bias in sources and how to use biased sources well
lessons.examTip: Students dismiss biased sources entirely — a biased source can be used as EVIDENCE OF a perspective or to demonstrate how a group framed an issue; the key is to acknowledge the bias and use it appropriately, not pretend it doesn't exist

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Your Argument Must Drive Your Research (Not the Other Way Around)
topics: Working thesis vs. finalized thesis
Research question development
Avoiding confirmation bias in source selection
lessons.examTip: Students use whatever sources support their pre-existing view — strong research requires actively seeking COUNTER-EVIDENCE and incorporating or refuting it; a paper that ignores opposing scholarship is academically weak regardless of how much support it accumulates

lessons.lessonTitle: Citation: How to Attribute Sources Without Interrupting Your Voice
topics: MLA in-text citation and works cited format
Signal phrases and attribution
Avoiding plagiarism through proper paraphrase
lessons.examTip: Students think paraphrasing means changing a few words — a proper paraphrase REPROCESSES the idea in your own sentence structure using your own vocabulary; just swapping synonyms while keeping the sentence structure is still considered plagiarism

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Structure a Long Argument That Doesn't Lose Its Thread
topics: Organizing by line of reasoning, not by source
Topic sentences that advance the argument
Transitions that show logical relationships
lessons.examTip: Students organize research papers by source (one paragraph per source) — papers must be organized by ARGUMENT; sources should appear wherever they support your claim in the argument structure, not in the order you found them

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Sentence Variety Is About Meaning, Not Just Sound
topics: Periodic vs. cumulative sentences and their effects
Short sentences for emphasis
Syntactic parallelism and its persuasive power
lessons.examTip: Students vary sentences randomly for 'style' — sentence length and type should serve MEANING; a very short sentence after long ones creates emphasis through contrast; use it where you want the reader to pause and feel the weight of an idea

lessons.lessonTitle: How Diction Shapes the Reader's Entire Experience
topics: Connotation vs. denotation and emotional weight
Formal vs. informal register and context
Precision of word choice in academic writing
lessons.examTip: Students use sophisticated vocabulary to 'sound smart' at the cost of clarity — diction should serve PRECISION and TONE, not display vocabulary; a simpler word used precisely is stronger than a complex word used vaguely

lessons.lessonTitle: How Tone Is Created and How to Analyze It Accurately
topics: Tone = author's attitude toward subject or audience
Multiple simultaneous tones
How diction, syntax, and figurative language converge to create tone
lessons.examTip: Students name a single broad tone word ('sad' or 'angry') — effective analysis uses SPECIFIC, nuanced tone words and traces which specific word choices and syntactic decisions CREATE that tone; 'melancholic' is better than 'sad'; showing HOW it's created is the actual skill

lessons.lessonTitle: How Figurative Language Compresses Meaning Into a Single Image
topics: Metaphor and simile: what the comparison reveals
Extended metaphor and conceit development
Irony types: verbal, situational, dramatic
lessons.examTip: Students identify the device but don't explain what the comparison REVEALS — 'the poet uses a metaphor comparing life to a river' is identification; the analysis must explain what the river comparison specifically says about the nature of life that a direct statement could not

lessons.lessonTitle: What Slope Really Means Beyond 'Rise Over Run'
topics: Slope as rate of change
Positive, negative, zero, and undefined slope
Interpreting slope in context (units matter)
lessons.examTip: Students calculate slope as Δx/Δy instead of Δy/Δx — slope is always VERTICAL change over HORIZONTAL change (rise/run = Δy/Δx); inverting the fraction gives the slope of the perpendicular line, which is a completely different line

lessons.lessonTitle: Three Forms of a Line — When to Use Which
topics: Slope-intercept: y = mx + b
Standard form: Ax + By = C
Point-slope: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
lessons.examTip: Students always convert to slope-intercept even when point-slope is faster — when given a point and a slope, point-slope form is directly applicable without solving for b; converting first wastes time and introduces arithmetic errors

lessons.lessonTitle: How Parallel and Perpendicular Lines Are Related
topics: Parallel lines: equal slopes
Perpendicular lines: slopes are negative reciprocals
Writing equations of parallel and perpendicular lines
lessons.examTip: Students negate the slope instead of taking the negative reciprocal for perpendicular lines — perpendicular slope = −1/m; for slope 2, perpendicular slope is −1/2, not −2; students who only negate get the sign right but still have the wrong answer

lessons.lessonTitle: Solving Systems by the Method That Fits the Problem
topics: Graphing, substitution, and elimination methods
When each method is most efficient
No solution vs. infinitely many solutions
lessons.examTip: Students always use substitution regardless of the equations — elimination is faster when coefficients are already equal or easily scaled; substitution requires extra algebra when both equations are in Ax + By = C form; choose method based on structure

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Solve and Graph Linear Inequalities
topics: Solving inequalities: same as equations except flip sign when dividing by negative
Graphing linear inequalities: dashed vs. solid line
Systems of inequalities: feasible region
lessons.examTip: Students forget to flip the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a NEGATIVE number — this is the single rule that makes inequalities different from equations; −2x > 6 gives x < −3, not x > −3; always check this when the variable has a negative coefficient

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Vertex Form Actually Tells You About the Parabola
topics: Vertex form: y = a(x − h)² + k
Vertex (h, k): h has sign flip
How 'a' controls width and direction of opening
lessons.examTip: Students read the vertex from y = a(x − h)² + k as (−h, k) without checking the sign — in y = (x − 3)² + 2, the vertex is (3, 2) because h = 3; in y = (x + 3)² + 2, the vertex is (−3, 2); the sign inside the parenthesis is OPPOSITE to the h-coordinate

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Factor Quadratics When the Leading Coefficient Isn't 1
topics: AC method for ax² + bx + c
Factoring by grouping
Checking factored form by expanding
lessons.examTip: Students apply trial-and-error factoring to ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 1 — the AC method is systematic: multiply a × c, find factors that add to b, split the middle term, then factor by grouping; random guessing is slow and misses answers

lessons.lessonTitle: The Quadratic Formula: When to Use It and How Not to Mess Up
topics: Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac)) / 2a
Discriminant: b² − 4ac and what it predicts
Setting quadratic = 0 before applying the formula
lessons.examTip: Students forget to set the equation equal to zero before applying the formula — the quadratic formula requires the form ax² + bx + c = 0; if the equation is x² + 3x = 4, rewrite as x² + 3x − 4 = 0 first, then identify a, b, c

lessons.lessonTitle: Completing the Square: The Technique Behind Everything
topics: Process: isolate x² term, add (b/2)² to both sides
Converting standard to vertex form
Why it works (creating a perfect square trinomial)
lessons.examTip: Students forget to add (b/2)² to BOTH sides — when completing the square, the value added to one side must also be added to the other; if a ≠ 1, divide through by a first before completing the square; skipping this step breaks the equation

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Discriminant Tells You Without Solving
topics: b² − 4ac > 0: two real roots
b² − 4ac = 0: one real (repeated) root
b² − 4ac < 0: no real roots (complex roots)
lessons.examTip: Students compute the discriminant but interpret a negative result as 'no answer' — b² − 4ac < 0 means no REAL roots; the quadratic has two COMPLEX (imaginary) conjugate roots; for Honors, these are ±i√|discriminant|/2a

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Add, Subtract, and Multiply Polynomials Without Losing Terms
topics: Combining like terms: matching degree and variable
Distributing multiplication: FOIL and beyond
Special products: (a+b)², (a−b)², (a+b)(a−b)
lessons.examTip: Students use FOIL for polynomials with more than two terms — FOIL only works for BINOMIAL × BINOMIAL; for trinomials, distribute each term of the first polynomial to every term of the second; using FOIL for (x²+x+1)(x+2) gives wrong answers

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Factoring Is Just Multiplication in Reverse
topics: GCF factoring first
Difference of squares: a² − b² = (a+b)(a−b)
Sum and difference of cubes
lessons.examTip: Students skip GCF factoring and proceed to more complex methods — always factor out the GCF FIRST; 2x² − 8 = 2(x² − 4) = 2(x+2)(x−2); students who skip GCF may not recognize the difference of squares pattern underneath

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Simplify Rational Expressions Without Canceling Too Much
topics: Factor completely before canceling
Domain restrictions from the original denominator
Simplifying vs. evaluating
lessons.examTip: Students cancel individual terms instead of factors — (x² + 3x) / x = x(x+3)/x = x+3; but (x + 3) / (x + 3) can ONLY be canceled as a unit; you cannot cancel part of a sum: (x+3)/(x+5) ≠ 3/5 even though students often do this

topics: Multiply: factor all, then cancel across numerators and denominators
Divide: multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor
Simplifying before multiplying reduces errors
lessons.examTip: Students forget to find the reciprocal when dividing rational expressions — division is multiplication by the RECIPROCAL of the second fraction; flip the second fraction, then multiply; taking the reciprocal of the entire expression, not just the numerator or denominator, is essential

lessons.lessonTitle: How Exponential Growth and Decay Models Work in Context
topics: y = a·bˣ: initial value a, growth/decay factor b
Growth (b > 1) vs. decay (0 < b < 1)
Finding b from a percent rate: b = 1 + r or 1 − r
lessons.examTip: Students write b = r (the rate) instead of b = 1 + r — for 6% annual growth, b = 1.06, not 0.06; writing y = a(0.06)ˣ gives a decay function; the base encodes the FACTOR, not the rate of change

lessons.lessonTitle: What Logarithms Ask and How to Evaluate Them
topics: log_b(x) = y ↔ bʸ = x
Common log (log₁₀) and natural log (ln)
Evaluating simple logarithms by asking 'what exponent?'
lessons.examTip: Students try to compute log₂(8) as 2÷8 or 2×8 — a logarithm asks 'what power of the base gives this number?'; rewrite as an exponential equation: 2? = 8 → ? = 3; this conversion is the only reliable method

topics: Taking log of both sides when bases can't be matched
Isolating the exponential before logging
Using change of base: log_b(x) = log(x)/log(b)
lessons.examTip: Students log both sides before isolating the exponential — solve 3·2ˣ = 48 by dividing both sides by 3 first to get 2ˣ = 16, THEN take the log; logging too early creates log(3·2ˣ) = log(48) which requires additional log rules to separate

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Describe a Data Set: Center and Spread
topics: Mean, median, mode: when each is appropriate
Range, IQR, standard deviation as spread measures
Effect of outliers on mean vs. median
lessons.examTip: Students report the mean for skewed data — mean is pulled toward outliers; for skewed distributions, the MEDIAN better represents the 'typical' value; always check the shape of the data before choosing a measure of center

topics: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A)
Independent vs. mutually exclusive events (not the same)
lessons.examTip: Students confuse mutually exclusive and independent events — mutually exclusive events CANNOT both happen (P(A and B) = 0); independent events DON'T AFFECT each other (P(A|B) = P(A)); these are different properties and a set of events can be one without being the other

lessons.lessonTitle: Counting Strategies: When to Multiply, Permute, or Combine
topics: Fundamental counting principle
Permutations nPr: order matters
Combinations nCr: order doesn't matter
lessons.examTip: Students use permutations when order doesn't matter (or vice versa) — ask: 'Does swapping two choices create a DIFFERENT outcome?' If yes, use permutation; if no, use combination; choosing a committee of 3 from 10 = combination (same people regardless of order)

lessons.lessonTitle: How Scatter Plots and Correlation Tell a Story
topics: Positive vs. negative vs. no correlation
Correlation coefficient r: strength and direction
Correlation ≠ causation
lessons.examTip: Students say a strong r-value means one variable CAUSES the other — correlation measures LINEAR ASSOCIATION, not causation; ice cream sales and drowning rates are correlated (both increase in summer) but neither causes the other; always ask about a lurking variable

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Three Distinct Colonial Regions Developed Different Societies
topics: New England: Puritan compact, town meetings, subsistence farming
Middle colonies: diversity and commerce
Southern colonies: plantation economy and indentured servitude to slavery
lessons.examTip: Students describe colonies as uniformly agricultural — the key regional distinction is ECONOMIC FOUNDATION; New England developed trade and manufacturing because rocky soil limited farming; this shapes later sectional conflict in ways that are heavily tested

lessons.lessonTitle: How Salutary Neglect Created the Conditions for Revolution
topics: Salutary neglect: British non-enforcement of trade laws pre-1763
Colonial self-governance through assemblies
Why colonists felt British interference post-1763 was tyranny
lessons.examTip: Students say colonists rebelled only over taxes — the deeper grievance was loss of SELF-GOVERNANCE; decades of running their own affairs meant colonists saw post-1763 enforcement as a violation of established rights, not just new taxation

lessons.lessonTitle: What 'No Taxation Without Representation' Really Meant
topics: Virtual vs. actual representation debate
Stamp Act, Townshend Acts, and colonial responses
Boston Massacre and Tea Party as escalation
lessons.examTip: Students say the Revolution was purely about taxes being too high — it was about the PRINCIPLE of parliamentary authority over the colonies; colonists often paid lower taxes than British citizens; the issue was legitimacy of Parliament's right to tax, not the amount

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Declaration of Independence Actually Argued (It's More Than a List of Grievances)
topics: Lockean natural rights foundation
Social contract theory and right to revolution
The rhetorical structure: philosophy → evidence → conclusion
lessons.examTip: Students treat the Declaration as primarily listing British abuses — the first two paragraphs establish the PHILOSOPHICAL JUSTIFICATION; the grievances come after to PROVE the contract was broken; Jefferson's logical structure is what essay questions target

lessons.lessonTitle: Why the Articles of Confederation Failed on Purpose
topics: Intentional weakness: fear of centralized power
Successes: Land Ordinance of 1785, Northwest Ordinance of 1787
Shays' Rebellion as catalyst for Constitution
lessons.examTip: Students say the Articles were just poorly designed — they were DELIBERATELY WEAK because the founders feared a powerful central government like Britain's; recognizing this intent explains why the Constitution required a political revolution in thinking, not just a technical fix

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Constitution's Framework Actually Created (and What It Left Unresolved)
topics: Federalism: concurrent and enumerated powers
Bill of Rights as Anti-Federalist compromise
What the Constitution deliberately left ambiguous
lessons.examTip: Students treat ratification as the end of debate — the Constitution's AMBIGUITIES (necessary and proper clause, commerce clause) became the source of ongoing conflict; the founders' failure to resolve slavery is the most consequential omission

lessons.lessonTitle: How Political Parties Emerged Despite the Founders' Wishes
topics: Federalists vs. Democratic-Republicans: Hamilton vs. Jefferson
Elastic clause vs. strict construction debate
Washington's Farewell Address warning about factions
lessons.examTip: Students say Hamilton and Jefferson disagreed only on economic policy — their disagreement was PHILOSOPHICAL; Hamilton believed in active government as a force for prosperity; Jefferson feared concentrated power as a threat to liberty; this tension defines US political history

lessons.lessonTitle: How Manifest Destiny Was Used to Justify Expansion (and at Whose Expense)
topics: Ideological basis: providential destiny and Anglo-Saxon superiority
Mexican-American War and territorial acquisition
Impact on Native American nations: Trail of Tears, Indian Removal Act
lessons.examTip: Students treat westward expansion as unambiguously positive — Honors-level analysis requires examining WHOSE COSTS paid for whose gains; Manifest Destiny was simultaneously nation-building and ethnic cleansing; both must appear in any analytical response

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Compromise Over Slavery Failed and What That Reveals
topics: Missouri Compromise, Compromise of 1850, Kansas-Nebraska Act
How each compromise pushed the crisis forward
Bleeding Kansas and the collapse of compromise
lessons.examTip: Students memorize the compromises as a list — the analytical point is that EACH COMPROMISE delayed rather than resolved the fundamental contradiction; each successive compromise required greater concessions from the North, making future agreement less likely, not more

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Civil War Decided — and What It Left Open
topics: Union victory: preserved union, ended slavery as institution
13th Amendment's scope and limits
Competing visions of Reconstruction as indicator of unresolved questions
lessons.examTip: Students say the Civil War 'ended' the slavery issue — the war ended slavery as a LEGAL INSTITUTION but left unanswered questions about the status, rights, and economic position of formerly enslaved people; Reconstruction debates show how much remained contested

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Reconstruction Was Both a Revolutionary Moment and a Failed Promise
topics: Radical Reconstruction: 14th and 15th Amendments, Freedmen's Bureau
Black political participation in the South 1867–1877
Compromise of 1877 and withdrawal of federal troops
lessons.examTip: Students say Reconstruction simply 'failed' — it had SIGNIFICANT achievements (Black officeholders, schools built, constitutional amendments passed); the failure was in DEFENDING those gains; the question is not whether it worked but why federal commitment collapsed

lessons.lessonTitle: How Industrialization Concentrated Power and Created Opposition
topics: Robber barons vs. captains of industry framing
Vertical and horizontal integration (Carnegie, Rockefeller)
Labor movement: Knights of Labor, AFL, Pullman Strike
lessons.examTip: Students describe Gilded Age business leaders as purely villainous or purely heroic — both framings are too simple; the analytical task is explaining HOW their business practices SIMULTANEOUSLY created national prosperity and concentrated power in ways that undermined democracy

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Progressive Movement Actually Reformed (and Who It Excluded)
topics: Muckrakers and investigative journalism as political force
Trust-busting, food safety, conservation under TR
Limits of Progressivism: race, women's suffrage, immigration
lessons.examTip: Students present Progressivism as broadly reformist — a critical analysis notes that most Progressive reforms were SEGREGATED or explicitly EXCLUDED Black Americans; many Progressives shared eugenic beliefs; 'progress' was defined by and for middle-class white Americans

lessons.lessonTitle: How WWI and Its Aftermath Changed American Foreign Policy
topics: Wilson's Fourteen Points and failed idealism
Senate rejection of League of Nations
Return to isolationism in the 1920s
lessons.examTip: Students say the US rejected the League because of isolationism — Senate rejection was driven by SPECIFIC reservations about Article X (requiring US military response to League decisions); many senators supported international engagement but opposed surrendering war power to an international body

lessons.lessonTitle: What Caused the Great Depression and Why the New Deal Was Controversial
topics: Causes: bank failures, Smoot-Hawley, credit collapse, speculation
New Deal: relief, recovery, reform — 3 Rs
Conservative critique: government overreach and debt
lessons.examTip: Students say Hoover 'did nothing' during the Depression — Hoover actually tried interventions (Reconstruction Finance Corporation, tariffs) but believed they were insufficient to act further; the more accurate critique is that his interventions were INADEQUATE and ideologically constrained

lessons.lessonTitle: How WWII Transformed the United States Domestically
topics: War production ending the Depression
Japanese American internment as civil liberties failure
Double V campaign: democracy abroad, democracy at home
lessons.examTip: Students describe the home front as uniformly patriotic — Honors analysis requires examining CONTRADICTIONS: the US fought fascist racism abroad while maintaining Jim Crow at home; the Double V campaign shows Black Americans' awareness of this hypocrisy; it sets up the civil rights movement

lessons.lessonTitle: How Cold War Logic Shaped Every Domestic and Foreign Decision
topics: Containment doctrine and Truman Doctrine
McCarthyism as domestic Cold War
Korea, Cuba, and Vietnam as containment in practice
lessons.examTip: Students treat Cold War foreign policy decisions as responses to specific events — Cold War decisions were driven by the DOCTRINE OF CONTAINMENT which shaped interpretation of every event; policymakers saw Vietnam, Korea, and Cuba through the lens of domino theory, not just their local context

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Civil Rights Movement Achieved and How It Did It
topics: Direct action strategy: boycotts, sit-ins, freedom rides
Legislative achievements: Civil Rights Act 1964, VRA 1965
Internal debates: SNCC, CORE, SCLC, Black Power
lessons.examTip: Students present the civil rights movement as monolithic — the movement had SIGNIFICANT internal disagreements about tactics, goals, and leadership; the tension between nonviolent gradualism (SCLC/MLK) and direct confrontation (SNCC) and Black Power (later) reflects genuine strategic debates

lessons.lessonTitle: How the 1970s Crisis Reshaped American Politics
topics: Vietnam's legacy: credibility gap and War Powers Act
Watergate: executive power and its limits
Economic stagflation and end of postwar consensus
lessons.examTip: Students treat Nixon's resignation as a story about personal corruption — Watergate is analytically important as a story about PRESIDENTIAL POWER and institutional checks; the constitutional crisis was about whether a president is above the law, not just Nixon's character

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Reagan Revolution Actually Changed
topics: Supply-side economics: tax cuts, deregulation, cutting social programs
Cold War escalation vs. détente
Cultural conservatism and the New Right coalition
lessons.examTip: Students evaluate Reagan purely as partisan liberals or conservatives do — the analytical task is explaining HOW Reaganism SHIFTED the ideological center of American politics; even Democrats moved rightward in the 1990s, showing the lasting structural impact of the Reagan coalition

lessons.lessonTitle: How Globalization and Technology Rewired American Society After the Cold War
topics: NAFTA, WTO, and deindustrialization
Internet economy and wealth concentration
9/11 and the transformation of national security state
lessons.examTip: Students treat 9/11 as a purely foreign policy story — 9/11 transformed DOMESTIC governance (Patriot Act, DHS, surveillance state); the tension between security and civil liberties that defines modern America begins here; connect to long-term debates about government power

lessons.lessonTitle: What Scientists Actually Do (It's Not a Checklist)
topics: Observation vs. inference
Scientific question vs. testable hypothesis
Why science is iterative, not linear
lessons.examTip: Students write hypotheses as questions — a hypothesis must be a TESTABLE STATEMENT in 'if...then...' form; 'Does sunlight affect plant growth?' is a question, not a hypothesis; 'If a plant receives more sunlight, then it will grow taller' is a testable prediction

lessons.lessonTitle: The Difference Between a Good Experiment and a Guess
topics: Independent variable (what you change), dependent variable (what you measure)
Control group and controlled variables
Why you can only change ONE variable at a time
lessons.examTip: Students confuse the control group with the controlled variables — the CONTROL GROUP is the untreated baseline for comparison; CONTROLLED VARIABLES are factors kept constant throughout; both are required for a valid experiment

topics: Accuracy vs. precision
Significant figures basics
Metric system: kilo-, centi-, milli-, conversions
lessons.examTip: Students use 'accurate' and 'precise' as synonyms — a dartboard analogy clarifies it: precise = clustered together (reproducible); accurate = close to the bullseye (correct); you can be precise and wrong, or accurate but inconsistent

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Read Data and Tell If It Supports Your Hypothesis
topics: Tables vs. graphs: when to use which
Interpreting line graphs: trends and outliers
Correlation: patterns in data without claiming cause
lessons.examTip: Students say data 'proves' a hypothesis — science never proves; data SUPPORTS or REFUTES a hypothesis; the correct language is 'the data is consistent with' or 'the data does not support'; one experiment never gives final proof

lessons.lessonTitle: What Matter Is Made Of and How We Know
topics: Atoms, elements, compounds, mixtures
Physical vs. chemical properties
States of matter and particle motion
lessons.examTip: Students confuse compounds and mixtures — in a COMPOUND, elements are chemically bonded in fixed ratios (water is always H₂O); in a MIXTURE, substances are physically combined and can be separated without a chemical reaction

lessons.lessonTitle: What a Chemical Reaction Is (and Isn't)
topics: Signs of a chemical reaction: gas, precipitate, color change, heat
Conservation of mass
Physical change vs. chemical change
lessons.examTip: Students say ice melting is a chemical change because 'it looks different' — a physical change alters form but NOT chemical identity; melting, dissolving, and cutting are physical; burning, rusting, and digesting are chemical; the substance identity either changes or it doesn't

lessons.lessonTitle: How Forces Change Motion (Newton's Laws in Plain Language)
topics: Force, mass, and acceleration: F = ma concept
Balanced vs. unbalanced forces
Friction and gravity as everyday forces
lessons.examTip: Students say an object moving at constant speed has no forces on it — constant speed means forces are BALANCED (net force = 0), not absent; a car cruising requires engine force to balance friction; zero net force ≠ no forces

lessons.lessonTitle: What Energy Is and Why It Can't Disappear
topics: Kinetic vs. potential energy
Law of conservation of energy
Energy transformations in everyday systems
lessons.examTip: Students say energy is 'lost' in a system — energy is TRANSFORMED, not destroyed; a roller coaster converts PE to KE to heat (friction); 'lost' energy became thermal energy; asking where the energy WENT is the correct scientific framing

topics: Seven characteristics of life: MRS GREN
Cell as basic unit of life
Unicellular vs. multicellular organisms
lessons.examTip: Students say fire and cars are alive because they grow and use energy — life requires ALL characteristics (reproduction, response to environment, homeostasis, cells); fire lacks cells and cannot reproduce; applying all criteria simultaneously is essential

lessons.lessonTitle: How Cells Get Energy: The Short Version
topics: Photosynthesis: light + CO₂ + water → glucose + oxygen
Cellular respiration: glucose + oxygen → CO₂ + water + energy
Why both processes are essential to life on Earth
lessons.examTip: Students say only plants do photosynthesis and only animals do respiration — ALL living cells perform cellular respiration; plants do BOTH photosynthesis AND respiration; in darkness, a plant only respires and actually releases CO₂

lessons.lessonTitle: How Traits Are Passed From Parents to Offspring
topics: DNA as hereditary molecule
Dominant and recessive alleles
Simple Punnett square predictions
lessons.examTip: Students say a dominant trait is more common in a population — dominant means it's expressed when present, NOT that it's more frequent; a dominant disease allele can be rare; frequency in a population has nothing to do with dominance

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Living Things Are Classified Into Groups
topics: Taxonomy: domain, kingdom, phylum...species
Binomial nomenclature (genus species)
Why shared characteristics drive classification
lessons.examTip: Students write binomial nomenclature with both words capitalized — only the GENUS is capitalized; the species epithet is lowercase: Homo sapiens, not Homo Sapiens; when handwritten, both words are underlined; when typed, both are italicized

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Rock Cycle Tells Us About Earth's History
topics: Three rock types: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic
How each type forms and transforms
Reading rock layers (strata) as a timeline
lessons.examTip: Students say rocks always follow the cycle in one direction — the rock cycle has NO fixed order; igneous rock can become metamorphic directly under heat/pressure without becoming sedimentary first; arrows go multiple directions

lessons.lessonTitle: How Plate Tectonics Explains Earthquakes, Volcanoes, and Mountains
topics: Convergent, divergent, and transform boundaries
Evidence for plate tectonics: seafloor spreading, fossil distribution
Why plate boundaries are where action happens
lessons.examTip: Students say earthquakes only occur at plate boundaries — MOST earthquakes occur at boundaries, but intraplate earthquakes exist; the New Madrid Seismic Zone in the US interior is a tested example; 'most' and 'only' are different claims

lessons.lessonTitle: What Weather vs. Climate Actually Means
topics: Weather = short-term atmospheric conditions; climate = long-term patterns
Factors affecting climate: latitude, altitude, ocean currents
Why 'it's cold today' doesn't disprove climate change
lessons.examTip: Students use weather events as evidence for or against climate change — weather is day-to-day; climate is 30+ year patterns; a cold snap is a weather event; climate change refers to shifts in the GLOBAL AVERAGE over decades, not individual days

lessons.lessonTitle: The Building Blocks: Points, Lines, and Planes Have Rules
topics: Undefined terms: point, line, plane
Postulates vs. theorems
Segment and angle notation
lessons.examTip: Students treat a postulate and a theorem as the same thing — a POSTULATE is assumed true without proof (a starting rule); a THEOREM is proved using postulates and other theorems; the difference matters when writing proofs

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Write a Two-Column Proof Without Getting Stuck
topics: Statement-reason format
Properties of equality and congruence
Common reasons: given, definition, postulate, theorem
lessons.examTip: Students write 'because it looks equal' or 'obvious' as reasons — every reason must be a named DEFINITION, POSTULATE, or THEOREM; acceptable reasons are formal mathematical names; informal observations earn no credit in a proof

lessons.lessonTitle: What Congruence Actually Means (Not Just 'Same Size')
topics: Congruent segments and angles: exact same measure
Congruence vs. equality (≅ vs. =)
Midpoint and angle bisector definitions
lessons.examTip: Students write AB = CD when they mean AB ≅ CD — segments and angles are CONGRUENT (≅); their MEASURES are equal (=); 'AB = CD' means the lengths are equal numbers; '∠A = ∠B' should be '∠A ≅ ∠B' unless referring to degree measures

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Triangles Always Add Up to 180° (and How to Use That)
topics: Triangle angle sum theorem
Exterior angle theorem
Finding missing angles in multi-triangle figures
lessons.examTip: Students apply the 180° rule to quadrilaterals — the interior angle sum is 180° only for TRIANGLES; for any polygon, sum = (n−2) × 180°; a quadrilateral sums to 360°, not 180°

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Prove Two Triangles Are Congruent (All Five Shortcuts)
topics: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL congruence shortcuts
Why SSA and AAA do NOT guarantee congruence
CPCTC as a reason after proving congruence
lessons.examTip: Students use SSA (Side-Side-Angle) as a congruence shortcut — SSA is NOT valid and can produce two different triangles (the ambiguous case); HL (Hypotenuse-Leg) is valid ONLY for right triangles; SSA for non-right triangles does not prove congruence

lessons.lessonTitle: What's Special About Isosceles and Equilateral Triangles
topics: Isosceles triangle theorem: base angles are equal
Converse: equal angles means equal sides
Equilateral = equiangular = 60° each
lessons.examTip: Students identify the 'base' of an isosceles triangle as the bottom side regardless of orientation — the BASE is the NON-EQUAL side (between the two equal sides); the figure can be rotated; always identify which two sides are equal first

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Pythagorean Theorem Works and When to Use It
topics: a² + b² = c² where c is the hypotenuse
Pythagorean triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17
Converse: if a²+b²=c², then it's a right triangle
lessons.examTip: Students assign c to any side — c is ALWAYS the hypotenuse (the longest side, opposite the right angle); assigning c to a leg and solving gives a wrong answer every time; identify the right angle first, then c is the side opposite it

lessons.lessonTitle: Special Right Triangles: The Two Shortcuts Worth Memorizing
topics: 45-45-90: legs = x, hypotenuse = x√2
30-60-90: short leg = x, long leg = x√3, hypotenuse = 2x
Recognizing when to apply each
lessons.examTip: Students multiply the SHORT leg by 2 to get the hypotenuse in a 30-60-90 — this is correct ONLY when the SHORT LEG is x; if given the hypotenuse or long leg, divide first to find x, then multiply; starting from the wrong side cascades into wrong answers

lessons.lessonTitle: The Hierarchy of Quadrilaterals (Every Square Is a Rectangle — Not Vice Versa)
topics: Quadrilateral → parallelogram → rectangle/rhombus → square
Properties of each type
Trapezoid and isosceles trapezoid
lessons.examTip: Students say 'a rectangle is a square' — a square IS a rectangle (all squares have 4 right angles) but a rectangle is NOT necessarily a square (it doesn't need equal sides); the hierarchy flows one way; Venn diagram thinking prevents this error

lessons.lessonTitle: What Parallelogram Properties Let You Solve Problems
topics: Opposite sides equal and parallel; opposite angles equal
Consecutive angles supplementary
Diagonals bisect each other
lessons.examTip: Students say diagonals of a parallelogram are equal — diagonals bisect each other in ALL parallelograms, but they are only EQUAL in a rectangle; only PERPENDICULAR in a rhombus; only BOTH in a square; don't over-apply properties

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Find Interior and Exterior Angles of Any Polygon
topics: Interior angle sum = (n−2) × 180°
Each interior angle of regular polygon = (n−2)×180°/n
Each exterior angle of regular polygon = 360°/n
lessons.examTip: Students confuse interior and exterior angle formulas — for a REGULAR polygon: each EXTERIOR angle = 360°/n (always); each INTERIOR angle = 180° − exterior angle; students frequently apply the 360°/n formula to find interior angles, getting the wrong answer

lessons.lessonTitle: All the Parts of a Circle and What They're Called
topics: Radius, diameter, chord, secant, tangent
Central angle, inscribed angle, arc
Arc measure vs. arc length
lessons.examTip: Students confuse arc MEASURE (in degrees) and arc LENGTH (in linear units) — arc measure equals the central angle in degrees; arc length = (arc measure/360) × 2πr; these require different formulas and are frequently mixed up

lessons.lessonTitle: The Inscribed Angle Theorem: Half the Central Angle
topics: Inscribed angle = half the intercepted arc
Inscribed angle in a semicircle = 90°
Two inscribed angles intercepting the same arc are equal
lessons.examTip: Students set inscribed angle equal to the arc instead of half the arc — the inscribed angle is HALF the intercepted arc; the central angle EQUALS the intercepted arc; confusing which is which produces exactly the wrong answer

lessons.lessonTitle: How Tangent Lines and the Radius Are Always Related
topics: Tangent perpendicular to radius at point of tangency
Two tangents from external point are equal length
Tangent-chord angle = half intercepted arc
lessons.examTip: Students forget the 90° angle at the point of tangency — when a tangent meets a radius, they form a RIGHT ANGLE; this creates right triangles in problems where none seem obvious; most tangent-line problems are secretly Pythagorean theorem problems

lessons.lessonTitle: How Distance and Midpoint Formulas Come From Pythagorean Theorem
topics: Distance formula: d = √[(x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²]
Midpoint formula: M = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2)
Applying to prove geometric properties
lessons.examTip: Students average the x-coordinates but subtract the y-coordinates in midpoint (or vice versa) — midpoint takes the AVERAGE of BOTH x AND y; both coordinates use the same averaging operation; students sometimes apply the distance formula operation to midpoint

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Prove a Shape Is What You Say It Is Using Coordinates
topics: Proving parallelogram: equal and parallel opposite sides
Proving rectangle: perpendicular adjacent sides (slopes are negative reciprocals)
Using distance and slope together
lessons.examTip: Students prove a rectangle by showing all four sides equal — equal sides proves a RHOMBUS, not a rectangle; to prove rectangle, show right angles using PERPENDICULAR SLOPES (negative reciprocal slopes); these two proofs are completely different

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Equation of a Circle Means Geometrically
topics: Standard form: (x−h)² + (y−k)² = r²
Identifying center (h,k) and radius from equation
Completing the square to convert general form
lessons.examTip: Students read center from (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r² as (−h, −k) — the center is (h, k) with the OPPOSITE signs of what appears in the equation; (x−3)²+(y+2)²=25 has center (3, −2), not (−3, 2); the sign flip is the same trap as vertex form of a parabola

lessons.lessonTitle: How Surface Area and Volume Are Different Problems
topics: Surface area: sum of all face areas
Volume: space inside the figure
Units: SA in square units, V in cubic units
lessons.examTip: Students use volume formula when asked for surface area (and vice versa) — SURFACE AREA measures the OUTSIDE wrapping (square units); VOLUME measures what it holds (cubic units); re-read the question to identify which is asked before selecting a formula

lessons.lessonTitle: The Formula Patterns for Prisms, Cylinders, Pyramids, and Cones
topics: Prism/cylinder: V = Bh (base area × height)
Pyramid/cone: V = ⅓Bh
Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³, SA = 4πr²
lessons.examTip: Students forget the ⅓ in pyramid and cone volume — pyramids and cones hold EXACTLY one-third the volume of the corresponding prism or cylinder with the same base and height; physically, three conical fills equal one cylinder; forgetting this gives volume 3× too large

lessons.lessonTitle: How Scale Factor Changes Size, Area, and Volume
topics: Linear scale factor k: lengths multiply by k
Area scale factor: k²
Volume scale factor: k³
lessons.examTip: Students apply the linear scale factor to area and volume — if a figure is scaled by k, LENGTHS multiply by k, AREAS by k², VOLUMES by k³; doubling all dimensions of a box makes it 8× the volume (2³), not 2× or 4×; students consistently under-apply the exponent

lessons.lessonTitle: What a Variable Actually Means (And Why x Isn't Scary)
topics: Variable as a placeholder for an unknown number
Evaluating expressions by substitution
Difference between an expression and an equation
lessons.examTip: Students add variables and numbers: 3x + 4 = 7x — you CANNOT combine 3x and 4 because they are unlike terms (different kinds); 3x + 4 is already fully simplified; only LIKE TERMS (same variable, same exponent) can be combined

lessons.lessonTitle: The Order of Operations Is Not Optional
topics: PEMDAS: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiply/Divide, Add/Subtract
Left-to-right for equal priority operations
Common mistakes with subtraction and division
lessons.examTip: Students do addition before subtraction because 'A comes before S' in PEMDAS — addition and subtraction have EQUAL priority; work LEFT TO RIGHT; 10 − 3 + 2 = 9 (not 5); the same applies to multiplication and division

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Combine Like Terms Without Losing Anything
topics: Identifying like terms: same variable, same exponent
The distributive property: a(b+c) = ab+ac
Simplifying expressions step by step
lessons.examTip: Students distribute only to the first term in parentheses: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 4 — the 3 must multiply EVERY term inside: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12; forgetting to distribute to the constant is the most common distributive property error

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Solve an Equation by Undoing What Was Done to x
topics: Inverse operations to isolate the variable
Two-step and multi-step equations
Checking solutions by substituting back
lessons.examTip: Students perform operations in PEMDAS order when solving — solving equations reverses PEMDAS; undo addition/subtraction FIRST (outermost operations), then multiplication/division (innermost); doing it in PEMDAS order locks the variable inside instead of isolating it

lessons.lessonTitle: What Happens When You Solve an Equation With Variables on Both Sides
topics: Moving all variable terms to one side
Combining like terms across the equals sign
Equations with no solution or infinitely many solutions
lessons.examTip: Students get 0 = 0 or 5 = 3 and say there's no solution in both cases — 0 = 0 (always true) means INFINITELY MANY solutions (all values work); 5 = 3 (always false) means NO solution; these are opposite conclusions from similar-looking steps

lessons.lessonTitle: The One Rule That Makes Inequalities Different from Equations
topics: Solving inequalities like equations — except one rule
Flip the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative
Graphing solutions on a number line: open vs. closed circle
lessons.examTip: Students flip the inequality sign every time they touch a negative number — only flip when MULTIPLYING or DIVIDING both sides by a negative; subtracting a negative (adding) does NOT flip the sign; the sign flip rule is specifically about the operation, not the presence of negatives

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Write and Solve Equations From Word Problems
topics: Defining the variable before writing an equation
Translating verbal phrases to algebraic expressions
Checking that your answer makes sense in context
lessons.examTip: Students define x as 'the problem' rather than a specific quantity — define x precisely: 'let x = the number of apples Sarah bought'; vague definitions lead to equations that solve for the wrong thing; the definition determines what your answer means

lessons.lessonTitle: What Makes a Relationship a Function (The Rule Every Graph Must Follow)
topics: Function: each input has exactly one output
Vertical line test on graphs
Function notation: f(x) means output when input is x
lessons.examTip: Students say x = 3 is a function because 'it's just a line' — a VERTICAL line fails the vertical line test and is NOT a function; every x must map to exactly one y; x = 3 maps one x-value to infinitely many y-values, violating the definition

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Graph a Line from an Equation Without Making a Table
topics: Slope-intercept form: y = mx + b
Plotting y-intercept, then using slope to find next point
Horizontal and vertical lines: y = k and x = h
lessons.examTip: Students plot the slope as a single point instead of a ratio — slope is RISE OVER RUN, meaning 'go up rise units, then right run units'; a slope of 3/4 means up 3 RIGHT 4 from any point; treating slope as just another coordinate to plot gives a random point, not the next point on the line

lessons.lessonTitle: How Domain and Range Describe What a Function Can Do
topics: Domain: all valid inputs (x-values)
Range: all resulting outputs (y-values)
Restrictions: no division by zero, no square root of negative
lessons.examTip: Students give range as all real numbers for y = x² — the RANGE of y = x² is y ≥ 0 because squaring any real number gives a non-negative result; the graph only exists at and above the x-axis; always consider what output values are actually achievable

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Add, Subtract, and Multiply Polynomials
topics: Combining like terms (same variable, same degree)
Distributing a monomial: multiply each term
FOIL for binomial multiplication
lessons.examTip: Students add exponents when adding like terms: x² + x² = x⁴ — adding like terms ADDS the coefficients, not the exponents: x² + x² = 2x²; MULTIPLYING terms adds exponents: x² · x² = x⁴; addition and multiplication are completely different operations

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Factor Out the GCF (The First Thing You Always Try)
topics: Finding the greatest common factor of all terms
Factoring GCF from a polynomial
Why factoring is the reverse of distributing
lessons.examTip: Students factor out a number that doesn't divide all terms evenly — the GCF must divide INTO every single term; to find it, list the factors of each coefficient and each variable, then pick the highest common value; after factoring, check by distributing back

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Factor a Trinomial x² + bx + c
topics: Finding two numbers that multiply to c and add to b
Writing as (x + p)(x + q)
Signs: when both positive, both negative, or mixed
lessons.examTip: Students guess factors without checking the signs systematically — for x² − 5x + 6: multiply to +6 and add to −5 means BOTH numbers must be negative (−2 × −3 = +6, −2 + −3 = −5); drawing a small table of factor pairs and their sums is faster than guessing

lessons.lessonTitle: What a Parabola's Vertex and Axis of Symmetry Tell You
topics: Vertex: minimum or maximum point
Axis of symmetry: x = −b/2a
Opening direction from sign of a
lessons.examTip: Students find the axis of symmetry as −b/a instead of −b/2a — the axis of symmetry formula is x = −b/(2a), where 2a is in the denominator; forgetting the 2 gives an axis that's off by a factor of 2; write the full formula before substituting

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Solve a Quadratic Equation Three Different Ways
topics: Factoring: set each factor = 0 (Zero Product Property)
Square root method: when no bx term
Quadratic formula: always works
lessons.examTip: Students apply the quadratic formula to every problem before trying to factor — factoring is faster and less error-prone when the quadratic factors nicely; use the discriminant (b²−4ac) first: if it's a perfect square, factor; if not, use the formula

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Discriminant Predicts Before You Solve
topics: b² − 4ac > 0: two real solutions
b² − 4ac = 0: one real solution
b² − 4ac < 0: no real solutions
lessons.examTip: Students compute the discriminant as b² − 4c (omitting a) — the discriminant is b² − 4AC, where ALL THREE of a, b, and c must be identified from ax² + bx + c = 0; omitting a (or using the unset equation) gives wrong discrimination results

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Find What the Author Is Really Saying
topics: Main idea vs. topic
Explicit vs. implicit meaning
Distinguishing major details from minor ones
lessons.examTip: Students confuse the topic with the main idea — the TOPIC is what it's about ('dogs'); the MAIN IDEA is what the author says about it ('Dogs make better companions than cats because...'); the main idea must be a STATEMENT, not just a label

lessons.lessonTitle: How Authors Use Evidence to Support Their Points
topics: Facts vs. opinions
How supporting details connect to the main idea
Evaluating whether evidence is relevant and sufficient
lessons.examTip: Students accept any statement as a fact if it sounds authoritative — a FACT is verifiable and can be proven true or false; an OPINION is a belief or judgment ('this is the best policy'); statements using 'should,' 'best,' 'worst,' or 'I believe' signal opinions

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Infer What the Author Didn't Say Directly
topics: Inference: using evidence + background knowledge
What 'reading between the lines' actually means
Avoiding inferences that go beyond the text
lessons.examTip: Students make inferences that the text doesn't support — a valid inference must be SUPPORTED BY TEXTUAL EVIDENCE; it's not a guess about anything beyond what the text implies; if no evidence points to your inference, it's speculation, not inference

lessons.lessonTitle: How Vocabulary Context Clues Help You Figure Out Unknown Words
topics: Definition context clues: the word is explained nearby
Contrast clues: antonym signals
Example clues: lists and illustrations
lessons.examTip: Students look up words in their head without checking context — the CONTEXT meaning may differ from the dictionary definition; a word like 'draft' or 'charge' has multiple meanings; always use the surrounding sentences to determine which meaning fits

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Write a Thesis That Actually Takes a Position
topics: Thesis = one arguable claim, not a topic announcement
Where the thesis goes: end of introduction
The difference between a topic sentence and a thesis
lessons.examTip: Students write 'In this essay I will discuss...' as a thesis — this announces a topic, not an argument; a thesis must make a CLAIM that can be agreed with or disagreed with; 'Social media harms teenagers because it disrupts sleep and amplifies anxiety' is a thesis

lessons.lessonTitle: What a Strong Body Paragraph Must Include
topics: Topic sentence that supports the thesis
Evidence: quote, example, or data
Commentary explaining what the evidence proves
lessons.examTip: Students end paragraphs after a quote — a quote needs COMMENTARY explaining what it means and how it proves the topic sentence; 'This quote shows...' followed by real explanation; ending with evidence alone leaves the reader to make the connection for you

lessons.lessonTitle: Common Grammar Mistakes That Change Your Meaning
topics: Run-on sentences and comma splices
Sentence fragments: missing subject or verb
Subject-verb agreement with tricky subjects
lessons.examTip: Students fix comma splices by adding a comma before 'however' — 'however' is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction; joining two independent clauses requires either a SEMICOLON before 'however' or a period; 'I tried, however I failed' is still a comma splice

lessons.lessonTitle: How Transitions Connect Ideas (Not Just Fill Space)
topics: Transitions showing addition, contrast, cause-effect, example
Using transitions to signal logical relationships
Overused transitions to replace
lessons.examTip: Students start every paragraph with 'Also' or 'Additionally' — these only show ADDITION; use transitions that reflect the actual logical relationship: contrast (however, although), cause-effect (therefore, as a result), emphasis (indeed, above all); 'also' for every paragraph suggests no logical structure

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Identify What a Story Is Really About (Theme vs. Plot)
topics: Plot = what happens; theme = what it means
