Universal themes across different stories
How multiple elements contribute to theme
lessons.examTip: Students write theme as one word ('friendship') — theme is a SENTENCE that makes a claim: 'True friendship requires accepting someone's flaws, not just their strengths'; the one-word version is a topic, not a theme; always push from the topic word to a full thematic statement

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Analyze a Character as More Than Just Their Traits
topics: How characters are revealed through actions, speech, thoughts
Dynamic vs. static characters
How characters change in response to conflict
lessons.examTip: Students list personality traits rather than analyzing them — describing a character as 'brave' earns no credit; analyzing HOW the author shows bravery through specific actions, what the bravery COSTS the character, and what it REVEALS about the theme is the actual analytical task

lessons.lessonTitle: How Figurative Language Creates Meaning Beyond Literal Words
topics: Simile and metaphor: comparison and what it reveals
Personification: giving human qualities to nonhuman things
Symbolism: objects that represent larger ideas
lessons.examTip: Students identify the device but stop there — 'The author uses a metaphor' earns minimal credit; the analysis must explain WHAT IS BEING COMPARED and WHAT THE COMPARISON REVEALS about the character, mood, or theme; identification is just step one

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Build an Argument That Actually Persuades Someone
topics: Claim supported by reasons and evidence
Acknowledging the other side
Why a counterargument makes your argument stronger
lessons.examTip: Students skip the counterargument because they think it weakens their position — addressing the opposing view and REFUTING it shows the reader you've thought carefully; ignoring it makes readers think you haven't considered it; concession + refutation builds credibility

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Use Sources Without Letting Them Take Over
topics: Introducing sources with signal phrases
Quoting vs. paraphrasing
Explaining what the source proves
lessons.examTip: Students drop in a quote and move on — every source needs: (1) introduction (who said it and why they're credible), (2) the quote or paraphrase, (3) explanation of what it proves for YOUR argument; skipping the explanation makes the source do all the work for you

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Tell If a Source Is Trustworthy
topics: Author credentials and purpose
Publication date and relevance
Bias: perspective vs. misinformation
lessons.examTip: Students accept any website as a source — evaluate AUTHOR expertise (does this person know the subject?), PURPOSE (is it trying to inform or sell/persuade?), and DATE (is it current enough for your topic?); a .org or .edu domain is not an automatic guarantee of accuracy

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Colonists Came to America (And Who Was Already There)
topics: Push-pull factors for European colonization
Native American cultures and early contact
Three main colonial regions and their differences
lessons.examTip: Students describe colonization as if America were empty — Native American nations were DISPLACED by colonization, not simply absent; the impact on indigenous peoples (disease, land loss, warfare) must be part of any account of colonial settlement

lessons.lessonTitle: Why the Colonists Decided to Break Away From Britain
topics: Taxation without representation: Stamp Act, Townshend Acts
Growing self-governance through colonial assemblies
Boston Massacre and Tea Party as turning points
lessons.examTip: Students say the Revolution was only about taxes — the deeper issue was SELF-GOVERNANCE; colonists had run their own assemblies for decades and saw Parliament's new assertiveness as an attack on rights they already had; taxes were the symptom, not the root cause

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Constitution Set Up and Why It Was Designed That Way
topics: Three branches and separation of powers
Checks and balances: each branch limiting the others
Federalism: national vs. state power
lessons.examTip: Students describe checks and balances as 'three equal branches' — the branches are equal in STATUS but not in every POWER; Congress overrides vetoes (2/3), the president nominates judges, Congress confirms them; each branch has specific powers OVER specific other branches

lessons.lessonTitle: How the North and South Became Two Different Economies
topics: Northern industrialization and wage labor
Southern plantation economy and slavery
How economic differences created political conflict
lessons.examTip: Students describe slavery as 'just a Southern issue' — slavery was economically connected to the ENTIRE country; Northern textile mills depended on Southern cotton; banks in New York financed plantations; slavery's reach was national, not regional, which made abolition politically explosive

lessons.lessonTitle: What Manifest Destiny Was and Who It Hurt
topics: Idea that westward expansion was America's destiny
Mexican-American War and territorial expansion
Displacement of Native Americans: Indian Removal Act, Trail of Tears
lessons.examTip: Students describe westward expansion only through the pioneers' perspective — a complete answer includes the COST paid by Native American nations and Mexicans; Manifest Destiny required taking land from people already living there; both perspectives must appear in analysis

lessons.lessonTitle: Why the Civil War Was Ultimately About Slavery
topics: States' rights debate centered on slavery specifically
Confederate Constitution explicitly protected slavery
Emancipation Proclamation's strategic purpose
lessons.examTip: Students say the Civil War was 'really about states' rights, not slavery' — the SPECIFIC right being claimed was the right to keep slavery; Confederate documents explicitly name slavery as the cause of secession; 'states' rights' is not a neutral term in this context

lessons.lessonTitle: How Big Business Changed American Life After the Civil War
topics: Railroads connecting national markets
Carnegie (steel) and Rockefeller (oil): vertical and horizontal integration
Why monopolies worried Americans
lessons.examTip: Students describe big business as purely negative — industrialization created jobs, lowered consumer prices, and connected the nation; the problem was CONCENTRATION OF POWER without accountability; both the benefits and the dangers are required for a complete answer

lessons.lessonTitle: What Immigrants and Workers Did to Shape American Society
topics: New immigration waves from Southern and Eastern Europe
Working conditions: hours, pay, child labor
Labor unions: strikes, collective bargaining, Pullman Strike
lessons.examTip: Students say unions immediately improved conditions — unions faced violent opposition (Homestead Strike, Pullman Strike) and won gains slowly over decades; the government often sided with business owners; early labor movement history is a story of struggle and setback, not quick victory

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Progressive Movement Tried to Fix the Problems of Industry
topics: Muckrakers exposing corruption and unsafe conditions
Theodore Roosevelt's trust-busting and conservation
Limits: Progressivism often excluded Black Americans
lessons.examTip: Students present Progressivism as solving all industrial problems — many Progressive reforms were LIMITED to white Americans; segregation intensified during the Progressive Era (Wilson re-segregated federal buildings); 'progressive' didn't mean equal rights for all

lessons.lessonTitle: How WWI and WWII Made America a World Power
topics: US entry into WWI: Zimmermann Telegram, unrestricted submarine warfare
WWII: from isolation to global war after Pearl Harbor
How wartime production ended the Great Depression
lessons.examTip: Students say the US was always willing to enter both wars — the US maintained ISOLATIONISM until specific events forced entry (Zimmermann Telegram for WWI, Pearl Harbor for WWII); Congress and the public strongly opposed involvement before these events; entry was not inevitable

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Cold War Was (It Wasn't Just About Nuclear Weapons)
topics: Containment: stopping Soviet expansion
Korean War and Vietnam as containment in practice
Space race and arms race as competition beyond military
lessons.examTip: Students say the Cold War was a military conflict between the US and USSR — it was a POLITICAL, ECONOMIC, and IDEOLOGICAL competition that rarely involved direct combat; 'hot' wars in Korea and Vietnam were proxy conflicts; the two superpowers never directly fought each other

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Civil Rights Movement Changed America
topics: Direct action: sit-ins, boycotts, freedom rides
Key legislation: Civil Rights Act 1964, Voting Rights Act 1965
Why legal equality and economic equality are different challenges
lessons.examTip: Students say the Civil Rights Act 'solved' racism — the legislation ended LEGAL discrimination but did not eliminate economic inequality or social racism; the movement's ongoing challenges (poverty, housing discrimination, police violence) show that legal rights and lived equality are different goals

lessons.lessonTitle: Everything Around You Is Matter — Here's How to Describe It
topics: Physical vs. chemical properties
Pure substance vs. mixture
Homogeneous vs. heterogeneous mixtures
lessons.examTip: Students classify solutions as pure substances because they look uniform — a solution is a HOMOGENEOUS MIXTURE, not a pure substance; saltwater looks uniform but can be separated by evaporation; pure substances (elements and compounds) cannot be physically separated

lessons.lessonTitle: How Scientists Measure Things in Chemistry
topics: SI units: mass (g), volume (mL or L), temperature (K)
Significant figures: what they mean and how to count them
Density: D = m/V and its uses
lessons.examTip: Students count ALL digits as significant — zeros are TRICKY: leading zeros are NOT significant (0.0045 has 2 sig figs); trailing zeros after a decimal ARE significant (2.50 has 3 sig figs); trailing zeros without a decimal are ambiguous; use scientific notation to be clear

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Convert Units Without Getting Confused
topics: Dimensional analysis (factor-label method)
Setting up conversion factors
Multi-step conversions
lessons.examTip: Students multiply by conversion factors without canceling units — in dimensional analysis, write units in EVERY step and cancel them like fractions; if you can't cancel the unit you want to eliminate, the conversion factor is upside down; units that remain are your answer's units

lessons.lessonTitle: What an Atom Is Made Of and Where Those Parts Are
topics: Protons and neutrons in the nucleus; electrons in orbitals
Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons
Ions: gaining or losing electrons changes charge, not identity
lessons.examTip: Students say an ion is a different ELEMENT — gaining or losing electrons changes the CHARGE, not the number of protons; an atom's IDENTITY is determined by proton count (atomic number); Na⁺ is still sodium; only changing protons creates a different element

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Periodic Table Organizes Every Element
topics: Periods (rows) and groups (columns)
Metals, nonmetals, metalloids location
Periodic trends: atomic radius, ionization energy, electronegativity
lessons.examTip: Students say ionization energy and atomic radius increase in the same direction — they move in OPPOSITE TRENDS across a period; as you go right, atomic radius DECREASES (more protons pull electrons closer); ionization energy INCREASES (harder to remove electrons held tighter)

lessons.lessonTitle: How Electrons Are Arranged and Why It Matters
topics: Electron configuration: filling order by energy level
Valence electrons determine reactivity
Why noble gases are unreactive
lessons.examTip: Students say all elements want to have 8 electrons — the octet rule applies to most main group elements, but EXCEPTIONS exist; hydrogen follows the duet rule (2 electrons); some elements like phosphorus and sulfur can expand beyond 8; hydrogen and helium are the key exceptions

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Read and Write Chemical Equations
topics: Reactants → products format
Conservation of mass: atoms balanced on both sides
State symbols: (s), (l), (g), (aq)
lessons.examTip: Students change subscripts to balance equations — NEVER change subscripts to balance; H₂O₂ ≠ H₂O; subscripts define the substance; only change COEFFICIENTS in front of formulas; changing a subscript creates an entirely different chemical

lessons.lessonTitle: The Five Types of Chemical Reactions and How to Recognize Them
topics: Synthesis (A+B→AB), decomposition (AB→A+B)
Single replacement, double replacement, combustion
Predicting products from reaction type
lessons.examTip: Students confuse single and double replacement — SINGLE: one element displaces another in a compound (A + BC → AC + B); DOUBLE: the cations of two compounds switch partners (AB + CD → AD + CB); identifying whether one or two elements are switching determines the type

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Use Moles to Predict How Much Product You Make
topics: Mole concept: 1 mol = 6.02×10²³ particles
Molar mass from periodic table
Mole ratio from balanced equation
lessons.examTip: Students convert grams directly to grams of product — stoichiometry requires going THROUGH MOLES: grams A → moles A → moles B → grams B; skipping the mole conversion and just using a mass ratio gives wrong answers except by coincidence

lessons.lessonTitle: What 'Dissolving' Actually Means at the Particle Level
topics: Solute and solvent roles
'Like dissolves like': polarity matching
Concentration: molarity = moles/liter
lessons.examTip: Students say 'water dissolves everything' — water only dissolves POLAR and IONIC substances ('like dissolves like'); oil doesn't dissolve in water because oil is nonpolar; this principle predicts what will dissolve before any experiment is run

lessons.lessonTitle: What Acids and Bases Actually Are
topics: Acids: donate H⁺; bases: accept H⁺ (Brønsted-Lowry)
pH scale: 0–14, neutral at 7
Strong vs. weak acids: complete vs. partial dissociation
lessons.examTip: Students say a low pH means 'a little acidic' — pH 2 is EXTREMELY acidic; each pH unit represents a 10× change in H⁺ concentration; pH 2 has 100× more H⁺ than pH 4; students confuse the magnitude of the number with the intensity of acidity

lessons.lessonTitle: What Happens When an Acid and a Base Are Mixed
topics: Neutralization: acid + base → salt + water
Net ionic equations
Titration: using a known concentration to find an unknown
lessons.examTip: Students say neutralization means the products are neutral — a neutralization REACTION produces a salt and water, but the resulting solution is not necessarily pH 7; strong acid + weak base → acidic salt; weak acid + strong base → basic salt; the product's pH depends on which reactant is stronger

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Every Living Thing Is Made of Cells
topics: Cell theory: all life made of cells
Prokaryotic vs. eukaryotic cells
Why cell size has limits
lessons.examTip: Students say plant cells have all the same organelles as animal cells — plants have CELL WALLS, CHLOROPLASTS, and a LARGE CENTRAL VACUOLE that animal cells lack; animal cells have CENTRIOLES that plant cells lack; the differences are directly tied to each cell's unique functions

lessons.lessonTitle: What Each Organelle Does and Why It Matters
topics: Nucleus, mitochondria, ribosome functions
Endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi: protein production line
Chloroplasts and cell wall in plant cells
lessons.examTip: Students say the nucleus makes proteins — the NUCLEUS contains the DNA instructions; RIBOSOMES make proteins using those instructions; the rough ER processes proteins, the Golgi modifies and ships them; this is a multi-step assembly line, not a single organelle job

lessons.lessonTitle: How Materials Get In and Out of Cells
topics: Diffusion and osmosis: passive transport
Active transport: energy required
Osmosis effects: crenation and lysis in different solutions
lessons.examTip: Students say a cell placed in salt water will swell — a cell in HIGH SALT (hypertonic) solution loses water by osmosis and SHRINKS (crenation in animal cells, plasmolysis in plant cells); a cell in PURE WATER (hypotonic) gains water and swells; water moves toward MORE solute

lessons.lessonTitle: How Traits Are Inherited From Parents
topics: Dominant and recessive alleles
Genotype vs. phenotype
Homozygous vs. heterozygous
lessons.examTip: Students say a dominant trait is 'stronger' or 'better' — dominant simply means it's expressed when present; it has NO relationship to being beneficial or common; a harmful dominant allele (like Huntington's disease) is expressed even with one copy

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Predict Offspring Using a Punnett Square
topics: Setting up monohybrid crosses
Reading probability from Punnett squares
Phenotype ratios vs. genotype ratios
lessons.examTip: Students report Punnett square results as exact numbers instead of probabilities — a 3:1 phenotype ratio means a 75% chance of the dominant phenotype per offspring, not that exactly 3 out of 4 offspring will show it; probability applies to EACH individual offspring, not a guaranteed count

lessons.lessonTitle: How DNA Carries the Instructions for Making You
topics: DNA structure: double helix, base pairing (A-T, G-C)
Gene: section of DNA coding for a protein
DNA replication: copying before cell division
lessons.examTip: Students say A pairs with G and T pairs with C — base pairing is A-T and G-C (in DNA); A pairs with T, not G; G pairs with C, not A; this rule is called complementary base pairing and determines both DNA replication and transcription accuracy

lessons.lessonTitle: What Natural Selection Actually Is (Evolution Explained Simply)
topics: Variation exists in populations
Traits that improve survival are inherited more
Natural selection acts on individuals; evolution happens to populations
lessons.examTip: Students say 'organisms evolve to survive' — organisms don't CHOOSE to evolve; individuals with EXISTING helpful traits survive and reproduce more; the population's allele frequencies shift over generations; no intentionality is involved; 'organisms develop traits they need' is Lamarckism, which is incorrect

topics: Fossil record showing change over time
Homologous structures in related species
DNA similarity as molecular evidence
lessons.examTip: Students say 'evolution is just a theory' as if theory means a guess — in science, a THEORY is an explanation supported by extensive evidence and testing; scientific theories explain HOW things happen (evolution, gravity, germ theory); a hypothesis is the guess; a theory is the tested explanation

lessons.lessonTitle: How Scientists Organize and Name All Living Things
topics: Classification hierarchy: domain to species
Binomial nomenclature rules
Phylogenetic trees and common ancestry
lessons.examTip: Students say species that look similar must be closely related — convergent evolution produces similar-looking organisms with NO close relationship (dolphins and fish look similar but are not closely related); classification must be based on EVOLUTIONARY HISTORY (genetics), not appearance

lessons.lessonTitle: How Energy Moves Through an Ecosystem
topics: Producers, consumers, decomposers roles
Food chains and food webs
10% energy transfer rule between trophic levels
lessons.examTip: Students say 50% of energy passes between trophic levels — only about 10% of energy transfers to the next level; 90% is LOST as heat through cellular respiration; this is why food chains are short and why there are more producers than top predators in any ecosystem

lessons.lessonTitle: How Populations Grow and What Controls Their Size
topics: Biotic and abiotic factors
Carrying capacity and population limits
Predator-prey relationships
lessons.examTip: Students say populations grow until 'there's no more room' — populations are limited by RESOURCES (food, water, space), PREDATION, and DISEASE, not just physical space; a meadow might have room for more rabbits but not enough food; food is usually the limiting resource before space

topics: Habitat destruction as leading cause of species loss
Pollution and its effects on food chains
Climate change and ecosystem shifts
lessons.examTip: Students list many causes of extinction as equally important — HABITAT DESTRUCTION is the SINGLE LARGEST cause of species extinction globally; pollution, invasive species, and climate change are significant but secondary; when asked to rank causes, habitat loss is the answer

lessons.lessonTitle: What Speed, Velocity, and Acceleration Are (They're Not the Same)
topics: Speed (scalar) vs. velocity (vector: speed + direction)
Acceleration: change in velocity, not just speeding up
Calculating average speed and velocity
lessons.examTip: Students say an object isn't accelerating if it's moving at constant speed in a curve — CHANGING DIRECTION is a change in velocity (direction changed), so it IS accelerating; a car going around a circular track at constant speed is constantly accelerating toward the center

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Read Distance-Time and Speed-Time Graphs
topics: Slope of distance-time graph = speed
Slope of speed-time graph = acceleration
Area under speed-time graph = distance
lessons.examTip: Students read a horizontal line on a speed-time graph as 'stopped' — a HORIZONTAL LINE on a speed-time graph means CONSTANT SPEED (not zero speed); the object is only stopped if the line is on the x-axis (speed = 0); a flat line at v = 5 m/s means moving steadily at 5 m/s

lessons.lessonTitle: How Gravity Pulls Everything Down the Same Way
topics: Free fall: all objects accelerate at g = 9.8 m/s²
Why mass doesn't affect fall time (ignoring air resistance)
Terminal velocity from air resistance
lessons.examTip: Students say heavier objects fall faster — in a VACUUM, all objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass (Galileo's experiment); air resistance makes a feather fall slower than a hammer in atmosphere; on the moon (no air), both hit the ground simultaneously

lessons.lessonTitle: What Work and Power Mean in Physics (Not in Life)
topics: Work = force × distance in direction of force
Zero work: perpendicular force or no movement
Power = work / time
lessons.examTip: Students say holding a heavy box is 'hard work' in physics — physics work requires DISPLACEMENT in the direction of force; holding a box with no movement does ZERO WORK no matter how tiring it is; work requires both force AND movement in the force's direction

lessons.lessonTitle: How Kinetic and Potential Energy Trade Off in Moving Objects
topics: KE = ½mv², PE = mgh
Conservation of mechanical energy (no friction)
Energy transformations on a roller coaster or pendulum
lessons.examTip: Students say a roller coaster has the most speed at the highest point — speed is maximum at the LOWEST point where KE is maximum (all PE converted to KE); at the highest point, PE is maximum and KE is minimum; height and speed are inversely related in a frictionless system

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Energy Is Never Actually Lost (It Just Changes Form)
topics: Law of conservation of energy
Thermal energy as the destination of 'lost' energy
Efficiency: useful energy output vs. total input
lessons.examTip: Students say friction 'destroys' energy — friction CONVERTS mechanical energy to THERMAL energy; total energy is conserved; the energy isn't gone, it's just in a less useful form; efficiency measures how much of the input energy becomes useful output

lessons.lessonTitle: What Waves Actually Are and How They Move
topics: Transverse vs. longitudinal waves
Wave speed, frequency, wavelength: v = fλ
Amplitude and energy: more amplitude = more energy
lessons.examTip: Students say faster waves have higher frequency — wave speed, frequency, and wavelength are related by v = fλ; if SPEED increases and frequency stays the same, WAVELENGTH increases; only frequency changes if you change the source, not the medium; medium changes speed and wavelength together

lessons.lessonTitle: How Light Behaves When It Hits Different Materials
topics: Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection
Refraction: light bends when changing medium
Total internal reflection and critical angle
lessons.examTip: Students say light bends TOWARD normal when going from fast to slow medium — light bends TOWARD the normal when entering a denser medium (slowing down); it bends AWAY when entering a less dense medium (speeding up); this is why a straw appears bent in water

lessons.lessonTitle: Why White Light Contains All Colors
topics: Electromagnetic spectrum: radio to gamma
Visible light: ROY G BIV and frequency order
Dispersion: prism separating white light
lessons.examTip: Students say red light has the highest frequency — RED has the LOWEST frequency and LONGEST wavelength in visible light; VIOLET has the highest frequency and shortest wavelength; energy increases with frequency: gamma rays have more energy than radio waves

lessons.lessonTitle: What Electric Charge Is and How It Creates Force
topics: Positive and negative charges; like charges repel
Static electricity and charge transfer
Insulators vs. conductors
lessons.examTip: Students say only electrons move when charging objects — in solids, only ELECTRONS (negative charges) move; protons are fixed in the nucleus; when a rod becomes positively charged, it LOST electrons, not GAINED protons; charging is always about electron transfer in solids

lessons.lessonTitle: How Voltage, Current, and Resistance Work Together (Ohm's Law)
topics: Voltage (V) = electric pressure; current (I) = flow rate
Resistance (R): opposition to current
Ohm's Law: V = IR
lessons.examTip: Students say higher voltage always means higher current — current depends on BOTH voltage and resistance: I = V/R; doubling voltage while also doubling resistance keeps current the SAME; you must consider both before predicting what happens to current

lessons.lessonTitle: What Happens to Current and Voltage in Series vs. Parallel Circuits
topics: Series: same current everywhere, voltage divides
Parallel: same voltage across branches, current divides
Why parallel is used in home wiring
lessons.examTip: Students say voltage divides in parallel circuits — in PARALLEL, each branch has the SAME voltage as the source; voltage DIVIDES in SERIES; this is why household circuits are parallel: every device gets the full voltage regardless of how many devices are on
